If it is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. It is the same for sign-language (*aṅgulipratyaya*) up to and including gestures (*nimitta*).
With the exception of the two [sexual] organs, regarding the act of matchmaking (*dūtīkarma*) at other locations, it has been stated that it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

For female deities, down to animals capable of transformation, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), if one speaks clearly regarding matchmaking, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it is not clear, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
*Dūṣaṇa* (offense of corruption). The same applies to finger-signs and so forth. If the animal is unable to transform its form, acting as a matchmaker for it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Acting as a matchmaker for a male is a *duṣkṛta*. If one acts as a matchmaker while perceiving another as a matchmaker, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one acts as a matchmaker while doubting whether it is a matchmaker, or if one acts as a matchmaker while perceiving it as not a matchmaker, or if one does not act as a matchmaker while perceiving it as a matchmaker, or if one does not act as a matchmaker while doubting whether it is a matchmaker—it is a *sthūlātyaya*. [The same applies to] a human female.
If one perceives a human female as a human female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one suspects she is a human female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If she is a human female but one perceives her as a non-human female, or if she is a non-human female but one perceives her as a human female, or if one suspects she is a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If a bhikṣu takes a letter and goes to deliver it without reading it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he performs other services for a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The rest is as before.

For the three classes of persons, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if a man and a woman have already had sexual relations and subsequently separated, and one brings a letter to reconcile them;
if, on account of a parent’s illness or imprisonment, one brings a letter while visiting them in prison;
if, for the sake of a faithful lay follower (*upāsaka*) who is ill or imprisoned, one brings a letter while visiting them in prison; or if it is for the sake of the Three Jewels.
And for a sick bhikṣu, one may take a letter and carry it to him.

If a bhikṣu seeks to build a dwelling for himself where there is no patron and he acts for his own sake, he must build it according to the prescribed measure. Regarding this, the measure is as follows:
It shall be twelve spans long according to the Buddha’s span, and seven spans wide inside. A monk shall lead another monk to point out the site;
that monk shall point out the site as a place free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a monk seeks to build a hut for himself where there are difficulties or obstructions, for which no owner exists and which is for his own use, yet he does not lead another monk to point out the site, and if it exceeds [the prescribed dimensions]...
Regarding the measure of the builder: it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense (six).
The Buddha permitted monks to build private dwellings. In the country of Aṭṭhakanāgara, there was a monk who built a large private dwelling for himself.

He possessed great power and constantly went about seeking [offerings]. The lay devotees feared and avoided him. There was a bhikṣu who wished to build a dwelling and was about to cut down a tree himself.
The tree deity thought, "If I strike this bhikṣu, I fear it would violate the principles of propriety. She went to inform the World-Honored One, who praised and comforted her.
At that time, Kāśyapa was begging for alms in the city of Kalandaka. The lay devotees avoided him from afar. Kāśyapa questioned them and learned of the situation.
The reason for this was that he informed the Buddha and the precept was established.
"To seek for oneself" means to beg and solicit from various places. "A house" refers to a dwelling. "Without an owner" means there is no person there.
Whether there be one, two, or many [beings], for one's own sake—that is, seeking for oneself and acting for oneself—one must deal with difficult places.
Such difficult places include tigers, wolves, and other malevolent beasts, down to even ants;
if a bhikṣu is not troubled by these insects and beasts while leveling the ground, and if there are stones, tree stumps, or thorns, he should have them excavated by others. If...
If there are ditches, pits, ponds, or reservoirs, one should have them filled. If one fears that water will flood the area, one should establish embankments in advance.
If the land is claimed by others, one should settle the matter together so that no disputes arise. Regarding "obstructed places":

these are locations where grass carts cannot pass, turn around, or travel back and forth. A bhikṣu, having inspected the site and confirmed it is free from such obstacles and difficulties, approaches the Saṃgha and [informs them]...
Baring the right shoulder and kneeling, he makes this formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am personally begging for materials to build a house for my own use, as there is no patron. I now request the Saṃgha to designate a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions.
This is repeated a second and a third time. At that time, the Saṃgha should examine whether the bhikṣu is trustworthy. If he is trustworthy, then...
It may be permitted. If [the person] is not trustworthy, the Saṃgha should go to inspect; or they should dispatch someone from within the Saṃgha who is trustworthy to go and inspect.
If there is an obstacle and an impediment, or if there is no obstacle but there is an impediment, or if there is an obstacle but no impediment, one should not grant permission.
If there is neither obstacle nor impediment, one should grant permission. From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed and should act as follows:
[The proclaimer] says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has requested materials himself to build a hut for his own use, as there is no donor.
He now requests from the Saṃgha the assignment of a site that is free from difficulties and obstacles. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
The Saṃgha shall assign to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, a site free from difficulties and obstacles. Thus is the announcement. Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, seeking to build a dwelling for himself where there is no owner and which is for his own use, requests from the Saṃgha a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions.
The Saṃgha now grants to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha assigning to the bhikṣu so-and-so a site that is free from difficulties and obstacles, let them remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak. The Sangha has approved; the assignment of a site free from difficulties and obstacles to the bhikṣu so-and-so is completed.
Because the Sangha has approved by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus. He who builds the hut should know that this is the initial placement.
Regarding timber, stone, earth, brick, or a lump of mud, up until the final stage of plastering:

if it has not been formally assigned by the Saṃgha, and it is excessive in size, or located in a place that is difficult or obstructive, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* (or *sthūlātyaya*) offenses.

Among these, for failing to have it assigned, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; for being excessive in size, one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; for being in a difficult place, one *duṣkṛta*; and for being in an obstructive place, one *duṣkṛta*.
Dukkata. The sequence of phrases may be understood accordingly. If it is constructed but not completed, there are two thullaccayas and two dukkatas.
If one causes another to construct it, the same applies whether it is completed or not. If one constructs a house for another and it is completed, there are two thullaccayas and two dukkatas;
if it is not completed, there are four dukkatas. If the Saṅgha has not authorized [the construction], and it is not authorized...

If one perceives it as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, yet suspects it is not a formal assignment (*an-adhiṣṭhita*), or perceives it as a formal assignment when it is not, or suspects it is a formal assignment when it is not, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

The same applies to exceeding the prescribed dimensions. If there is a danger and one perceives it as such, or suspects it, or perceives it as no danger when there is danger, or perceives it as danger when there is none, or suspects it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This also applies to obstructing the site.
It is also thus: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

There is no offense if one builds according to the prescribed measure, or less than the measure, or if it is a construction authorized by the Saṃgha, or if it is free from obstacles and difficulties, or if it is laid out according to the Dharma, or if it is built for the sake of the Saṃgha, or for a Buddhist temple, a lecture hall, a grass hut, a leaf hut, or a small shelter sufficient for the body.
In a place where many people reside, if a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, he should take other bhikṣus with him to inspect it and designate the site.
Those bhikṣus should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions. If a bhikṣu...
If one builds a large dwelling with a patron for oneself in a place that is difficult or obstructed,
and does not take other bhikṣus to inspect and designate the site, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense (the seventh).
King Udayana was on intimate terms with the Venerable Channa and permitted him to construct a large dwelling near the city of Kauśāmbī.
There was a Nyagrodha deity-tree there where many travelers used to rest; Channa cut it down, which led householders to criticize and resent him.
Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.

The "large" [construction] involves the extensive use of wealth and materials. Regarding those with an owner: whether it be one person, two people, or many people, "for oneself" means constructing for one's own person.
"Difficult places" and "obstructed places" are as explained above. A bhikṣu goes to the midst of the Saṃgha to request its formal authorization (*adhikaraṇa*).
The assembly of monks performs the authorization; the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is as explained above. If the Saṃgha does not appoint someone to direct the work, there are difficulties and...

Regarding the obstruction of a site: one case constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; two cases constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses. If one acts but does not complete it: one case constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense; two cases constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
It is the same when instructing another to act. All other matters and those involving no offense are as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, being overcome by anger, slanders another bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense,
desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct, and if at a later time— whether he is questioned or not—
he knows that this matter was groundlessly stated and says, "I spoke thus because of my anger," if a bhikṣu speaks such words, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa (8). The Venerable Ṭhapassamitaputta was distributing bedding and assigning invitations to monks in order of seniority.
A bhikkhu named Mettiya arrived and, having been assigned an inferior room and bedding according to that sequence, became angry. The next day, when it was time to assign invitations, the donor...
Upon hearing this, Maitrībala spread out a worn-out sitting mat outside the gate and prepared coarse food.

Maitrībala’s anger redoubled, and he then hired his sister, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī, to falsely accuse the Venerable One of having committed an offense against her. The Buddha questioned them thoroughly and learned the truth of the matter.
He rebuked them and established the precept.

There are three roots: namely, seeing, hearing, and suspecting. As for the root of seeing: it is when one actually sees someone committing an act contrary to the pure life (*brahmacarya*), or sees them stealing five *kārsāpaṇa* coins or more than five, or sees them taking the life of a human being; or if another person has seen it, one hears of it from that person—this is called the root of seeing.

The root of hearing (*śruta-mūla*) consists of hearing that one has violated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), heard that one has stolen five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five, heard that one has taken a human life, heard that one has praised oneself, or heard that one has attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). If one says, "I heard this from such-and-such a person," this is called the root of hearing.

There are two roots of doubt (*vicikitsā-mūla*): those arising from what has been seen and those arising from what has been heard. Regarding those arising from what has been seen: if one sees [the accused] entering a forest with a woman.

Emerging from the forest, one is naked and without clothing, with the body defiled by impurities and holding a blood-stained blade, accompanied by evil associates—this is called doubt arising from what is seen.
That which arises from hearing is as follows: if, in a dark place, one hears the sound of a bed, or grass mats being shifted as a body turns over.
The sound of bodily movement; the sound of conversing together; the sound of sexual intercourse; the sound of "I have violated the holy life";

the sound of saying "I have stolen five coins or more than five coins"; the sound of saying "I have killed a person"; the sound of saying "I have attained the state of a superior person"—these are called "hearing with doubt.
Having excluded these three bases, to further defame another by means of other methods is called "without basis. If that person is not pure...
Having seen, heard, or suspected that another has committed a *pārājika* offense, one says: "I have seen, heard, or suspected that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.

Thus, with groundless charges, one slanders him with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If that person is actually not pure, and one had produced the perception of having seen, heard, or suspected a *pārājika* offense when in fact there was no such seeing, hearing, or suspecting, but later forgets that perception and says: "I saw, heard... [or "I suspected..."].
Suspecting that he has committed a *pārājika* offense, one slanders him with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, yet one has neither seen, heard, nor suspected that he committed a *pārājika*, and after having such a suspicion, one then says:
"I have no doubt regarding this; I have seen, heard, or suspected that he committed a *pārājika," and thus slanders him with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*—in this matter...
He was without doubt, yet he spoke as if there were doubt; he slandered [another] with a groundless charge of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

In this matter, he was without doubt, yet later, having forgotten his lack of doubt, he slandered [another] with a groundless charge of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In this case, the phrases regarding "not seeing, hearing, or doubting" are interwoven with those regarding "seeing, hearing, or doubting.
The text is too voluminous to record here in full. If a bhikṣu slanders another bhikṣu with four groundless matters...
The Buddha said: "If it is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if it is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

It is the same for using a finger-seal, sending a messenger, or making signs of recognition. Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, if one further slanders another with other non-monastic qualities, saying:

'You have committed an extreme offense (*antimavatthu*); you have violated a nun; you received the precepts with a thieving mind; you have broken the inner and outer [vows],' [it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*]."
The Path. [Regarding] eunuchs, those with both sexual organs, those who kill their father, kill their mother, kill an Arhat, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or shed the blood of a Buddha:
if one speaks [of these acts] clearly to a non-human or an animal, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if not clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses signs such as pointing with a finger, writing, or making gestures to cause [a monk] to be known [as having committed an offense], it is likewise.
Having excluded these non-monk-like methods, if one further slanders a monk with other groundless charges (*amūlaka-dharma*), he incurs the same offense as previously specified.
If one slanders a bhikṣuṇī by means of the eight groundless *pārājika* dharmas, if the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a finger-seal, a written document, or causes another to act as a witness, it is likewise.

Apart from these eight *pārājika* offenses, if one slanders another with other groundless charges that are not *bhikṣuṇī*-dharma, if the meaning is clear, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a finger-seal, a written document, or causes another to act as a witness, it is likewise. This excludes cases that are not *bhikṣuṇī*-dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the case where one slanders with groundless charges (*amūlaka-dharma*): for a nun, it is according to her previous offense.
Excluding monks and nuns, if one slanders others with groundless charges of an offense, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for a monk and a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) for a nun.
For the other three groups of persons, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one speaks based on what was seen, heard, or suspected; if one speaks in jest;
if one speaks hurriedly; if one speaks alone; if one speaks in a dream; or if one speaks erroneously.

If a bhikṣu, out of malice, takes a portion from a matter belonging to a different category and, regarding a bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense, slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy his pure conduct;
and at a later time, whether questioned or not, it is known that he took a portion from a matter belonging to a different category, and that bhikṣu says of himself: "I did this out of malice."
Having spoken these words—those who speak such words commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense (the ninth).
Maitrāyanī, descending from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, saw a large ram engaging in sexual intercourse with a ewe.
She then compared the ram to the Venerable One and the ewe to herself, the Bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī, and immediately said to the bhikṣus: "My relative..."
Having seen it with his own eyes, the bhikṣu examined the facts and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.

Regarding "a different matter": if a bhikṣu has not committed a *pārājika* offense, yet claims to have seen him commit a *pārājika*, and thus defames another with groundless charges of a different matter—a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*—or if a bhikṣu has not committed a *pārājika* offense, yet claims he has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one slanders another with a *pārājika* offense that belongs to a different category and lacks a basis, claiming it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
or if a bhikṣu has not committed a *pārājika*, yet [the accuser] sees him as having committed a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *sthūlātyaya*, or a *duṣkṛta*.
If one slanders [a monk] with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category, claiming he has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a monk has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and one says he has committed a *pārājika*—slandering him with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category—claiming he has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a monk has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and another claims he has committed a *pāyattika*, or even down to a groundless charge of a different category. This is called "evil speech" (*durvacana*). Slandering with a groundless charge of a different category.

Regarding the *pārājika* offense of slandering [a monk] with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: it is impure; it is similar to an impure person; the names, surnames, and physical characteristics are identical;
and one slanders this person by means of these very matters. That person is slandered by means of a different category, namely, a groundless *pārājika* offense.
One who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense is like one who is pure; one who is pure is like one who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
one who is pure is like one who is pure—it is also thus. If one sees them as they were originally when living at home...
At that time, having committed an act of sexual misconduct, theft of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, or the taking of human life, one speaks to others, saying:

"I have seen this bhikṣu commit sexual misconduct and so forth," thereby slandering him with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category, namely a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one hears [such a report], it is likewise [an offense].
Thus it is: if a bhikṣu defames another with a groundless *pārājika* offense based on a different matter, and his speech is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The same applies to using a signet ring, a letter, or a messenger to convey such an indication.
Excluding the four grave offenses (*pārājika*), if one slanders [another] with other distinct matters that are groundless and not the dharma of a bhikṣu, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

This applies even down to using a finger-seal, a letter, or a messenger to convey such signs; it is the same for all these cases. Excluding the aforementioned matters, if one further uses other distinct matters...
If one slanders a bhikṣu with groundless charges, it is treated according to the offense previously mentioned; the same applies to other persons and so forth, as explained before.
If a bhikṣu seeks to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, employing the means to adopt the methods for causing a schism, and persists in holding to them without relinquishing them.
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not accept the principles that lead to a schism and persist in them without relinquishing them. Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha; [be] with the Saṃgha."
Living in harmony and joy without dispute, studying under the same teacher like water and milk blending together, they shall increase within the Buddha’s Dharma and abide in peace and well-being.
When that bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists in his refusal to relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should [admonish him] up to three times.

Because he was admonished to abandon this matter, if he abandoned it after being admonished up to three times, it was well; if he did not abandon it, it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).
Since Devadatta desired to harm the Buddha and further instructed Ajātaśatru to kill his father, his evil reputation spread, and [he received] gain.

Their sustenance was cut off, and they were thus joined by five others. They went from house to house begging for alms; however, the Buddha had established a rule that one must not eat in a separate group.
Devadatta then conceived this thought: "Gautama has cut off the people's food; I should rather break his rule."
The Saṃgha-cakra. He then instructed the bhikṣus with five dharmas for as long as they lived:

begging for food, wearing rag-robes, sitting in the open air, abstaining from consuming ghee or salt, and abstaining from eating fish or meat. Causing them to have faith and delight in these, he used skillful means to break up that Saṃgha.
The monks reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to admonish him and then established this precept.
"In harmony" means performing the same *karmavācanā* and reciting the same *prātimokṣa*. "Saṃgha" refers to four or more bhikṣus.

Regarding the enumeration: there are eighteen matters concerning what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, what is an offense and what is not an offense, what is light and what is heavy, what is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension) and what is not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, what is grave and what is not grave, what is customary practice and what is not customary practice, what is prescribed and what is not prescribed, and what is spoken and what is not spoken.
It is said: One who abides by the dharma of causing a schism in the Saṃgha abides by these eighteen matters.

If a bhikṣu, through skillful means, desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the dharma of causing a schism, and stubbornly maintains it without relinquishing it, that bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu.
"Venerable sir, do not employ means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha. Do not accept the methods for breaking the Saṃgha. Firmly hold [your view] and do not abandon it.
Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha; be joyful and without dispute, like water and milk blended as one, within the Buddha-dharma."

Within this there is the increase of well-being and a peaceful dwelling. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter; do not cause the Saṃgha to issue a formal reprimand and thereby commit a grave offense.
If you accept this advice, it is well; if you do not accept this advice, [the Saṃgha] shall further cause the bhikṣus to [address you].

If nuns, male lay followers (upāsakas), or female lay followers (upāsikās), or kings, great ministers, non-Buddhist śramaṇas, or brahmins seek [the Dharma], or if bhikṣus from other regions hear of this and know that such persons will place their trust in his words, they should come; provided that they will indeed place their trust in his words.
"Very well. If you do not comply with these words, you should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, you should further request:
'Venerable sirs, I have already made the announcement; the remaining *karmavācanā* is yet to come. You should now relinquish this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform the *karma*.'"
If one commits a grave offense again, it is well if they heed the instruction; if they do not heed the instruction, one should perform the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed it, one should further request of the Venerable Ones: "I have completed the proclamation and the first *karmavācanā*; there remain two more *karmavācanās*."
[He] said: "It is possible that you may abandon this matter so as not to cause the Saṃgha to perform the *karmavācanā* again and thereby incur a grave offense.
If you accept these words, it is well; if you do not accept these words, then a second *karmavācanā* should be performed. Once it is finished, [you] should further request the Venerable One: 'I..."

The first *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* has been completed; one *karman* remains. You should relinquish this matter so as not to cause the Saṃgha to perform another *karman* and thereby incur a grave offense.
If you can relinquish it, that is well; if you do not relinquish it, I shall proclaim it to you.

If one abandons [the offense] after the third *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one abandons it after the second *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) has been completed, it is three *sthūlātyaya*s.

If one abandons it after the first *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-ekadhā-karman*) has been completed, it is two *sthūlātyaya*s. If one abandons it after the *jñapti* has been completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya*.
[The Buddha] prohibited it. If one abandons [the intent] before the initial announcement (*jñapti*) is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, while nothing has yet been announced, one employs means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha and accepts the methods for breaking the Saṃgha without abandoning them, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies even if the Saṃgha acts to break the Saṃgha.
When performing the *karmavācanā*, if a monk instructs [another] saying, "Do not abandon the *sthūlātyaya*," and does not rebuke or admonish him, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
It is the same if a *bhikṣuṇī* instructs [another] not to abandon it. This applies except for monks and *bhikṣuṇīs*; if there are other persons besides these, it is likewise.
If one does not relinquish [the offense] after being instructed, it is a *dukkaṭa*; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if one relinquishes it immediately upon the first admonition; or if the admonition was made by an illegal separate assembly (*adharma-vibhakta-gaṇa*); or if it was made by an illegal united assembly (*adharma-samagra*).

The formal act of admonition performed by a united assembly; the formal act of a separate assembly; a formal act resembling that of a separate assembly; a formal act resembling that of a united assembly;

that which is not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not taught by the Buddha; if no one has yet performed the formal act of admonition; or if one causes a separation from evil friends.
Regarding evil associates: if one employs means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, one must obstruct them so that the schism does not occur.
If one employs means to cause a schism and assists in such a schism through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) by two or three people; or if one intends to perform an illegal *vinaya* formal act;

or if it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, for a stūpa, for an upādhyāya, for those who share an upādhyāya, or for those who share an ācārya—[one must intervene] for the sake of knowledge [of the Dharma].
If one deprecates consciousness, or acts as one who destroys it by asserting that it has no abiding place, there is no offense.
If a group of bhikṣus—whether one, two, three, or even countless—speaks thus to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sirs, do not admonish this bhikṣu. This bhikṣu is a speaker of the Dharma; this bhikṣu is a speaker of the Vinaya.
We delight in what this bhikṣu says; we accept what this bhikṣu says. That bhikṣu said, "Venerable sirs, do not say: 'This bhikṣu is a speaker of the Dharma; this bhikṣu is a speaker of the Vinaya.'"
"O Bhikkhus, what this bhikkhu has spoken, we delight in; what this bhikkhu has spoken, we approve of.
Nevertheless, this bhikkhu is not one who speaks according to the Dhamma, nor is he one who speaks according to the Vinaya. Venerable sirs, do not seek to cause a schism."
"A harmonious Saṃgha—this you should delight in. You who desire a harmonious Saṃgha, O Venerable One, should bring the Saṃgha into harmony;
being joyful and without dispute, let them study under the same teacher, blending like water and milk, so that within the Buddha’s Dharma there may be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
When this bhikṣu is thus admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish his position, that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times for the sake of making him relinquish that matter.
If, after up to three admonitions, he relinquishes [the course], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense (eleven).
Devadatta’s faction said to the bhikṣus, "Do not admonish Devadatta. The bhikṣus reported this.
The Buddha, having instructed the Saṃgha to admonish him, established this precept.
There are two kinds of compliance: compliance regarding the Dharma and compliance regarding robes and food. Compliance regarding the Dharma means being taught by means of the Dharma.
Those who increase their virtue, concentration, and wisdom; those who respectfully recite and receive [the teachings]; those who comply with [the rules for] clothing and food;
those who provide robes, bedding, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites; and those who form a group—whether four people or more—who assist by speaking on behalf of the group.
Whether there be one, two, three, or many, if a group of bhikṣus acts contrary to the Dharma, those bhikṣus should admonish them.
If they follow the advice, it is well; if they do not follow the advice, a formal motion (*jñapti*) and the threefold proclamation (*karmavācanā*) should be performed for them.
Whether there is an offense or no offense, all is as previously explained.

If a bhikṣu, residing in dependence upon a village or a town, defiles families and performs evil deeds—such that his defiling of families is both seen and heard, and his performance of evil deeds is both seen and heard—the other bhikṣus should address him. That bhikṣu shall say:
"Venerable sirs, I have defiled families and performed evil deeds; my defiling of families is both seen and heard, and my performance of evil deeds is both seen and heard."
[He] hears: "Venerable sir, you have defiled a family and committed evil conduct. You should now depart from this village;
you must not remain here. That bhikṣu says to that other bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, the bhikṣus possess affection, hatred, fear, and delusion.
There are bhikṣus who commit such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not. The bhikṣus...
The Buddha replied, "Venerable sir, do not speak such words. There may be affection, there may be hatred, there may be fear, and there may be delusion.
Among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not; yet these bhikṣus are free from affection, hatred, fear, and delusion.
Venerable sir, you have defiled families and committed evil deeds; that you have defiled families has been both seen and heard. [He continued: "You have committed evil deeds..."
If a bhikṣu, when being thus admonished, persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣu should be admonished a second and a third time so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense (twelfth).
There were two bhikṣus who were bound together by ties: one was named Aśvaka and the other was named Punarvasuka.
They engaged in unlawful conduct, such as planting flowering trees themselves and instructing others to plant flowering trees, even accepting wages for performing acts of merriment and the like.

There were a group of bhikṣus begging for alms; they moved with measured steps, maintaining proper decorum, with eyes cast downward as they walked straight ahead. The lay devotees, however, considered this a transgression.
When the bhikṣus became aware of this, they reported it in full to the Buddha. The Buddha dispatched Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to perform the *brahmadanda* (act of suspension) against them.
While the formal act was being performed, the two bhikṣus said, "The Saṃgha is subject to favoritism and the like. Śāriputra—
Maudgalyāyana returned and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to censure him and then established this precept.
There are four ways of defiling another's household: first, defiling a household by means of that household—taking goods from one family and giving them to another.
When he hears of the place where goods have been obtained, he is not pleased; yet when he considers the place where goods were given, he thinks of repaying that kindness.
He then says: "If they give to me, I shall give to them; if they do not give to me, why should I give? Second, there is defiling the family through gain and offerings.
If a bhikṣu obtains gain in accordance with the Dharma—even down to the remnants in his alms bowl—and gives it to one...
"Householder, [if] one householder does not give [to another], the recipient thinks: 'I must repay his kindness; since he gave to me, I shall repay him.
If he had not given to me, why should I have given? Thirdly, there is the defilement of the family through reliance on relatives and friends.
If a bhikṣu relies upon a king or a great minister, or for the sake of one householder and not for the sake of another householder, whatever [he receives] therein..."

"Those who do [me] a favor," he thinks, "are those to whom I shall repay my gratitude; those who act for my benefit are those whom I shall honor; those who do not act for my benefit are those whom I shall not honor.

Fourth, the monastic community defiles the household: if a bhikṣu takes flowers or fruit belonging to the Saṃgha and gives them to one layperson while not giving them to another, that person immediately forms this thought: "Those who give me [these things] are those whom I shall honor; those who do not..."
As for "I": I do not make offerings. One who practices evil deeds plants flowering trees oneself and instructs others to plant flowering trees;

one waters them oneself and instructs others to water them; one plucks flowers oneself and instructs others to pluck flowers; one makes flower garlands oneself and instructs others to make flower garlands;
one threads them with string oneself or ties them, and instructs others to thread them with string or tie them; one holds the flowers oneself.
He teaches others to hold flowers; he holds flower garlands himself and gives them to others; he teaches others to hold flower garlands and give them to others.
He sits and rises on the same seat as women and young girls; they share food and drink from the same vessel, converse, and joke together.

He may personally perform songs, dances, and music, or join in singing and chanting when others perform; he may engage in comic recitations, or play drums, blow pipes and horns, and sound conch shells.
He imitates the cry of a peacock, makes the sounds of various birds, or feigns lameness as he walks, or accepts invitations for amusement and laughter.

If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village settlement and defiles that family by committing evil deeds, and these acts are witnessed and heard by all, that bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, you have defiled that family by committing evil deeds; these things have been witnessed and heard by all. You should abandon them."
Regarding this matter, do not allow yourself to be rebuked by the Saṃgha, lest you further commit a grave offense. If you follow these instructions, it is well;
if you do not follow them, you should perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and three rounds of *karmavācanā*, all as previously described.

There is no offense if you relinquish [the object] upon the first instruction, or if you are dealing with one's parents, the sick, small children, pregnant women, or those imprisoned in a jail within the monastery.
Working as a laborer: if one plants flowers or trees for the sake of the Triple Gem and instructs others to gather flowers to make offerings to the Triple Gem;
or if one runs to avoid dangers; or if one leaps over ditches and channels; or if one whistles and calls out to companions while walking.

If a bhikṣu is of a wicked nature and does not accept the words of others, and when the bhikṣus admonish him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the precepts, he himself does not accept their admonition, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me, whether it be good or bad;
nor will I speak to the venerable sirs, whether it be good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me. That bhikṣu...
Kāśyapa admonished that bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not yourself refuse to accept admonition. Venerable sir, you yourself ought to accept admonition.
Venerable sir, when you admonish other bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, those bhikṣus shall likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the disciples of the Buddha attain increase; they admonish one another, they instruct one another, and they confess to one another."
[The offense is] a *pācittiya*. When that bhikṣu is thus admonished and persists in not relinquishing [his position], those bhikṣus should admonish him three times to relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it upon being admonished up to three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (thirteenth).
Cchanda was of an evil nature and would not accept the words of others. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to reprove and admonish him, and thus established this precept.
One of an evil nature who does not accept words means one who cannot endure being instructed by others.
Regarding those who teach according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, there are seven groups of offenses: pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, and prātideśanika.
*Tiśani*, *sthūlātyaya*, *duṣkṛta*. Regarding what is spoken according to the Dharma: that which is in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instruction.

If a bhikṣu is of evil character and does not accept the words of others, and while the bhikṣus instruct him according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, he himself acts in a manner that makes it impossible to converse with him, another bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu. If...

If one complies with the instruction, it is well. If one does not comply, a formal motion (*jñapti*) and three proclamations (*karmavācanā*) should be performed. Upon the completion of the third proclamation, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one relinquishes [the offense] after a motion followed by two proclamations (*jñaptidvitīyakarman*), it is three *sthūlātyaya*s. If one relinquishes it after a single proclamation (*ekakarmavācanā*), it is two *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one relinquishes it after the motion is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Prior to the motion, for one who is of evil character and refuses to accept [the instruction], it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding verbal *duṣkṛta*: when one is being exhorted and admonished, if other monks or nuns instruct them, "Do not abandon [the offense]," it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Before the exhortation has been given, such instruction constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. Furthermore, if others instruct one who is being exhorted, as long as the exhortation has not yet been completed, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:
if at the time of the first speech one abandons the illegal separate assembly; up until the point where it is not the instruction of the Buddha; before the formal admonition has been issued;
or if a person lacking wisdom offers the admonition, to whom one should say: "The conduct of your preceptor and ācārya is also like this; you may [proceed] further."

Regarding the study and recitation of the scriptures: if the matter is as described above, even if spoken in jest or through error, it constitutes the third of the two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*).
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a screened place, or a place suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks indecently...

The Dharma Discourse: There was a female lay follower established in faith who explained each of the three categories of offenses—whether a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*. A monk sitting there then declared of himself, "I have committed this offense."

Among these three categories of offenses, each should be dealt with individually—whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*—in accordance with what has been stated by a laywoman (*upāsikā*) of verified faith. One should discipline that bhikṣu according to the Dharma;
this is called an *aniyata-dharma* (1).
Kāḷodāyin was mutually infatuated with a female lay disciple (*upāsikā*) who was his relative.
When it was time for almsround, he went to her house and sat upon the same bed with her, speaking improper words. Visākhā Mātā heard the sound.
Having observed this, he reported it to the Buddha, who established the precept:
"A solitary person" refers to one bhikṣu and one woman. There are two kinds of seclusion: first, seclusion by sight, such as when there is dust, mist, or darkness, and they do not see each other;
second, seclusion by hearing, which extends to the point where, even while speaking normally, they do not hear each other's voices.

"Place. "Obstructed" means: if there is an obstruction such as a tree, a wall, a fence, a cloth, or other objects that can serve as a place for sexual intercourse—provided it is a space sufficient to engage in sexual acts.
"Speaking unrighteous words" means speaking of the dharma of lust.

"A laywoman who abides in faith" means one who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, upholds the five precepts, and is well-versed in retaining the facts so that her speech is not erroneous and is truthful.

And it is not false. If a bhikṣu himself declares the place toward which he was heading, the place he reached, and whether he was sitting, lying down, or acting, he should be dealt with according to the bhikṣu’s own words.
If he himself declares the place toward which he was heading, and so on up to lying down, but does not declare that he acted;
or if he himself declares the place toward which he was heading, and so on up to sitting, but does not declare...
Sitting or lying down; or if one speaks of the place toward which one is heading and the place reached, but does not speak of sitting or lying down;
or if one speaks of the place toward which one is heading, but does not speak of the place reached as well as sitting or lying down;
or if one says nothing at all—all these cases should be dealt with according to what was stated regarding the *upāsikā*. There is no fixed rule in this matter; therefore, it is so stated.
Indeterminate.
If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an exposed place, in a spot where sexual intercourse is impossible, and utters coarse and wicked words,
and a faithful upāsikā accuses him of one of two offenses, either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or [an offense of wrong-doing].
If it is a *pāyattika*, the monk who was sitting there shall himself declare, "I have committed this offense.
He should then be dealt with according to each of the two rules: either as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or as a *pāyattika*, exactly as stated by the faithful laywoman (*upāsikā*).
This bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma; this is called the *aniyata* (undetermined) rule (1).
The origin story (*nidāna*) is the same as before.
"An open place" means a location without walls, fences, hedges, or other obstructions. "Not a place suitable for sexual intercourse" means...

Regarding the place where one commits sexual misconduct: as for "coarse speech," it refers to speaking of the methods of sexual desire regarding the two paths [the anus and the mouth], whether they be good or bad. The rest is as previously explained.
This is the fourth of the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas.
If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been removed, he may obtain an extra robe;
he may keep it for ten days without having performed the formal act of "unclean giving" (apariśuddha-dāna). If it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (1).
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to possess three robes, but not in excess.

The group of six bhikṣus, however, possessed extra robes—either robes for early morning, robes for midday, or robes for late afternoon—and it was therefore prohibited. Ānanda obtained a single robe made of discarded rags (pāṃsukūla).
He wished to offer it to Mahākāśyapa, but Kāśyapa was away. Ānanda informed the Buddha, who asked Kāśyapa when he would return.
He replied that he would return in ten days. Thereupon, [the Buddha] permitted him to keep it for ten days.

"Having finished with robes" refers to the three robes (the *kaṭhina* robe—this is translated as the "robe of merit"—which is received at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat; during the five months [of its validity], one obtains five benefits, as detailed in the *Kaṭhina-vastu*).
Regarding "extra robes": these are those that are eight finger-breadths long or four finger-breadths wide according to the Buddha's measurement.

If a bhikṣu acquires a robe on the first day and keeps it, and acquires another robe on the second day, continuing in this manner until he acquires a robe on the tenth day and keeps it, then upon reaching the eleventh day...

When the light of dawn appears, all [items] become *niḥsargika* (requiring forfeiture). If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, up to the tenth day, and then obtains a robe on the eleventh day when the light of dawn appears, then all robes obtained during the nine intervening days become *niḥsargika*.
(In this case, although he obtained robes for nine days, he did not obtain one for one day; because of that one day of non-attainment, the count shifts from the second day to the tenth. Thus it is.
2nd day: not obtained; 8th day: obtained; 3rd day: not obtained; 7th day: obtained;
4th day: not obtained; 6th day: obtained; 5th day: not obtained; 5th day: obtained; 6th day: not obtained; 4th day: obtained;
7th day: not obtained; 3rd day: obtained; 8th day: not obtained; 2nd day: obtained; 9th day: not obtained; 1st day: obtained; 1st [day]: not obtained.

In all cases, because [the robe] has not been obtained, one forms successive permutations of the sentences; yet in every sentence, the fact that the first day’s possession of the robe remains unchanged applies.

Thus, all such permutations result in a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and does not perform a formal relinquishment (*pariṇāmanā*), but obtains a robe on the second day and performs a formal relinquishment, and then from the third day up to the tenth day does not perform a formal relinquishment, reaching the dawn of the eleventh day—
[The robe] comes into being. Any robes obtained during the nine days are all subject to the *niḥsargika* [offense]. Thus, one should construct the phrases by successive substitution as follows:
if one sends it to another; if the robe is lost; if it is intentionally damaged; if it is made into something other than a robe;
if it is taken with the intent of a close friend; or if it is forgotten and left behind—each of these phrases should be substituted in place of the phrase "pure gift" (*śuddha-dāna*).
The formulation of the rule is as above. It is a *niḥsargika* offense in its entirety.

If one possesses a robe subject to forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*)—so called because it must be forfeited—and does not forfeit it but instead exchanges it for another robe, there is one *niḥsargika* offense and one *duṣkṛta* (the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* is here translated as "forfeiture-and-fall"; henceforth, for brevity, it shall be referred to simply as "forfeiture-and-fall").

This robe subject to forfeiture must be surrendered to the Saṃgha; it may not be surrendered to a group of people or to a single individual, nor may it be surrendered outside of the formal assembly. If...

If one relinquishes [the robe] improperly, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. At the time of relinquishing, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, kneel on the right knee, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept this surplus robe for more than ten days, thereby committing an offense requiring relinquishment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha. Having completed the relinquishment, one should perform confession. The person receiving the confession shall then perform the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Thereafter, one should accept the confession. Make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
This bhikṣu [Name] has intentionally kept such a surplus robe and committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha grants its consent, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name]. Having made this announcement, one should accept the confession and say to him: "By yourself..."

"Reprove your mind. He replies, "So be it. If the Saṃgha is difficult to assemble and this bhikṣu has business that requires him to travel far away, one should ask him, "To whom shall you give your robe?
According to his response, one should immediately give it to the Saṃgha and return the robe to this bhikṣu by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
It should be done as follows: among the members of the Saṃgha, one capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed.

A person makes this formal announcement: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen. The bhikṣu so-and-so has intentionally kept such a number of extra robes, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha. If it is the time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha permits, let this robe be given to the bhikṣu so-and-so;
that bhikṣu so-and-so shall then return it to this bhikṣu. Thus is the announcement made to the venerable Saṃgha.
Listen. This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept such an excess robe and thereby committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to that bhikṣu, so-and-so; that bhikṣu, so-and-so, shall then return it to this bhikṣu.
Which elders consent to the Saṃgha taking this robe and giving it to that bhikṣu, so-and-so? That bhikṣu, so-and-so...
"O Bhikṣus, let him who approves of returning this robe to that Bhikṣu remain silent. Whoever does not approve, let them speak. The Saṃgha has approved;
the robe has been returned to that Bhikṣu named so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If that Bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the robe within the Saṃgha, does not return it, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he returns it, and someone says:"

If one does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one makes it a *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure gift), or sends it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes it into a *pārihārika-cīvara* (miscellaneous robe), or intentionally destroys it, or burns it, or makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined—all these constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases: if the purification (*pariśuddhi*) occurs within ten days; if it is given away to another;

if there is the perception that the robe has been seized, lost, burned, or swept away; if it was not purified and not given away, yet one takes and wears it after it has been seized, lost, burned, or swept away;
if someone else gives it to one to wear; if someone else makes it for one; or if the person who received the entrusted robe passes away or goes far away.

[The robe] has been brought out. If it is stolen by bandits, destroyed by wild beasts, or swept away by water, and one does not perform the ritual of *pariṣkāra* (purification/dedication) nor give it away to another person, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the *kaṭhina* period has ended, and he separates from any one of his three robes, [he commits an offense].
If one leaves one's robes behind while traveling, except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (2).
The group of six monks went wandering among the people and entrusted their robes to a friendly bhikṣu, repeatedly leaving them out in the sun to dry.

When the other bhikṣus questioned them and learned the reason for this, they reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established the precept. At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu suffering from pulmonary consumption (*śoṣa*).
A sick monk wished to travel among the people, but his *pāṃsukūla-saṃghāṭī* was heavy and he was unable to carry it while traveling. His companion informed the Buddha on his behalf.

The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to establish for the sick bhikṣu the *anāpatti-vastu* (the rule of not losing the robe). This is to be performed by a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
The three robes are the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antaravāsaka. Regarding the "Saṃgha": there is one boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa and one boundary for the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "not losing the robe": within the monastery, there is a single boundary. Regarding "losing the robe":
within the monastery, there are several boundaries. Regarding "not losing the robe" under a tree: a tree has one boundary. Regarding "losing the robe" under a tree: a tree has [several boundaries].
There are several types of boundaries (*sīmā*). The same applies to threshing floors, carts, ships, villages, houses, halls, treasuries, and granaries.
Regarding the four kinds of monasteries (*saṃghārāma*), they are as described above. As for a "tree," it is one that provides enough shade for a person to sit cross-legged beneath it.
A "threshing floor" is a place where the five grains are processed. A "cart" is a place where a cart turns around. A "ship" is a place where a ship turns around.

"Village" is as described above. "Hall" refers to those that are mostly dilapidated and exposed. "Storehouse" refers to where vehicles, carriages, litters, and goods for sale are stored and accumulated.
"Granary" refers to where rice and grain are stored and accumulated. Regarding the "boundary of a saṃghārāma":
this is the boundary of this saṃghārāma, not the boundary of that saṃghārāma; this is the boundary of this saṃghārāma, not the boundary of its trees, and so on, up to the granary.
The same applies to the *koṭṭa* (fortress) boundary; it is not the boundary of its granary. Other formulations are likewise. Regarding the *ārāma* (monastery) boundary:
it is located at the edge of the monastery, extending as far as a person of average height can reach by throwing a stone or a brick; this is called the boundary.

It is the same up to the boundary of the granary. If a bhikṣu places his robe within a monastery and stays overnight under a tree, and before the dawn has appeared, he either leaves the robe, holds the robe in his hand, or goes to a place where a thrown stone would reach;

or if he does not leave the robe and so forth, and the dawn appears, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the distance from which he stayed overnight separated from the robe. If he leaves it...
If one leaves one's robe within the monastery and goes to the threshing floor, or even to the place of the storehouse or granary to stay overnight;
or if one leaves the robe under a tree and goes to the threshing floor, or even to the monastery to stay overnight—the same applies: there is no loss of the robe.
If one is in an araṇya (wilderness) where there is no boundary, it is the space between eight trees; the distance between two trees is seven *dhanus*.
According to the method for making a *dhanus* in the country of Cāmara, its length is four *madhyama-hastas*.

If a bhikṣu is in an araṇya where there is no village, he may leave his robe within this space between the eight trees and stay overnight in another location. As long as the dawn has not appeared, he does not relinquish the robe, nor does he need to hold it in his hand.

Regarding robes: if they do not reach the place where a stone can be thrown, and the dawn light appears, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. With the exception of the three robes, to be separated from any other robe constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. The method for relinquishing [the robe] is as explained above. For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
