Before the appearance of dawn, one may hold onto the robe, or relinquish it, or go as far as the distance a stone can be thrown;

or if there is the perception that it has been seized, lost, burned, washed away, or destroyed; or if there is a great flood, or the road is dangerous and difficult, or there is danger from thieves and robbers, or danger from wild beasts.
If one is seized by force, or is bound, or faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life;
or if a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina cloth has been relinquished, and that bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it.
Having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, he may keep an extra portion for up to one month.
Because the moon is for the purpose of fulfillment. If one keeps [the robe] beyond that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (3).
There was a bhikṣu whose *saṃghāṭī* was old, worn out, and tattered; within ten days he could not provide a replacement, fearing he would violate the preceding precept.
His companion informed the Buddha on his behalf, and consequently, [the Buddha] permitted him to keep [the robe] until it was fulfilled. The group of six had excrement...

Regarding discarded robes (*pāṃśukūla*) and other types of robes, if those of the same kind are insufficient, one should take a discarded robe of middling quality, wash it, dye it, mark it to make it pure, and entrust it to a friend or relative bhikṣu before departing on a journey.
As for the bhikṣu who received the entrustment, because the traveler has been gone for a long time and has not yet returned—
He then took it out to dry. The bhikṣus, having learned the reason for this, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept:
"The proper time" refers to one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, or five months after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
"Improper time" refers to exceeding these limits; however, if within ten days the requisite amount of cloth is obtained, it is permissible.

One should cut, sew together the seams, and make it into a robe. Whether it is given as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) or sent to another person, if one does not do so by the time the dawn of the eleventh day appears, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the number of robes [received].

If the requisite robes are incomplete on that day but become complete by the eleventh day, one must then cut and so forth as described above. If one does not cut and so forth... [until] the eleventh day... [the offense applies].

On the twelfth day, when the dawn appears, according to the quantity of robes [received], they must all be relinquished as a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This applies likewise up to the twenty-ninth day.

If the same type of robe is insufficient by one day of the thirty, whether it be sufficient or insufficient, whether it be the same type of robe or a different type of robe, one should cut and alter them that very day;
if not, then upon the appearance of dawn on the thirty-first day, it becomes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The procedure for relinquishing the object is as explained above. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if, within ten days, one completes the robe by cutting, sewing, and joining with thread using the cloth already possessed, or if the cloth has been formally dedicated through *viśuddha-dāna*.
If it is sent to another person, the same applies up until the twenty-ninth day.

On the thirtieth day, whether the number of robes is complete or incomplete, whether they are of the same type or different types, one must cut and sew them that very day, or even send them to another person;
the rest is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (4).
There was a certain bhikṣu wearing a tattered rag-robe; when the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā saw him, she felt compassion and immediately gave him the one she herself was wearing.
He bartered the robe for its price and later wore this worn-out garment. When he saw the Buddha, the Buddha said, "It is not proper to be like this.

I allow you to keep and wear five robes that are complete and sturdy; as for other robes, you may give them away to others as you wish. Thereupon, the assembly was gathered and the precept was established.
From then on, the bhikṣus did not dare to take robes from their own relatives. The Buddha said, "If they are relatives, one may take them after consultation."
One should ascertain through measurement whether something exists or not, whether it is acceptable or unacceptable, whether it is good or bad, and whether it is new or old;

therefore, one may take from relatives. Furthermore, when the two divisions of the Saṃgha were dividing robes received as offerings within the Jeta Grove, a bhikṣu mistakenly received a robe belonging to a bhikṣuṇī, and a bhikṣuṇī mistakenly received a robe belonging to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣuṇī then exchanged the robes with one another, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
Therefore, trading is permitted.
"Relatives" refers to those related by blood on the father’s or mother’s side, extending back seven generations.
"Trading" means exchanging clothing for clothing, or exchanging clothing for non-clothing, or exchanging non-clothing for clothing—whether it be needles, tubes, knives, or [other such items].
Thread. If it is a small piece of material, even down to a single pill of medicine, the method of picking it up is as explained above. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if [the action] is for the sake of the Saṃgha or for the sake of taking [it] for a Buddhist shrine (*stūpa*).
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (5).
Kāḷudāyin sat with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in the nude; they gazed at one another with lustful intent and were overcome.
[The robe] was impure and stained. A *bhikṣuṇī* requested that he wash his *antarvāsaka*. She took the impurity and placed it in her mouth and her urinary tract;

subsequently, she became pregnant. When the other *bhikṣuṇīs* questioned her, they learned the reason and informed the *bhikṣus*, who in turn reported it to the World-Honored One, who then established a precept.
Thereupon, the *bhikṣus* did not dare to have their relatives—whether *bhikṣuṇīs* or others—wash, dye, or beat their old robes. The Buddha said: [This is the rule].
It is permitted to have it washed by a relative.

Regarding "old clothes": even those that have been worn on the body once. If a bhikṣu has a nun who is not a relative wash old clothes, or dye them, or beat them (to soften them), it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If he instructs her to wash, dye, and beat them, and she washes and dyes them but does not beat them; or if...
If one has them washed but does not have them dyed or beaten, or if one has them dyed or beaten but does not have them washed, there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses and one *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another to wash, dye, and beat [the cloth] but they ultimately do not do so, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If one instructs a non-relative *śrāmaṇerī* or *śikṣamāṇā* to wash, dye, or beat an old garment, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one instructs a non-relative *bhikṣuṇī* to wash, dye, or beat [a garment], it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
To wear new clothes is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For the other four assemblies, it is also a *duṣkṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one is ill, or if it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, or for the sake of a Buddhist monastery (*stūpa*), or if one is washing, dyeing, or beating clothes borrowed from another.
If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The "appropriate time" refers to when a bhikṣu’s robes have been snatched away, lost, burnt, or carried off by water;
these are called the appropriate times. (6)
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who went to a park for recreation. Turning his carriage around, he went to Jetavana and saw Baddhananda. He paid his respects and listened to the Dharma.
Baddhananda preached the Dharma to transform and edify him, exhorting him until he was filled with joy.

The elder asked what he required; Baddhananda replied that he required nothing. The elder pressed him further, but Baddhananda said, "Stop, stop! Do not give me anything. The elder insisted, saying, "If you have something you require..."
He could not bring himself to give it. The householder requested it once more, whereupon he said, "You may give me that which you are wearing.
At that time, the householder was wearing a costly, wide, and long white woolen cloth (*karpāsa*). He replied, "Come to my home tomorrow; I shall give it to you then."

Bhadrananda pressed his request persistently and would not stop. The elder was displeased; he took off his garment and gave it to him, then boarded the carriage wearing only a single robe and entered the city.
The gatekeeper suspected he had been robbed by bandits, but the elder explained the circumstances in detail.

Because householders criticized and disapproved, [the Buddha] established a rule. Consequently, the bhikṣus did not dare to solicit robes from their relatives. The Buddha said, "I permit it. Furthermore, the community...
A bhikṣu was traveling on the road when he was plundered by bandits. Standing outside the gate of Jetavana with his body exposed, the other bhikṣus suspected him of being a Nirgrantha.
Upon reporting this to Upāli, they learned the circumstances; he immediately borrowed a robe, put it on, and went to see the Buddha.

The Buddha questioned him and he fully explained the causes and conditions. Thereupon, the Buddha decreed that walking about naked is a *duṣkṛta* offense, and that one should instead [use] soft grass [as a covering].
If her body is covered by tree leaves, she should go to the vicinity of a monastery. If she has an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), she should take it and wear it;

if she has none, she may use an extra robe belonging to a companion bhikṣu, or a robe that can be distributed from the Sangha, or bedding and such items, to cover her body while going outside to beg for robes.
At that time, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to beg for robes from those who are not her relatives.

This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. For the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one begs on behalf of another, if another begs for oneself, or if one obtains it without having sought it.
If a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried off by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him at will and offers him many robes,
that bhikṣu should accept the robes with contentment. If he accepts more than that,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (seventh).
There were a number of bhikṣus who, having encountered bandits and lost their robes, came to the Jetavana. At that time, there was an upāsaka who possessed many fine robes;
he allowed the bhikṣus to take whichever they desired. The bhikṣus, however, already possessed their own three robes (tricīvara) and replied that they would not take them.
The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus said to them, "Why do you not take them? Will you give them to others? Thereupon, the bhikṣus took them.
He gave it to him. Those of few desires complained and rebuked him. He informed the Buddha, who therefore established this rule:

If one loses a single robe, one should not take [another]. If two robes are lost and only one remains, whether it be a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsa*, if it is double-layered, triple-layered, or quadruple-layered, one should tear it down [to the standard size]. If... [the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, or the *antarvāsa*...]
If all three robes are lost, one should receive robes with contentment. There are two kinds of contentment.
For a layperson, contentment means accepting whatever robe the white-clad householder provides. For an ordained person, contentment consists of the three robes.
If a householder makes an open invitation and gives many robes—whether they be fine, thin, or not durable—one should take them and have them made into [robes]. Second.
One should place the three layers or four layers upon the shoulder, ensuring that the edges are tucked against any areas prone to dirt or grease.
Hooks and buttons should be attached. If there is any remnant, one should ask the layperson: "What shall this leftover cloth be cut into?
If the donor says, "I did not give this to you because I lost my own garment; I gave it to you of my own accord," then if he...
If one who desires to receive it does so, the bhikṣuṇī commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a householder or a householder’s wife prepares the price for robes for a bhikṣu, intending to buy such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, goes to the householder’s home and speaks thus: "It is well..."
"O householder, you have bought such a robe for me because you wish to do me a favor. If one obtains such a robe [in this manner], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (8)."

A certain bhikṣu entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Upon arriving at the house of a lay devotee, he overheard the husband and wife discussing how they were preparing the price for a robe for Bāḷhaṇḍa.
He returned and informed Bāḷhaṇḍa. When Bāḷhaṇḍa asked him about it, the bhikṣu learned of the household's plans;
the next day he went to their home and said, "If you wish to give me a robe, it should be made thus—spacious, large, and of fine quality—for such as that I shall accept and wear."
Because laypeople criticized and disparaged [the monks], the rule was established. Subsequently, when laypeople personally invited monks, saying, "Venerable Sir, what kind of robe do you require?
the monks, harboring doubts, did not answer. There were also laypeople who wished to provide monks with robes of high value;

those monks, being content and desiring only what they needed, felt hesitant even regarding items that were inferior to their wishes, and did not dare to ask for them as they pleased. The Buddha then granted permission [for them to accept such offerings].
Regarding those who have previously accepted an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*:
as for the price of robes, it may be money, gold, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, necklaces, raw gold, or wrought gold.
There are two kinds of seeking: first, seeking the price, even down to an increase of one-sixteenth of a coin; second, [seeking the specific item].
Seeking robes: up to the point where one obtains a robe by adding even a single thread, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;

failure to obtain one constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one seeks on behalf of another, if another seeks on one's own behalf, or if one obtains it without seeking.
If two householders or a householder and his wife provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣu,
intending to purchase such a robe with that price and give it to a certain bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu has not previously accepted an invitation from those householders.
He went to the houses of two lay devotees and spoke thus: "Excellent! Prepare such a price for robes as this and make a single robe for me together, so that it may be fine.
If he obtains a robe [in this manner], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (9)."
The causal conditions are the same as before. Whether it constitutes an offense or not is also as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu, or a king, or a high minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a householder’s wife sends a messenger.
Someone is sending the price for robes to a bhikṣu, intending to give such a price for robes to a certain bhikṣu.
When that messenger arrives at the bhikṣu’s location, he says to the bhikṣu: “Venerable sir, this robe-price has been sent for your sake;
please accept it. That bhikṣu should say to the messenger: “I should not accept this robe-price. If I need a robe...”
When the time is right and one is pure, one should accept it. That messenger should say to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, is there an attendant?
The bhikṣu who requires robes should say, "There is a monastery attendant, or an upāsaka;
this person is the bhikṣus' attendant and constantly performs services for the bhikṣus. Then that messenger shall go to the attendant and give him the robe-cloth.
Having paid the price, he returns to the bhikṣu and says: "Venerable sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the attendant designated by you.
Venerable sir, please know the time and go there; you shall obtain the robe. The bhikṣu who requires a robe should go to the place of the attendant.
If he reminds him two or three times, he should say: "I require a robe. If [he does this] two or...
He should remind [the donor] three times. If he obtains the robe, it is well.

If he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before [the donor] four times, five times, and six times. If he obtains the robe by standing silently before him four times, five times, and six times, it is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain it beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If he does not...
Having obtained the robe, [the agent] should go to the place where the price for the robe was received—either going there in person or sending a messenger—and say:
"You have now sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu; that bhikṣu has ultimately not obtained the robe. You should take it back;
do not let it be lost. This is the tenth case.
In the city of Rājagṛha, a high minister sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to Baddhālī (Upananda).
Baddhālī took this messenger into the city and gave the price for the robe to an old friend, a householder, to hold for him.
At another time, the minister asked the messenger, "Has Baddhālī put it on? The messenger replied, "He has not. Thereupon, the minister sent another messenger to demand the robe back.
Regarding the price of the robe: Vāḍananda immediately went quickly to the house of the elder to solicit the robe.

At that time, the elders of the city had assembled, and there was a prior regulation that anyone who did not attend would be fined five hundred coins. The elder replied, "Venerable sir, please wait a moment while I return from the assembly.
Vāḍananda did not grant permission. After the elder had finished making the robe for him, the assembly had already sat down.
The payment of five hundred coins was abolished; this rule was established because [the monks] were immediately subject to mutual derision and suspicion by householders.
Regarding "recollection": if an official in charge goes to such places—whether at home, in the marketplace, or at a place of labor—[he should act with mindfulness].
A second and a third time, one should say: "I now require a robe; please make a robe for me. If one obtains a robe after two or three requests, that is well.
If one does not obtain a robe, one should stand silently before [the agent] for four, five, or six times.
If the attendant asks, "For what reason are you standing here? one should reply, "You should know for yourself. If he says:
"I do not know. If there is another who knows, one should say that person knows it. If a bhikṣu makes one utterance and breaks two periods of silence;
or two utterances and breaks four periods of silence; or three utterances and breaks six periods of silence;

or if he exceeds three utterances in seeking [the robe] by speech, or exceeds six periods of silence in seeking it, and obtains the robe, it is an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if she goes to the owner of the robe and says to him, "I do not need it;
I shall give it to you. This bhikṣu should request it at the proper time, request it with gentle speech, and request it through skillful means;
in doing so, he does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using mixed wild silk cotton, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (eleventh).
The group of six [bhikṣus] made a new bedding using mixed wild silk cotton; they went to a silkworm-raising household to request silk, saying, "Wait until the silkworms are ripe.
At that time, the group of six went to wait and watch as the cocoons and silkworm pupae made sounds. Because of this, the laypeople censured them.

The Regulation on Mixed Materials: If it is made of wool, cotton, *koccha* cloth, *kappāsa* grass, *kusa* grass, *śāṇa* hemp, or flax, and if a bhikṣu makes it himself, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The same applies if he instructs another to make it.
It is so. If one acts on behalf of another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the relinquishment of this [material]:
one should finely chop it with axes and hatchets, mix it with mud, and apply it as plaster to walls or mounds. For a *bhikṣuṇī* and the three other assemblies, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one obtains what is already finished; or if one uses an axe or hatchet to chop and hack wool into pieces to mix with mud for plastering walls or floors;
or if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using entirely new, pure black sheep’s wool, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
(12) The Licchavis frequently engaged in sexual misconduct. They made blankets from pure black sheep’s wool and wore them while walking at night so that people would not see them.
The group of six [monks] imitated this practice. The Licchavis said: "We [did this] for..."
"Because of lust, what is the purpose of your doing this? The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "It was done for that reason.
Regarding the "pure black": it may be black by birth or black by dyeing. If one performs it oneself, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if not, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same when instructing another to make one. If one causes another to make it, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The method for relinquishing [the object] is as explained in the section on "extra robes" (*atirekacīvara*). There is no offense in the following cases: if one obtains what is already finished; if it has been cut or damaged;
if it is thin and folded to make it double-layered; or if it is made into a mattress, a pillow, a small square sitting mat, or a bed-cover.
Woolen cloth: one may use it to make a bowl-cloth, a shaving-bag, a cap, socks, a towel for removing heat from tongs, or a cloth for wrapping leather sandals.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding cover, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of... [gray].
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (thirteen).

The group of six monks made bedding that was entirely white. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying it resembled that of kings or high ministers; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule:
"White" refers to either naturally white or dyed white; "spotted color" refers to the hair on the head, the hair on the ears, or the hair on the legs.
If one makes a woolen bedding of forty *pala* using other brindled-colored wool, it consists of twenty *pala* of black, ten *pala* of white, and ten *pala* of brindled.
If one makes it of thirty *pala*, it consists of fifteen *pala* of black, fifteen *pala* of white, and half [of that] brindled. If one makes it of twenty *pala*, ten *pala*...
Black hair: five *pātra*s; white hair: five *pātra*s; variegated hair: five *pātra*s. The gravity of the offense is the same as above.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Non-offense is as above.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat and uses it for six years or less than six years, and without relinquishing the old one, he makes another new one—
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma)— it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense (14).
The group of six monks took offense at their bedding and requisites—whether they were heavy or light, thin or coarse—and because they refused to discard the old, they would instead make new ones.
As these accumulated in great numbers, the Buddha established a rule against it. Later, a certain monk contracted the disease of consumption (śoṣa).

Having a reason to travel among the people, he found his refuse-rag bedding too heavy to carry on his journey. The monks informed the Buddha, and the Buddha granted permission [to use lighter materials].
The Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for him; the gravity of the offense is as stated above. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), he must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one.

[The Buddha said: "Because it must be dyed a discolored color (*kāṣāya*). If one makes a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and does not take a piece from an old one—measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length and breadth—and affix it to the top of the new one for the purpose of dyeing it a discolored color, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the fifteenth)."
When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he sent someone to invite [the monks] for a meal.

It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that after the bhikṣus have accepted an invitation, they go through all the rooms and see that the old sitting cloths are scattered about everywhere in disorder. Thereupon, [the Buddha] ordered the bhikṣus to make new sitting cloths;
they were to take a piece from the old ones measuring one span in length and breadth and patch it onto the new ones to ensure the color was faded. (6)
Because the multitude did not rely upon the Buddha’s instructions, he established this precept.
When a bhikṣu is making a new sitting mat (niṣīdana), if his old mat has not yet worn out and there are no holes in it, he must wash, dye, repair, and stretch it;
having made it wide and long enough, he should cut a piece measuring one span (vitasti) to be pasted onto the new mat. If it is at the edge...
If it is of medium quality, for the purpose of discoloring it, the gravity of the offense is the same as above. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one does not possess it oneself; or if another has made it for one's sake; or if one obtains what is already finished; or if one makes it from pure, old materials.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, obtains wool and there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three yojanas.
If he carries it himself beyond three yojanas when there is no one to carry it, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense (16).

While traveling on the road, Upananda obtained a great deal of wool; he threaded it onto the tip of a staff and carried it along the way. A householder looked upon this with resentment and reproached him.
It was for the sake of such trade in wool that the rule was established.
Monks, if a monk is traveling on a road or staying at a residence and obtains wool that he requires, he may take it.
If there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three *yojanas*. If there is someone to carry it, he should say to them, "I have this item;
please help me carry it" as far as that destination. During this interval, the monk must not assist in carrying it [on his own behalf].

If one assists in carrying [the robe], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one causes the other four groups of the Saṃgha to carry it beyond three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense, except in the case of wool.
If one carries other *kośaka* materials—such as milk-tree bark, leaves, grass, *kusa* grass, hemp, or *celā-paṇi*—and carries them beyond three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, if one carries other items on a staff, [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense].
The leader of the procession also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. The forfeiture of the object is as previously described. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one carries it for three *yojanas* or less than three *yojanas*;

or if someone speaks with the carrier and instructs them to carry it to a certain place, and the carrier does not assist in carrying it further along the way; or if one instructs a *bhikṣuṇī* or the other three assemblies [to carry it].
If one is within three yojanas of reaching [the destination], there is no offense in carrying wool, woolen garments, or woolen ropes; nor in carrying hair from the head, neck, or feet;
nor in making hats, socks, tweezers, or hot-cloth headbands; nor in wrapping leather sandals. All such acts are without fault.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (seventeenth).
The group of six [bhikṣus] took wool to make a sitting mat and had Mahāprajāpatī wash, dye, and card it; the dye stained her hands.
He went to see the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One questioned him and learned the reason for this; he rebuked him and established a precept.
Thereafter, the bhikṣus did not dare to allow their own relatives to act as *bhikṣuṇīs*. The Buddha said, "I permit it."
If one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card [wool], it is each a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one causes her to wash but she does not wash, and so forth, it is each a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes a *śrāmaṇerī* or a *śikṣamāṇā* who is not a relative to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if it is for the sake of a sick person, for the sake of the Saṃgha, or for the sake of the Buddha or a stūpa;
or if a bhikṣu takes money or gold and silver with his own hand, or instructs another to take it, or receives it by placing it on the ground. This applies to a bhikṣuṇī as well.

Saṃghāvaśeṣa (18): Because of the householder at the marketplace to whom Upāli’s brother, Upananda, entrusted money while he was at the residence of a high minister, and because of the resulting reproach and suspicion, this rule was established.
Regarding "money": it has inscribed images upon it. Regarding "one who renounces it therein":
if there is a faithful and devoted garden-keeper or an upāsaka, one should say to them, "This is not for me to keep; you should know this.
If that person takes it back and gives it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu, for the sake of that person's property, should instruct a pure attendant (kappiyakāraka) to receive it.
Take charge of them. If one obtains a pure robe, alms bowl, needle case, or sitting mat (niṣīdana), one should trade for them and maintain possession of them.
If a lay follower (upāsaka) takes them and gives a pure robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, or needle case to a bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should take and maintain them.
If he takes them and does not return them, one should have another bhikṣu speak to him, saying: "The Buddha has given this instruction."
Because it has been purified, I have given it to you; you ought to return this object to that bhikṣu. If other bhikṣus do not speak up, you should go there yourself and say:
"The Buddha has instructed that because it was given to you for the sake of purification, you may now give it to the Saṃgha or to a stūpa."

If one returns [an item] to its original owner together with one's *upādhyāya*, or together with one's *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*, or together with one's *ācārya* and various relatives, acquaintances, and friends—for what reason?
It is because one does not wish to cause the loss of that person’s faithful offering (*śraddhā-deya*).

If one does not inform them, saying, "Know this" or "Look at this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *bhikṣu*; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
[The Nineteenth Rule: If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[This was established] because Upananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for more money while carrying it away; since householders criticized and disparaged this, the rule was enacted.
Regarding various forms of buying and selling: one exchanges finished gold for unfinished gold, unfinished gold for finished gold, or finished and unfinished gold;

one exchanges them for finished silver, unfinished silver, or finished and unfinished silver; one exchanges them for coin. One exchanges unfinished gold for finished gold, unfinished gold for [finished and unfinished gold], and so on up to exchanging it for coin.
One exchanges finished and unfinished gold for finished gold, and so on up to exchanging it for silver or coin.
The formulation regarding coins is explained in the same way. There are eight kinds of coins:
gold coins, silver coins, copper coins, iron coins, wooden coins, white wax coins, lead and tin coins, and foreign resin coins. The procedure for relinquishing them is the same as above.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one uses money to exchange for necklaces.
[If] one uses jewelry to exchange for money for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha;
or if a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling: [this constitutes] a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) [twenty].
In a village without a permanent residence, Upananda took fresh ginger and exchanged it for food before departing.

When Śāriputra went to that house while begging for alms, the man immediately demanded the price. Furthermore, in Śrāvastī, a non-Buddhist obtained a costly garment and brought it to the monastery to trade;
Upananda pounded and mended an old robe and exchanged it for it, after which the non-Buddhist returned to his own place.

While staying in the garden, someone informed him, saying, "You have been deceived by another. He immediately took his robes to the monastery intending to return them, but Baddhananda would not consent.
Because the non-Buddhists criticized and disparaged this, [the Buddha] established the rule.

Regarding those who engage in various kinds of trade: exchanging at the proper time for the proper time; exchanging at the proper time for the improper time; exchanging within seven days; exchanging for as long as one lives;
and *pālikāla* (temporary exchange)—the remaining four modes of exchange are also described in this same way. As for the seller: if the price is worth one coin, they repeatedly lower or raise it;
as for the over-seller: if the price is worth one coin, they claim it is worth three coins; as for the excessive over-seller: [they claim it is worth even more].

If an item worth one *kārsāpaṇa* is described as being worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, and it is purchased accordingly, the same applies. If one acquires [an item] through various forms of trade, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if one does not acquire it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The method of relinquishment (*pratikṣepa-dharma*) is as previously explained.
There is no offense if one trades with the five classes of renunciants, having personally determined that there is no disparity in value, according to the rules of market exchange.
If one engages in trade with others, or if one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") to engage in trade, it should be returned if regret arises.
If one exchanges ghee for oil, or exchanges oil for ghee.

If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms bowl without having performed the ritual of pure donation (*viśuddhi-dāna*), he may keep it for up to ten days; if he exceeds this period, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). (21)

The group of six [monks] kept their fine alms bowls and set aside those that were not good. A lay devotee visited their quarters to look at them and criticized them with disdain, saying it was like a potter’s shop selling earthenware.
Therefore, a regulation was established. At that time, Ānanda obtained a high-priced bowl from the kingdom of Soma.

He wished to give it to Kāśyapa, but as the latter was temporarily away, he feared he might violate this precept. The Buddha asked how long it would be before Kāśyapa returned, and Kāśyapa replied that it would be ten days.
Thereupon, [the Buddha] permitted him to keep it for up to ten days.
There are two kinds of bowls: iron bowls and clay bowls. The large ones hold three *dōns*, and the small ones hold one and a half *dōns*.

Such bowls should be kept and purified through formal donation (*pariṣkāra-dāna*). If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, and continues obtaining bowls up until the tenth day, and keeps them until the dawn of the eleventh day, all the bowls obtained during those ten days constitute an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If he obtains [a bowl] on the first day...

[If] he does not obtain a bowl on the second day, but obtains one on the third day, or even up to the tenth day, and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, then all the bowls obtained during those nine days constitute a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. (The same applies in descending order down to the case where he does not obtain a bowl for ten days; the formulation is as above.
Likewise, if he does not obtain one on the second day, but obtains one on the eighth day, or even if he does not obtain one for nine days, but obtains one on the first day, it is also [the same].

It is so. It is so. Whether it has been given as a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*), or sent to another, or lost, or intentionally damaged, or made into something other than a bowl, or taken with the intent of a close friend, or forgotten and left behind—[the phrase "one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense" applies to each case above, substituting "pure gift" and so forth for the word "cannot"].

In all these cases, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Regarding the bowl that was not relinquished: if one trades it for another bowl, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense.

*Śāṭī*. Regarding the forfeiture of the *dharmaka* (robe-material) as in the case of the *atirekacīvara* (extra robe): for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if, within ten days, one performs a *viśuddhi-dāna* (pure gift), or if one sends it to another person, or if it is seized, lost, destroyed, or carried away by water.
If the bowl is stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water; if it is taken for use, or used because another person gave it;

or if one has accepted a bowl as a deposit, and the bhikṣu subsequently dies, travels far away, renounces the path, or is seized by bandits or wild beasts—under these circumstances, not returning the bowl to the person does not constitute an offense.
If a bhikṣu possesses an alms bowl that has fewer than five mends and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; the Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among those present and give it to him, instructing him to keep it until it breaks. This is the proper course of action. (22)
When Ba-nan-da’s bowl broke, he went to various laypeople to request bowls; having broken one bowl, he obtained many.
On another occasion, when those laypeople gathered in one place, each said that they had acquired immeasurable merit because they had purchased bowls to give to Ba-nan-da.
Consequently, they began to criticize and disparage him, and [the Buddha] therefore established this rule.
Regarding the "five patches": a patch is placed at intervals of two finger-widths apart.

If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken but has less than five patches and does not leak, and he seeks a new bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If it has exactly five patches and does not leak, yet he seeks a new bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the relinquishing [of the bowl] therein: one should relinquish it within the Saṃgha at this dwelling place. One should bare the right shoulder, remove one’s sandals, prostrate toward the Elder, and kneel with palms joined in repentance.
The person receiving the repentance shall first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then accept the repentance.
If this bhikṣu’s bowl is of high value and fine quality, it should be set aside; one should take the lowest-quality one that is inferior and give it to him. This is the announcement.
When the second *karmavācanā* has been completed, that bhikṣu’s bowl should be presented after making a formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made the motion to the Saṃgha in this way: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, [I shall ask] regarding this bowl, starting with the Elder;
the motion is as follows. Having made this motion, he should hold it out to the Elder. If the Elder wishes to take this bowl...
Give it to him. He should take the bowl of the senior monk (sthavira) and give it to the next seat. If he gives it to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should take it;
he should not withhold it for the sake of protecting the Saṃgha, nor should he fail to take it. For this reason, one should accept and keep the lowest bowl;
if one does not accept it, it is a duṣkṛta offense. If the second senior monk takes this bowl, he should take the second [bowl].
The senior elder’s bowl is given to the third senior elder. If it is given to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should accept it but should not keep it for the Saṃgha;
therefore, he should not take it. For this reason, one should hold onto the very lowest bowl. If one accepts [the higher ones], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
In this manner, it is passed down successively until it reaches the junior-most seat. If one returns the bowl of this bhikṣu [to its original owner], [there is no fault].

If this bhikṣu takes the bowl of the lowest-ranking seat and gives it to that bhikṣu, he shall perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one subsequent proclamation), making the following announcement:

"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now give this bowl of the lowest-ranking seat to the bhikṣu [Name] to receive and keep, until it breaks; it should be kept in this manner. Thus is the announcement. Great!
Venerable sirs, listen. The Saṃgha now bestows this bowl of the lowest-ranking seat upon the bhikṣu so-and-so for him to receive and maintain, and he shall keep it until it breaks.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s bestowing of this bowl upon this bhikṣu, remain silent.
Those who do not consent, speak. The Saṃgha has consented; the bestowing of the bowl upon this bhikṣu is concluded. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, it is thus.
One should maintain it in this manner. That bhikṣu must guard this bowl;

he must not place it where tiles or stones may fall upon it, nor beneath hanging weapons or staffs, nor beneath suspended objects. He must not place it on a path, on a stone, beneath a fruit tree, or on uneven ground.
He must not hold two bowls with one hand, except when separating them with his fingers in the middle. He must not [hold] one...

Holding two bowls in one's hands, one should open the door. With care, one must not place them within the threshold, beneath the door leaf, beneath a rope bed, beneath a wooden bed, between a rope bed and a wooden bed, or at the corner of a bed. One may place them there only temporarily;
one must not stand and shake the bowls until they are broken by one's feet. One should not intentionally damage them, nor should one act so as to lose them intentionally.
If one has discarded a bowl among the Sangha for use as something other than a bowl and does not return it, or instructs another not to return it, both incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one makes a formal gift (*śuddhaka-dāna*) of it to someone else, or causes it to be lost or destroyed, or uses it repeatedly as something other than a bowl, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense each time.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:

if it has fewer than five patches and leaks and she seeks another; if she solicits it on behalf of another; if another solicits it for her; if she obtains it without having solicited it; if she receives it in turn when a bowl is being offered to the Saṃgha;
or if she purchases it herself with her own funds and keeps it.
If a bhikṣu himself solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into the three robes,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (twenty-third).
Bhadanta wished to sew a great robe (saṃghāṭī). He went to the house of a lay devotee and sought thread everywhere; having obtained a great deal of thread, he then had a weaver weave it.
He himself made the shuttle, himself oversaw the weaving, and personally inspected the work. Because the lay devotee criticized and disapproved of this, the rule was established.
Regarding "soliciting oneself": in various places, one solicits weavers who are not relatives to provide thread that is not from a relative.

If a weaver is not a relative and the thread is provided by someone who is not a relative, it is an offense. Or, if the weaver is a relative but the thread is provided by someone who is not a relative, it is an offense.

Or, if the weaver is not a relative and the thread is provided by someone who is not a relative, it is an offense. If the weaver is a relative but the thread is provided by someone who is not a relative, it is an offense as before.
This is formed through weaving. If nine or eight sentences [of the rule] are violated, one commits an offense.

If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver weave it to make a robe, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If he supervises the weaving, weaves it himself, or winds the thread himself, he commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in each case.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies (*saṃgha*), it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if he weaves it himself.

The teacher gives thread; both [the teacher and the pupil] are kinsmen. If he weaves it himself, he makes a bowl bag, a sandal bag, a needle-case, a felt mat, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, tweezers, a hot-water towel, and a cloth for wrapping leather sandals.

If a monk, when a householder or a householder’s wife has sent a weaver to weave a robe for that monk, goes to the weaver’s place before having been invited by a formal request and says: “Weave this robe for me;
weave it very well, making it broad, large, and firm. I shall give you some small amount of payment. If that monk gives him such payment, [he commits an offense].
Even for the value of a single meal, if one obtains a robe [in such circumstances], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the twenty-fourth).
In Śrāvastī, there was a householder who provided high-quality thread and had a weaver weave a robe for Upananda.
The weaver told this to Bāḍhananda, who immediately sent him to weave something vast and of fine quality. [The weaver] said, "There is too little thread.
He went to the householder’s home and asked for more thread; [the weaver] replied, "The price is too low. He then agreed to provide a higher price.

The householder criticized and disparaged this, and thus [the Buddha] established the rule. Thereafter, the bhikṣus, out of doubt, did not dare to accept invitations for self-indulgent requests, nor to seek anything that was inferior.
The Buddha said: "It is permitted.
If one obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if it was for another's sake, if another acted for one's own sake, or if one obtained it without having sought it."
If a bhikṣu has previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or causes another to seize it,
saying, "Bring my robe back; I will not give it to you," and that other bhikṣu returns the robe and he takes it,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (the twenty-fifth).
Nanda’s disciple was skilled at exhortation and conversion. Upananda said to him, "Travel through the human world together with me, and I shall give you a robe.
Other bhikṣus asked him, "For what purpose do you travel with Upananda?
That foolish man does not know how to recite the precepts, nor the formal recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), nor the *karmavācanā* procedures. Thereupon, that bhikṣu no longer traveled with him.
Baddhananda then demanded back his previous robe. When the bhikṣu did not return it, he became angry and forcibly seized it. Therefore, the rule was established:
if one seizes and hides [the robe], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not hide it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This applies whether it is placed upon a tree, a wall, a fence, a stake, a "dragon-tooth" peg, a clothes rack, a rope bed, a wooden bed, a small mat, a large mat, a mechanical device, a floor covering, or similar items.
If one takes [the robe] from its place, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if not from its place, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one says without anger, "I am repentant;
therefore, I will not give you the robe. Return my robe to me. If the other person knows of the repentance and immediately returns it, or if another person says, "This... [and so forth].
A bhikṣu may take back a robe that was given to him for the purpose of repentance. If he has borrowed another's robe and that other person is wearing it, he must not take it away by force;

however, he may take it if there is fear of its being lost or damaged, or if the owner has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his conduct, or if he has been suspended or expelled, or if his life or his holy life (*brahmacarya*) is in danger because of that robe. In such cases, he may take it away without having to store it or return it.
If a bhikṣu is ill, he may consume leftover medicines—namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—for up to seven days.
If he consumes them beyond seven days, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika (offense involving forfeiture). (26)
"O bhikṣus, in the autumn months, those with wind-disorders (vāta) find their bodies parched and develop malignant sores.

The Buddha has permitted the consumption of the five kinds of medicine, both at the proper time and outside the proper time. At that time, Piṅgala-vatsa was residing in Rājagṛha; he was widely renowned for his extensive knowledge."
He also had many followers and received great offerings of ghee, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.

His disciples accumulated and stored these in such abundance that they overflowed everywhere, making the dwellings foul and stinking; those who saw this censured him with disdain. Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.
When a patient is instructed by a physician to take a certain medicine, that medicine consists of ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar.

If a bhikṣu acquires medicine on the first day and stores it, and continues to acquire and store it on the second day, and so on up to the seventh day, such that when the dawn of the eighth day appears, he has kept all that was acquired during the seven days, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If he acquires medicine on the first day and stores it, but does not [acquire any] on the second day...
It is permitted. One may store medicine obtained on the third day up to the seventh day. When the dawn of the eighth day appears, whatever was obtained on the sixth day must be relinquished;
otherwise, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. (In this manner, the phrase "not obtained" is successively moved down to the seventh day to form the sentences. Thus for two days:

if one does not obtain [medicine] on the second day, obtains it on the fifth day, and likewise does not obtain it on the sixth day but obtains it on the first day, the formation of the sentences is as above. This applies similarly if there is a *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure gift).

If one gives it away to another, if it is lost, if it is intentionally destroyed, if it is made into something that is not medicine, if it is taken with the intent of treating it as a personal gift, or if it is forgotten and carried off—[the phrase "one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense" applies to each of these cases, substituting "pure gift" (*pariśuddha-dāna*) for the word "cannot"]. In all such cases, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense regarding the medicine and does not relinquish it, but instead trades it for other medicine, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *dukkaṭa*. The procedure for relinquishment is as previously described.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the other three groups of followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:
if those medicines kept beyond seven days, or ghee and oil used for smearing on door-sills; if honey or *phāṇita* (molasses) given to a garden-keeper;
if, upon reaching the seventh day, they are relinquished and given to a bhikṣu to eat; or if, before the seven days have elapsed, they are returned to that bhikṣu, who may then use them.
Anointing the feet or lighting lamps.
If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the summer retreat, he should seek a rain-bathing robe; he should use it for bathing during the final half-month [of the retreat].

If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bathing robe more than one month before [the end of the retreat], or uses it for bathing more than half a month [before the end of the retreat], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
27. Viśākhā, the Mother of Migāra, invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. At that time, there was heavy rain. The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to bathe in the rain.

When the maidservant came to announce that it was time [for the meal], she saw from afar a bhikṣu bathing naked; suspecting him to be a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), she returned and informed her mistress.
After the World-Honored One had accepted her offering, the mother requested that he grant the bhikṣus rain-bathing robes (vārṣika-cīvara). The Buddha permitted this.

Thereupon, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks constantly sought rain-bathing robes at all times; they did not relinquish their own rain robes but instead used them for other purposes. This was made manifest.
There was a rain-cloak, yet [monks] still bathed naked in the rain; therefore, it was prescribed.
Regarding the rain-cloak: a bhikṣu shall use it for bathing during the rainy season. On the sixteenth day of the third month, he should seek a rain-bathing robe.

It should be used on the first day of the fourth month. If one seeks it before the sixteenth day of the third month and uses it before the first day of the fourth month, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
for the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if, having already relinquished the rain-cloak, one subsequently makes another use of it;
or if one wears a bathing-cloth to bathe; or if one has no rain-cloak; or if one is making a bathing-cloth; or if one is washing [the robe].
[The offense of] *niḥsargika-pācattika* for attachment:
If there is attachment to the place where [the robe] was found; or if a bhikṣu, before the three months of the summer retreat have concluded, receives an urgent offering of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

The bhikṣu, knowing it is an urgent offering of robes, should accept it. Having accepted it, he may keep it until the time for robes [at the end of the rainy season]. If he keeps it beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
**Saṃghāvaśeṣa 28.** The Buddha was staying at Vairaṇyā.
When the summer retreat (varṣā) had concluded, a brahmin prepared an offering and bestowed robes. The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to accept these summer robes.
However, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks constantly begged for robes at all times, even before the retreat had ended.

[The Buddha said: "One may accept robes; one may also accept [additional] robes. Furthermore, after Vāḍananda had completed his rains retreat in one place, he heard that robes had been obtained in great abundance elsewhere.

He then distributed them everywhere and received a share of the robes. When the Buddha heard of this, he rebuked him. At that time, two high ministers from Śrāvastī were going on an expedition against rebels.
They thought to themselves, "We do not yet know whether we will return or not. We wish to provide food for the Saṃgha and offer robes as a gift."
Because the rainy season retreat had not yet concluded, the bhikṣus did not dare accept the robes. The Buddha then permitted them to accept them and established this precept:

regarding "urgent robe-giving," if one accepts it, one obtains the robe; if one does not accept it, one loses the robe. Regarding "the time," it refers to the period after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, provided that one has not yet accepted [the robe].

The kaṭhina robe may be received for one month; the kaṭhina robe [period] lasts for five months. When ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, if one obtains an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), it should be accepted and kept until the time for the distribution of robes.
If nine days remain, and one obtains an urgent gift of robes, it should be accepted and kept until the time for the distribution of robes.
Furthermore, one day is added to the count. Likewise, if eight days remain, two days are added; if seven days remain...
On the third day, increase it by four days; continuing in this manner until on the first day, one increases it by nine days—all as explained above.
If [the period] exceeds the former limit or falls short of the latter, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if the robes are seized; if they are lost; if they are burned; if they are carried away by water; or if more than the prescribed time has elapsed;
or if one perceives them as being seized, lost, burned, or carried away; or if the road is dangerous and impassable; or if there are many thieves, wild beasts, or a great flood;
or if one is beset by the danger of royal command or the danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if the monk to whom they were entrusted has died or gone abroad.
After being ravaged by bandits, plundered by wild beasts,
or swept away by floods, if a bhikṣu, after the completion of the three months of the summer retreat and at the end of the month of Kārttika,
dwells in an araṇya— a place of apprehension and fear— a bhikṣu dwelling in such a place may wish to leave one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling.
29. If any bhikṣus, having a legitimate reason, stay apart from their robes for up to six nights, and if they exceed that period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

When the bhikṣus had completed the rainy season retreat and one month of the *kārttika* period remained, those staying in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*) encountered many dangers from bandits and all went to Jetavana to dwell together. The Buddha then permitted them to leave one robe each inside their dwellings.

The group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) monks immediately left their robes inside the dwellings, entrusted them to their friends and acquaintances among the bhikṣus, and departed; the ones who had received the entrustment then came out.
He hung his robe out to dry. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who established this precept:
"A forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) is located five hundred bow-lengths from a village. In the country of Cāmara, a bow is four cubits long;
this measurement shall be based on the medium cubit. 'A place of suspicion' means there is suspicion of thieves and robbers. 'A place of terror' means there are terrifying thieves within it."

"Stealing from within a dwelling" refers to a village settlement. During the seventh night, before the first light of dawn has appeared, if one does not relinquish the three robes, does not hold them in hand, and does not go to a place where a stone can be thrown, but remains elsewhere, then when the first light of dawn appears, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya). This excludes the case of being separated from the three robes;
for other garments, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense if one has the perception that they have been seized, lost, burned, or swept away.
If a ferry is not available for crossing, the road is dangerous and difficult, there are robbers or wild beasts, the waters are swollen and one is detained, life is in peril,
or the practice of the holy life is threatened— if a bhikṣu, knowing it to be property belonging to the Saṃgha, seeks to appropriate it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (thirty).
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a householder who wished to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as to offer fine robes.

Baddhananda said to him, "Those who give to the Saṃgha receive much merit; you should now eat, and you may give the robes to the Saṃgha, but you should give [one] to me. The householder agreed to this.
On the following day, the monks went to the invitation. Seeing that their deportment was perfect, the lay devotee cried out in remorse, saying, "I shall not give the robe.
When the bhikṣus asked him about the reason, he explained it to them. They reported this to the Buddha, who established a precept.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether an item was the property of the Saṃgha or not the property of the Saṃgha, nor whether it had been granted to the Saṃgha or not granted to the Saṃgha; only later did they realize it was the property of the Saṃgha and that it had already been granted to the Saṃgha.
One may perform a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* confession, or feel shame and remorse. The Buddha said: "If one does not know [it is monastic property], there is no offense.
Regarding "monastic property" (*saṃghika-vastu*): it refers to items made for the Saṃgha, already given to the Saṃgha, or promised to the Saṃgha;

such items include robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, down to drinking vessels and water containers. If a bhikṣu knows these are monastic property and seeks to take them for himself, he must relinquish them.
If one diverts property intended for the Saṃgha to a stūpa; intended for a stūpa to the Saṃgha;
intended for the Saṃgha of the four directions to the present Saṃgha; intended for the present Saṃgha to the Saṃgha of the four directions;
intended for bhikṣus to bhikṣuṇīs; intended for bhikṣuṇīs to bhikṣus; or intended for one location to another location—it is all a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If it has already been consented to, and one perceives it as such, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If it has already been consented to, but one is in doubt, or if it has not yet been consented to, but one perceives it as such, or is in doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [if it is] not [as described above].
If one does not know; if one has already consented to do something but then thinks one has not; if one consents to giving a small amount but encourages the giving of much;
if one consents to giving to few people but encourages giving to many; if one intends to consent to what is inferior but encourages giving what is superior;
or if it is spoken in jest, spoken while alone, spoken in sleep, or spoken erroneously.

Compiled by the Monk Guangcheng of the Wu-ling region, a Bodhisattva Precept-holder of the Ming Dynasty.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu of Chìchéng, Guǎnghǎo;
revised by the Dharma-heir Bhikṣu, Dàzhēn;
and supplemented by the Bhikṣu of Gǔwú, Zhìxù.
The ninety *pāyattika* rules, Chapter Five:
If a bhikṣu speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it is a *pāyattika*.
(1) When the elephant-strong son of the Śākyas was debating with a brahmin, if he did not respond at the proper time, he would contradict his previous words. If...
When this was asked among the Saṃgha, he again contradicted his previous statements. Because the brahmins censured and disparaged him, [the Buddha] established the rule:

"To speak falsely while knowing the truth—saying one has seen what one has not seen, saying one has heard what one has not heard, saying one has touched what one has not touched, saying one knows what one does not know;
or saying one has not seen what one has seen, saying one has not heard what one has heard, saying one has not touched what one has touched, saying one does not know what one knows. If...
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet says, "I have seen, heard, touched, or known," knowing this to be a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, but perceives that they have seen, heard, touched, or known, and then says, "I have not seen, heard, touched, or known," it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, and doubt arises in their mind, yet they say, "I have no doubt," it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has seen, heard, touched, or known [something], it is a *pāyattika* offense if one says, "I have no doubt; I have not seen, heard, touched, or known it.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known [something], it is a *pāyattika* offense if one has doubt in one's mind but says, "I have no doubt; I have not seen, heard, touched, or known it.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known [something], it is a *pāyattika* offense if one has no doubt in one's mind but says, "I have doubt; I have not seen, heard, touched, or known it."

This should be explained in detail. One originally forms this thought: "I shall speak falsely. (1) At the moment of speaking the falsehood, one knows it is a falsehood; (2) having spoken the falsehood, one knows it is a falsehood;
(3) one speaks falsely intentionally. This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Thus, there are cases where one knows at the beginning and middle but not at the end;
where one does not know at the beginning but knows at the middle and end; and where one knows at the beginning and end but not at the middle.

A *pāyattika* offense. To have a different view, a different tolerance, a different desire, a different contact, a different perception, and a different intention—these various matters are all false speech.
If one knowingly speaks falsely in the midst of the great assembly, it is a *pāyattika* if the meaning is clear;
it is a *dukkaṭa* if the meaning is not clear. This applies even when the precepts are being recited and the question is asked up to three times.
If one remembers a transgression but does not speak of it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if, having perceived it with one's own mind, one speaks of it immediately.
If a bhikṣu uses disparaging speech regarding another’s lineage, it is a pāyattika (2).

When the group of six [bhikṣus] settled a dispute by reviling a bhikṣu according to his lineage, that bhikṣu was so ashamed and humiliated that he forgot what preceded and followed and was unable to speak;
therefore, this rule was established.
Regarding those who disparage others by class: they are born into low-caste families; their occupations are base; their arts and crafts are base.
They say: "You are a transgressor; you have many fetters; you are a bald man and blind; you are a bald man and sightless. They are lowly ones:
the *caṇḍāla* caste, the scavenger caste, the bamboo-worker caste, the wagon-maker caste, and the low-caste *kukkuṭa*.
Kauśika, Vāsiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Ātreya, and Bhāradvāja—if one was not originally of low birth but practices a low craft, one is then of low birth.

Low occupations include: trading in pigs and sheep, slaughtering oxen, falconers and hunters, netting fish, committing robbery, capturing thieves, guarding cities, and serving as jailers. Low crafts include: smithing and carpentry.

[Those who] work with clay or tiles, those who work with leather, those who shave hair, and those who work with winnowing baskets—if such persons commit an offense, it is a *pārājika* [offense], up to and including "evil speech.
As for those bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*), from those possessed of anger up to those with five hundred fetters;

as for those who are blind or sightless, those who are bald, lame, crippled, deaf, mute, or afflicted by other various ailments—if a bhikṣu reviles another bhikṣu [in this manner, he commits an offense].
To speak thus: "You were born into a low and base family," and so forth, up to "you are a blind, shaven-headed wretch.
This includes verbal abuse to the face, metaphorical abuse, and abuse by comparison to oneself. Regarding "verbal abuse to the face": it means saying, "You were born into a *caṇḍāla* family;

you were born into a family of scavengers," and so forth, up to "you are a blind, sightless, shaven-headed, crippled, lame, mute, deaf person, or one afflicted by various ailments. This refers to metaphorical abuse.
Regarding "abusive speech": [If a monk says], "You resemble one of the *caṇḍāla* caste," and so on, up to "you resemble one afflicted by manifold ailments";

and the other replies in self-comparison, "I am not of the *caṇḍāla* caste," and so on, up to "I am not one afflicted by manifold ailments"—if a bhikṣu speaks such words of disparagement regarding lineage as described above, and they are clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if they are not clearly understood, [it is a *dukkaṭa*].

It is a *duṣkṛta*. If, while speaking of the wholesome Dharma, one reviles by way of direct address, by way of metaphorical address, or by way of self-comparison—referring to those who speak of the wholesome Dharma as "forest-dwellers," "alms-seekers," "rag-robe wearers," and so forth, up to "those who practice meditation"—then:
"direct address" means saying, "You are a forest-dweller," and so on; "metaphorical address" means saying, "You resemble a forest-dweller," and so on; "self-comparison" means saying, "I..."
Whether it concerns non-araṇya sites and so forth, or whether it is clear or not clear, all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if one speaks for the sake of mutual benefit, for the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of the Vinaya, for the sake of instruction, for the sake of intimacy, or if speaking in jest.
[He] speaks. Or, due to the flow of conversation, he speaks inadvertently; or he speaks alone; or he speaks in a dream;
or he speaks erroneously. If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a pāyattika (3).
The group of six monks spread rumors back and forth, causing strife to arise where none existed among the Saṃgha and preventing existing strife from being extinguished;
therefore, this was prescribed.
As for "slanderous speech": a bhikṣu incites discord between bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or [śrāmaṇerīs].

Māṇavas, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, tīrthikas, heterodox śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—these twelve groups mutually engage in strife and discord, forming twelve propositions. As for "strife and discord," it means that one person says this to another:
"You are of the caṇḍāla caste; you are of the scavenger caste," and so on, down to "you are bald, blind, one-eyed, or lame."
If one speaks clearly to someone who is lame, deaf, or mute, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not speak clearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in the following cases: when breaking away from evil associates; when breaking away from evil companions;
when breaking away from those who employ means to destroy the Saṃgha; when breaking away from those who assist in destroying the Saṃgha; or when breaking away from two or three [such individuals].
When a person performs a *karmavācanā* (formal act), they violate it by performing it as something that is non-Dharma and non-Vinaya. This constitutes a violation of the formal procedure;
it is meaningless and without benefit, being an expedient intended to produce what is meaningless and disadvantageous.
If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika (4).
When Aniruddha arrived at the village of Anāthapiṇḍada, he took up lodging under the door of a courtesan’s house. There were several elders there.
He also came to seek lodging. As they sat close together, the courtesan took pity on the Venerable One and invited him inside the house.
The Venerable One sat cross-legged, fixing his mindfulness before him. At the first watch of the night, the courtesan came to solicit him as her husband, but he remained silent and gave no answer.
He did not even look at her. Later in the night, the courtesan again removed her clothes and stepped forward to seize him. The Venerable One leaped into the air;
the courtesan was filled with shame, put on her clothes, and repented. The Venerable One descended to his original place and preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

The courtesan attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, received the precepts of refuge, and became a laywoman (*upāsikā*). On the following day, the Venerable One accepted her offerings, preached the Dharma, and departed.

Upon returning to the monastery, he recounted the matter to the assembly of monks. Those of few desires criticized and disapproved of this, and they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
Regarding "filled with women": it refers to a woman who is conscious and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has not been severed.

Regarding "enclosed" (*śālā*): there are four types. First, that which is surrounded by walls and barriers with a roof above; second, that which is open at the front and lacks walls; third, that which, though roofed, is not completely enclosed;
and fourth, that which, though completely roofed, has openings. If a bhikṣu stays overnight first and a woman arrives later, or if a woman arrives first...
If he arrives later than the bhikṣu, or if both arrive at the same time, and he lies down on his side with his flank touching the ground, it is a pāyattika.

For every subsequent turn over onto his side, it is a pāyattika. If he sleeps in the same room as a female deva, a female nāga, a female asura, a female yakṣa, a female preta, or a female animal—whether she possesses the power of transformation or not—it is likewise [an offense].
It is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one sleeps in the same room as a eunuch or a person with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, during the day, a woman is standing while a bhikṣu is lying down, it is a *duṣkṛta* for the bhikṣu; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one was unaware that a woman was present, or if the room had a roof but lacked an enclosure.
Or it may be entirely covered with half-obstruction; or entirely covered with little obstruction; or entirely obstructed without being covered; or entirely obstructed with little covering;
or half-covered and half-obstructed, or little covered and little obstructed; or neither covered nor obstructed;
or else one may be in the open air, or walking or sitting within this room, or falling to the ground from a dizziness of the head, or lying down due to illness, or [overpowered] by a forceful person.
If one is seized, or if one is bound by others, or if there is danger to life or danger to pure conduct;
except in these cases, if a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received the full ordination for more than two nights, reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika (5).
The group of six monks were staying together with several elders in a lecture hall. One monk fell asleep with a distracted mind; as he turned over, his body was exposed.
Another monk covered him with a robe, but he turned over again and his body was once more exposed.
This happened three times. The elders criticized and mocked this, which led to the establishment of the rule. Later, because the monks [did not know] that Rāhula had not yet received...

Having been expelled for violating the major precepts, Rāhula went to stay overnight in the latrines. The World-Honored One, knowing this, went to the latrines, led him into his own room, and stayed there with him for one night.
He then permitted bhikṣus to stay together with those who have not received the full precepts for two nights.
If they reach a third night, before the dawn has appeared, they must depart. If they reach a fourth night, they must leave of their own accord.

If one causes such a person to leave—referring to those who have not received the full ordination (upasampadā), excluding bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—it constitutes an offense for all others who have not received the full ordination.
Whether it is an offense or not is as explained above. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu recites the scriptures together with a person who has not received the precepts, it is a pāyattika (6).
The group of six bhikṣus was reciting the Buddha’s sūtras together with several elders in a lecture hall;
their voices were so loud that they resembled the sound of Brahmins reciting their texts, disturbing those engaged in meditation. Therefore, this rule was established.
The meaning of phrases is not the meaning of phrases; the flavor of phrases is not the flavor of phrases; the meaning of syllables is not the meaning of syllables. As for the meaning of phrases:
reciting together with others, neither ahead nor behind, [one says]: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify one's own mind."

These are the teachings of the Buddhas. Regarding that which is not a "phrase-meaning" (*pada-artha*): it is as when one person says, "Commit no evil," and before he has finished, a second person repeats the preceding words, "Commit no evil.

Regarding that which is a "phrase-flavor" (*pada-rasa*): it is when two people recite together, neither ahead of nor behind the other, such as "The eye is impermanent," up to "The mind is impermanent.
Regarding that which is not a "phrase-flavor": it is as when one person has not yet uttered the word "eye."
