"Impermanent. The second person repeats the previous statement, "The eye is impermanent. Regarding the meaning of the syllables (*akṣara*):

when two people recite together, neither before nor after the other, saying "A-ra-pa-ca-na," this is the meaning of the syllables. Regarding that which is not the meaning of the syllables: it is like one person who has not yet uttered the word "A."
The second person repeats the preceding words: "Regarding 'Dharma': it is that which is spoken by the Buddha, spoken by the Śrāvakas, spoken by the Ṛṣis, or spoken by the devas.

If a bhikṣu recites it together with one who has not received the precepts—if he teaches it orally and it is clearly understood—it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

It is a *duṣkṛta*. If a son of a deva, a son of an asura, a son of a yakṣa, a son of a nāga, a son of a gandharva, or a transformed being among animals speaks once, twice, or thrice—whether clearly or unclearly—it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the teacher does not instruct, saying, "I have finished speaking; you may speak now," it is a *duṣkṛta* for the teacher. [This applies to] a bhikṣuṇī.
A *pāyattika* offense. For the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if [the recitation] has already been completed by me and you then recite;
or if one person finishes the recitation and another writes it down; or if two people are practicing together and recite in unison, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination—
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha— it is a pāyattika (7).
There were *pārivāsika* and *mānāttika* bhikṣus sitting in the lower row. The group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) spoke to the laypeople, saying, "These [bhikṣus] have committed such offenses;

therefore, they are punished by sitting in the lower row. Other bhikṣus who had committed transgressions, as well as other bhikṣus, felt ashamed and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. At that time, some bhikṣus did not know whether an act was grave or not grave.

[He committed] an offense; only later did he realize it was a grave one. He either performed a *pāyattika* confession or felt apprehensive. The Buddha said: "If one did not know [the gravity of the offense], there is no transgression.
Furthermore, Śāriputra was appointed by the Saṃgha to speak of Devadatta’s faults among the king’s retinue and the masses of people.
He felt apprehension. The Buddha said: "Being appointed by the Saṃgha, there is no transgression."

Regarding grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*): these are *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding the Saṃgha: [if one speaks] during a formal act (*karmavācanā*) or during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, if it is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Apart from grave offenses, if one speaks of other offenses to a person who has not yet received the six precepts, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one has committed a grave offense oneself and speaks of it to a person who has not yet received the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*].

[If one] speaks [of such matters], it is a *duṣkṛta*. With the exception of monks and nuns, if one speaks of the grave offenses (*pārājika*) of others to a person who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding a grave offense: if there is the perception that it is a grave offense, it is a *pāyattika*; if there is doubt as to whether it is a grave offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not a grave offense but there is the perception that it is a grave offense, or if there is doubt as to whether it is not a grave offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

There is no offense if she does not know [of the charge], if she has been appointed by the Saṃgha, if it is a grave offense but she perceives it as not being a grave offense, or if a layperson has already heard of this grave offense beforehand.
If a bhikṣu speaks to one who has not received the precepts concerning a superhuman state (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), saying, "I have seen this;
I have known this," and it is true, it is a pāyattika (8).
The causal conditions are the same as for the fourth precept on great falsehoods.

Regarding the "state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*): it refers to the various dharmas that constitute the path of transcendence. To claim for oneself: "I possess mindfulness of the body; I possess right reflection; I possess morality;
I possess desire [for the goal]; I possess non-negligence; I possess diligence; I possess concentration; I possess right concentration; I possess the Path; I possess cultivation."

"Wisdom. "There is seeing. "There is attainment. "There is fruition. If one speaks clearly to a person who has not yet received the full ordination (upasampadā) regarding these as being truly so, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if unclearly, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If by hand gesture, writing, making a sign of knowledge, or sending another person, and the meaning is clear, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if unclear, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If toward...
O Devaputra, if one ordains a son of an asura or similar being by means of the full precepts (mahā-śīla), it is declared a *duṣkṛta* for those who do not agree;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in cases as explained in the section on the four *pārājikas*.
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a pāyattika (9).
Kāḷudāyin, while at the house of an elder, whispered the Dharma into the ear of his son’s wife in the presence of her mother-in-law. Her mother-in-law...

Seeing that doubts arose, [the Buddha] established a rule. Thereafter, the bhikṣus did not dare to preach the Dharma to women; therefore, he opened the permission [to do so]. Regarding the "five phrases":

they are "form is non-self," and "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self. Regarding the "six phrases": they are "the eye is impermanent," and "the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent.
If there is a man present who understands what constitutes a coarse offense and what does not, one does not commit an offense.
The gravity [of the offense] is as explained above. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if one speaks five or six words; or if one speaks more than that in the presence of a man who understands;

or if, in the absence of a man who understands, one bestows the five precepts upon an upāsikā and explains the dharma of the five precepts, or bestows the eightfold fast-precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) and explains them.

Regarding the Dharma of the Eight Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa): if one explains the Eightfold Noble Path, the ten unwholesome paths of action, or answers the questions posed by women, and if they do not understand, one should explain them extensively.
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika (10).

When the group of six bhikṣus were constructing a lecture hall for the Buddha, they dug the earth around the hall themselves; the elder householders criticized them, saying, "They are severing the life-roots of other beings."
Therefore, a rule was established. Subsequently, people were further instructed to say: "Dig this; place that. The elder again offered criticism. The Buddha then formulated another precept:

Regarding "ground," it refers to ground already dug or ground not yet dug. If it is ground that has been dug and, after four months have passed, has been soaked by rain until it returns to its original state, then one may use a hoe, or a pickaxe, or a mallet, or a sickle, or a dagger, or even one's finger.
To scratch the ground with one's nails, to drive a stake into the ground, or to set fire upon the ground—all these constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is actual earth and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not instruct another by saying, "Look at this" or "Know this," it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one says, "Know this."
Observe this: if one drags bamboo or wood; if a fence falls to the ground and one rights it; if one turns over bricks or stones;
if one takes cow dung or earth from a collapsed bank; if one takes earth from a rat hole; if one removes earth from a walking path (*caṅkrama*); if one removes earth from within a house;
if one walks back and forth on a path; if one sweeps the ground; if one strikes the ground with a staff—provided one does not intentionally dig.
If a bhikṣu destroys the village of spirits or ghosts, it is a pāyattika (11).
This was established because there was once a wilderness bhikṣu who, while repairing a dwelling, cut down trees himself.
"Ghost" (*peta*) refers to non-human beings. "Village" (*gāma*) refers to all grasses and trees; because they are cut down and fall, it is called "destroying. There are five kinds of villages:
those propagated from roots, those propagated from stems, those produced from joints, those propagated from slips, and those propagated from seeds.

If one cuts them oneself while perceiving them as living, or instructs another to cut them; or if one roasts them oneself, or instructs another to roast them; or if one cooks them oneself, or instructs another to cook them—it is a *pāyattika* offense.

"Ānanda. If one harbors doubt, or perceives what is not living as living, or perceives what is living as not living, or harbors doubt regarding what is not living—whether one cuts it oneself or teaches another to cut it, roasts it oneself or teaches another to roast it, or cooks it oneself or teaches another to cook it—it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one drives a stake into a living tree, or applies fire to living grasses or trees, or cuts more than half of a living grass or tree, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation)."
To cut half-dry, half-living grass or wood is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not say, "Look at this," yet knows it is so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one says, "Look at this," and knows it is so;
or if one cuts withered, dry grass or wood; or if one drags timber or drags [materials] over living grass or wood.
[If one encounters] bamboo, upright fences, or screens; if there are bricks or stones; if there is cow dung; or if living plants and grasses cover the path, one should clear them away using a staff.
If there are tiles or stones propped against [the vegetation], one may break the plants and grasses.

If one is removing soil from a walking path (caṅkrama), or sweeping the ground of the walking area, and by mistake knocks down or breaks living plants and grasses, or again uses a staff to strike them—[these are offenses].
If one cuts down growing grass or trees by mistake, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If a bhikṣu speaks falsely to annoy another, it is a *pāyattika* (twelfth).
When the bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense and the other bhikṣus questioned him about it, he replied with an irrelevant matter, saying: "To whom were you speaking?"
"What matter did you speak of? What principle did you discuss? Were you speaking of the precepts? To whom were you speaking? Who committed the offense?
From what did the offense arise? I do not see any offense; why do you say that I am guilty? At that time, the bhikṣus criticized him and reported the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) against him for "speaking otherwise" (*anyavāda*). Thereupon, he established the precept, saying: "If..."
"A bhikṣu who uses evasive speech commits a pāyattika offense. This was later regarding Chanda, who, because he did not use evasive speech, caused distress to the Saṃgha:
when summoned he would not come; when not summoned he would come; when he should rise he would not rise; when he should not rise he would rise;
when he should speak he would not speak; when he should not speak he would speak. When the Buddha heard this, he further established this precept.
Regarding "irrelevant speech": if one utters irrelevant speech before the Sangha has made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one speaks in such a manner after the announcement has been made, it is entirely a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding "causing annoyance": if, before the announcement has been made, one calls someone to come and they do not come, and so forth.
In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). After the formal announcement (*jñapti*), if it is as described above, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If the elder summons [a person] and they do not come, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one does not understand the previous words because of a lack of attention or due to a discrepancy; or if it appears to be different speech; or if one intends to act otherwise.

It is the Dharma, not the Vinaya; it is a formal act (kamma) that lacks benefit. For example, if one eats in a single sitting and does not perform the ritual for leftover food (atireka-bhojana-vidhi), yet eats [further], except in cases such as illness or even life-threatening danger, or danger to the holy life (brahmacariya), it constitutes an offense of "annoyance and provocation."
If a bhikṣu reviles [another], it is a pāyattika (thirteen).

When Trapusa-māra knew of the distribution of the Saṃgha’s bedding and the assignment of meals for the Saṃgha, Cīrṇī spoke of him as being possessed of affection, hatred, fear, and delusion in a place where she could see him but not hear him;
therefore, this was established. Later, he again heard of it where he could not see her but could hear her.
Regarding the "points of view" (*diṭṭhi-ṭhāna*), it refers to those who possess craving and so forth; thus, he further established the precept:

if one reviles another face-to-face, or if one scolds them behind their back, it is a *pāyattika* offense if the meaning is clearly understood, and a *dukkaṭa* offense if it is not clearly understood.
If a senior monk (*upādhyāya*) instructs someone to revile or scold, and that person carries out the instruction by reviling or scolding, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the bhikṣu.
For a nun, it is a *niḥpāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if the person actually possesses love, hatred, fear, or delusion, and speaks thus to cause them to confess according to the Dharma out of fear that they might later feel regret; or if it was spoken in jest, or even if it was spoken by mistake.
If a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, a wooden bed, bedding, a sitting mat, or a rug for spreading on open ground, and having instructed someone else to spread it,
departs without himself putting it away or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika (14).

A householder was providing a meal for the Saṃgha. The group of seventeen took the monks' sitting cloths and spread them out on the open ground; they then paced back and forth, waiting for the time of the meal to arrive.
When the time had come, they did not gather them up and went directly to the meal. Consequently, the monks' sitting cloths were covered with wind-blown dust and dirt.
Dust accumulates; insects and birds peck at it, making it filthy and impure.
Therefore, the following regulations were established: there are five types of rope beds—those with curved legs, straight legs, bent legs, those with steps, and those without legs.
Wooden beds are likewise. As for bedding, it may be used for sitting or for lying down. A cushion is used for sitting. If a bhikṣu...

If one has spread out the Sangha’s rope beds, wooden beds, bedding, or sitting mats on an open space, or has had someone else spread them out, then upon departing—if there are resident bhikṣus there, or a *māmātika* (steward), or a supervisor—one should say to them:
"I now entrust these to you; you should guard and look after them. If there is no one at all, one should fold them up and store them in a concealed place.

One should depart. If there is no secluded place, and one knows for certain that this spot will not be damaged and will remain secure, one should cover the fine [seat] with the coarse [cloth] and depart. If one can return immediately, one should go.

If the rain falls heavily but one can return quickly without damaging the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one should go. If it rains moderately and one can travel and return within that time, one should go.
One may go. If there is little rain and little travel, or if one can return, one should go. That bhikṣu should depart by employing such expedients in due order.
If he goes without employing such expedients, at the moment he first steps out the door, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is outside the door and one foot is inside the door, and though he intends to go he does not go, but returns—[the offense is as follows].
[If one] regrets [the offense], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. If two people sit together on one bed, the junior person should fold [the bedding] and leave.
If the junior person thinks the senior person should fold it, but the senior person does not, the junior person commits a *pāyattika* offense;
furthermore, because it was improper conduct, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the senior person thinks the junior person should fold it, but the junior person does not...
If [the bedding] has not been gathered up, it is an *upāli* offense for the senior monk. If two people neither go first nor last and both fail to gather it up, both commit an *upāli* offense.
If there is an empty rope bed, wooden bed, squatting stool, or ordinary bed; or a bathing stool; or a mat spread on the ground; or the outer and inner linings of bedding;
or if one takes a rope, cord, wool, or hemp and places them in the open air, and then departs without gathering them up, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one spreads out a monastic bedding in an open space and enters a room to sit in meditation without first putting it away, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;

for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is constrained by force, or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If a bhikṣu, having spread bedding belonging to the Saṃgha within a monastery cell— whether spreading it himself or instructing another to do so—
and then sitting or lying upon it, fails to remove it himself or instruct another to remove it when departing, it is a pāyattika (fifteen).
A visiting bhikṣu spoke to a resident bhikṣu, saying, "I shall spread bedding in an outlying monk's cell and stay there.
Later, without informing the resident, he departed. The monastic bedding became moldy and ruined; it was gnawed by insects and its color faded.
Because the resident did not see the visiting bhikṣu, he went to the cell to inspect it. Having seen this state of affairs, he informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.

When that bhikṣu spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha within the monastic quarters—whether spreading it himself or instructing another to do so—and whether sitting or lying down, upon departing he should say to any resident bhikṣu, monastery attendant, or *māmaka*:
"Please take charge of this and store it securely. If there is no one to whom it can be entrusted and he does not fear its loss or damage, he should move the bed.
He should leave the wall. He should raise the legs of the bed high, place pillows, mattresses, and bedding inside, and cover them with other bedding before departing.
If he fears they might be damaged, he should take the pillows, mattresses, and bedding and place them on a clothing rack, then stand the bed upright and depart.
If he departs without doing so, and his feet are such that one foot is outside the boundary and one foot is inside, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one is outside [the boundary], feels regret, yet does not return; or if one has agreed to go but does not go—these are all *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one returns immediately and stays outside the boundary for two nights, and on the third night, before the dawn light has appeared, one goes to one's own quarters; [there is no offense].
If one sends a messenger to tell the *māmāte* or the official in charge, "You must take charge of and protect this object," yet they do not act accordingly, it is a *pāyattika* offense for the monk;
for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if the dwelling collapses, or in cases such as threats to life, or if it is due to water.
There are obstacles on the road, such as thieves, wild beasts, rising waters, or being detained. One is unable to go there oneself and does not send word by messenger.
If a bhikṣu, knowing the dwelling place of a previously resident bhikṣu, arrives later and forcibly spreads out bedding in the interim to stay overnight, thinking:
"If he finds it cramped, he will naturally avoid me and leave," acting with such a motive and no other—this constitutes [an offense].
Regarding the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*): This is the sixteenth *pāyattika*.
When the group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling to the village of Anāthapiṇḍada, the group of seventeen said to the group of six, "You are our senior (*sthavira*);
you should first seek out a dwelling place. The group of six replied, "You all go ahead yourselves; as for me—"
They did not seek a place to stay. At that time, the group of seventeen immediately sought a place to stay for the night. The group of six then went to them and said, "You must rise;

you shall stay according to the order of seniority. The group of seventeen would not agree, so the group of six forcibly spread out bedding and took up residence there. Therefore, this rule was established.
It is not an offense if one is unaware, as previously explained. Regarding "in between": this refers to the head-side, the foot-side, or the side of the bed.
Regarding "bedding": it includes mats of grass, mats of leaves, or even bedding spread directly upon the ground.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already obtained a place to stay, later comes and forcibly spreads his bedding in the space between them to dwell there, and turns over onto his side against him—[this constitutes an offense].
Lying down on a bed is a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣu; it is a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand; or if [the person] has already spoken and then stops; or if they previously opened the door; or if it is spacious and does not cause obstruction;
or if a relative or acquaintance instructs them, saying, "Simply spread [your bedding] within this space; I myself will speak to the owner. Or...
If one falls to the ground, or rolls over while ill, or falls upon another; or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

or if a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, does not wish for him to stay in the monastery quarters, and either drags him out himself or instructs another to drag him out—this is a *pāyattika* (seventeenth).
This was also established as a rule due to the incidents involving the group of six and the group of seventeen.
Depending on the number of people led out and the number of times one exits the door, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one carries another's belongings out, or throws objects outside the door, or shuts others out by keeping them outside the door, these are all *dukkaṭa* offenses.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if one has no mind of malice and departs in due order;
or if, after staying together for two nights, at the third night, one sends away a person who has not received the precepts;
or if that person has broken the precepts, broken their view, or broken their decorum; or if they have been formally accused by another, or expelled, or are subject to such measures.
Expulsion. For these reasons, there is danger to life and danger to the holy life; therefore, driving someone away is not an offense.
If a bhikṣu sits or lies down on a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs, whether in a room or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, it is a pāyattika (eighteen).
There was a bhikṣu staying atop a multi-storied building who sat on a stool with removable legs. As he sat, he was not composed;
the legs of the stool came loose and struck a bhikṣu who was staying below, causing him bodily injury and drawing blood. Therefore, this rule was established.
"Room" refers to either a communal monastic room or a private room. "Multi-storied building" refers to one where the head of a standing person does not reach the upper level.

"Bed with removable legs" refers to one whose legs extend below the floorboards. If a bhikṣu, while on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down on such a bed with removable legs, and his side touches the bed as he turns over, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
This applies even if he is on a single-person seat or a single-plank bed used for bathing.
If one sits or lies down on a bed, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if one sits with legs tucked up, legs extended straight, legs bent, or without legs; or if it is a rope bed; or if the supports of the bed are large;
or if it is a bed with removable legs fitted with narrow spindles; or if there is a wooden floor covering above that upper story.
If one covers [the bowl] with a wooden flower-patterned cover; or if one uses a thick, heavy cover; or if one sits on the bowl upside down;

or if one sits on the bowl with its legs removed—if a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, washes mud himself, or pours it over grass, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika (nineteen).

Chanda built a large house using mud mixed with water containing living organisms. Because he instructed others to mix it in this way, the Elder [Mahākāśyapa] censured him, and thus the rule was established:
if one knows that water contains living organisms and yet throws grass or soil into it, it is a *pāyattika* offense. This excludes the case of [using] water itself.
If one uses worm-infested buttermilk, clear buttermilk, vinegar, or malt-fermented gruel to pour over mud or grass, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places soil or grass into clear buttermilk that contains worms, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.

If one soaks [them] in vinegar or in a gruel of fermented barley, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are insects in water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*.

If there are insects in water but one suspects it, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are no insects in water but one perceives them as such, or if there are no insects in water but one suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense if one does not know there are insects and perceives them as being non-existent;
or if the insects are large and one touches the water with the hand to make them leave; or if one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground;
or if one instructs another person to sprinkle it.
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, including its doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, he must direct that the roofing and thatching be limited to two or three layers.
If it exceeds this, it is a pāyattika (offense of expiation). (20)
Candana constructed a large room; after covering it once, there was still excess straw, so he covered it again, and did so a third time without stopping. The roof then collapsed and broke.
Because the lay devotees expressed their disapproval and reproached him, [the Buddha] established this rule.

Regarding "large-scale construction": it involves using many materials and various ornaments, such as carvings, engravings, and painted decorations. There are two types of roofing: longitudinal roofing and transverse roofing.
If a bhikṣu directs the work for two sections of roofing and then departs while the third section has not yet been completed, he must go to a place where he is neither seen nor heard.
If he does not depart, and the third section is completed, it is a pāyattika offense. If...

If one leaves the place where one has heard [the Dharma] to go to the place where one sees it, or leaves the place where one sees it to go to the place where one has heard it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for a male lay follower (*upāsaka*), a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī, and a *duṣkṛta* offense for the other three assemblies.

There is no offense if the path by water or land is cut off, or if there are robbers, wild beasts, rising waters, imprisonment, danger to life, or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); in such cases, not going and thus neither seeing nor hearing [the Dharma] is not an offense.
[The Twenty-first Pāyattika]: "If a bhikṣu instructs and admonishes bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
Mahāprajāpatī requested the Buddha to permit the bhikṣus to instruct, admonish, and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha then commanded Ānanda.

In accordance with the sequence, an elder was dispatched to go [and instruct]. However, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) went themselves to teach and admonish, not expounding the True Dharma, but speaking only of all worldly treatises and the like.
Mahāprajāpatī informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established the rule that persons must be appointed from within the Saṃgha to instruct the nuns.

After the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) had been performed, the group of six monks immediately went outside the boundary and appointed one another [as instructors].

Mahāprajāpatī once again addressed the Buddha. The Buddha established the rule that one must accomplish ten qualities before being permitted to instruct nuns; thus the precepts were fully established.

He is learned; he has recited the precepts of both divisions and possesses decisive judgment free from doubt; he is skilled at preaching the Dharma; he is of noble birth and has left the household life;
his appearance is upright and handsome, such that the community of nuns rejoices upon seeing him; he is capable of preaching the Dharma to the nuns and encouraging them to rejoice;
he did not don the religious robes for the sake of becoming a monk under the Buddha and commit a grave offense; and he is twenty years of age or older.
If she has passed twenty years [of age], such a person may be granted the instruction and precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*. Thus this rule was established.

"The Saṃgha" refers to those who recite the *Prātimokṣa* together and perform the *karmavācanā* together. "Appointed" means one appointed from within the Saṃgha by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

"Instructor" refers to the eight rules that must not be transgressed; the first is: when a *bhikṣuṇī* of one hundred *varṣas* sees a *bhikṣu* who has been ordained for only one summer, [she must show him respect].
One should rise to meet them, inquire after their well-being, prostrate, and invite them to sit. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised;

for as long as one lives, it must not be transgressed. Second, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor must she slander him by saying that he has broken his precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment (the remainder is as stated previously; the same applies hereafter). Third, a bhikṣuṇī...
One must not expose the offenses of a bhikṣu by saying, "What you have done is such," or "What you have done is not so. One must not make a self-accusation.
One must not obstruct another from seeking out their own offense. One must not obstruct another from reciting the precepts or performing the *pravāraṇā*.
A bhikṣuṇī may not speak of the faults of a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu may speak of the faults of a bhikṣuṇī. Fourth, one who has already trained in the training rules.
1. A *śikṣamāṇā* must seek to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the community of monks. 2.
If a bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (*guru-dharma*), she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both communities (*ubhayasaṃgha*). 3.
A bhikṣuṇī must, every half-month, request from the Saṃgha a person who will provide her with instruction. 4. A bhikṣuṇī must not remain in a place where there is no...

When a bhikṣu is staying for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), there are eight [rules]. When a bhikṣuṇī has completed her summer retreat, she must go before the community of monks (*saṃgha*) and request three matters:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected, and the invitation to admonition (*pravāraṇā*). At the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the elder (*sthavira*) should ask:
"Which person has the bhikṣuṇīs sent? If there is one, he should immediately rise and announce: "The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony."

She should prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and request instruction and exhortation (*anuśāsanī*). The elder (*sthavira*) should further ask: "Who shall provide the instruction and exhortation?
If there is a bhikṣuṇī [who is qualified], she should be appointed. If there are many who could provide the instruction and exhortation, he should send a messenger to tell the bhikṣuṇī:
"There are many here who can provide instruction and exhortation; whom have you requested? If that bhikṣuṇī says, "I have requested so-and-so," [he should appoint her].
If a person further replies, "I shall follow the Sangha's instructions," the Sangha should appoint someone in the regular order of those who instruct nuns.
The bhikṣu-saṃgha should arrive at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇīs should also go out to meet them at the appointed time.
If they do not arrive at the appointed time, or if they do arrive but do not go out to meet them, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. If they hear that the instructor is coming...
A bhikṣuṇī should go out half a yojana to welcome [the visiting bhikṣus], provide for their needs, prepare bathing requisites, and prepare various drinks and meals.

If she does not make such provisions, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If she goes to preach the eight rules that must not be transgressed (*aṣṭau dharmā avinipātayitavyāḥ*) when the Saṃgha has not dispatched her, or on a day other than the designated teaching day, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the Saṃgha has not...
If one goes to deliver a Dharma talk [to them], it is a *pāyattika*. If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha is ill, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health.
If the Saṃgha is not in harmony or if the assembly is incomplete, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health.
If the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha is ill, not in harmony, or incomplete, one should likewise send someone to pay respects and inquire after the health of the Bhikṣus.
Monks, if one does not do so, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a *pāyattika* (22).
Nanda was fond of melodious voices. While preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, his listeners were so delighted by the sound that it continued until sunset.

When the bhikṣuṇīs left Jetavana and entered the city, the city gates were already closed. They consequently took up residence for the night within the moat surrounding the city wall. At dawn, when the gates opened, they entered the city ahead of him.
The elders slandered him, claiming he had stayed overnight with the bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.
Except when giving instruction. If one receives, recites, or inquires about the sūtras, or engages in other such matters until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This does not apply to bhikṣuṇīs. If one recites the sūtras or performs similar acts for other women until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is sunset and one perceives it as sunset, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is doubt regarding sunset, or if it is sunset but one does not perceive it as such, [it is likewise].
If it is not evening, yet one perceives it as evening, or if there is doubt that it is not evening, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one is preaching the Dharma at a ferry crossing and a bhikṣuṇī comes to listen; or if traveling with merchants and preaching the Dharma during the night;
or if preaching the Dharma within a bhikṣuṇī monastery; or if on the day of the *poṣadha*, one has come to invite a teacher and happens to encounter a preaching of the Dharma.
Listen.
If a bhikṣu speaks to other bhikṣus in this way: "A bhikṣu teaches bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika (twenty-three).
When the nuns heard that the instructor was coming, they went out half a yojana to welcome her, settled her in a dwelling, and provided food, drink, bedding, seats, and bathing facilities.
At that time, the group of six [monks] who had not been appointed felt jealousy in their hearts and spoke as follows; therefore, this rule was established.
If it is finished [by the accused], it is a *pāyattika*; if not finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if the matter is indeed so; or if spoken in jest, in private, in a dream, or by mistake.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for trade, it is a pāyattika (24).
In Śrāvastī, there was a certain bhikṣu who begged for alms and was fully endowed with dignified deportment. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī saw him and immediately conceived a wholesome mind;
she repeatedly invited the bhikṣu [to accept robes], but the bhikṣu did not accept them. On another occasion, when the Saṃgha was distributing clothing and requisites, this bhikṣu...
The Bhikṣu Ānanda took his robe and went out through the gate of Jetavana. Seeing this nun approaching, he immediately gave it to her, intending that she would not accept it;
however, the nun accepted it at once. Because the Bhikṣu repeatedly expressed his disapproval and reproach to others regarding this matter, [the Buddha] established this rule.
Regarding trade: exchanging clothing for clothing, or exchanging clothing for non-clothing, and so forth. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if [the items] are given to a stūpa, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika (offense no. 25).
Kālodāyin made a robe for a certain bhikṣuṇī, depicting the act of sexual intercourse between a man and a woman; he folded it up and gave it to her, saying:
"You must not open it and look at it recklessly, nor show it to others. When the time comes for the white [robes], you shall wear it."
This occurred when [a monk] walked behind a nun. The nun followed his instructions. A layperson saw this and mocked them; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule:
for every portion cut with a knife, it is a *pāyattika*; for every stitch or needle, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one opens it to look at it, pulls it, drags it, irons it, strokes it with the hand, or grasps the corners to pull it into shape and smooths out the borders and seams, [each such act constitutes an offense].
If one threads the needle, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For the other four assemblies, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one does so for the sake of the Saṃgha, or for the sake of a stūpa, or if one borrows [the robe], wears it, washes, dyes, or repairs it, and then returns it to the owner.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika (26).
Kāḷudāyin went to the dwelling of Thullanandā and sat together with her in one place outside the gate; because householders criticized and disparaged this, the rule was established.
If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one stands still, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion; or if there is a wise person present;
or if while walking he suddenly falls to the ground; or if he falls while ill; or if he is overcome by force; or if he is imprisoned; or if his life...
It is difficult. It is difficult to practice the holy life.
If a bhikṣu agrees with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together along the same road from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The "appropriate times" are: when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or dread; these are called the appropriate times.
(27) The group of six monks and the group of six nuns were traveling through the human settlements. Because householders complained about this, [the Buddha] established a rule.

Consequently, when they met on the road, those who encountered them were fearful and cautious, not daring to travel together with them. The Buddha said: "If there was no prior appointment, there is no offense. Furthermore, the assembly...
When monks and nuns traveled from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī, they were unable to travel together;
because the nuns remained behind and were plundered by bandits, the rule was further relaxed for this exceptional circumstance.

"Agreed upon" (*saṃvidhāna*) means: "We shall go together to such-and-such a village, such-and-such a city, or such-and-such a country. "The path" (*mārga*) refers to the designated route between villages.

If one makes an agreement with a nun to travel, then for every portion of the path up to the boundary of a village—according to the number of people and the number of boundaries involved—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each. If it is not a village but an open space, [the offense applies] even up to ten *krośas*.
A *pāyattika* offense. If it is less than one village or less than ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If there are many villages between them but they travel within the same boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one employs the means to go, having made an appointment and being adorned [for the journey], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is constrained by force, if one is bound, or if there is danger to life or to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
It is difficult [to avoid]. If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to board the same boat, whether going upstream or downstream—
except when crossing directly across— a pāyattika offense (twenty-eight).
The causal conditions are the same as before. Regarding "crossing directly": there were many bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who wished to cross the Gaṅgā River. The bhikṣuṇīs were at the rear;
a heavy rain caused the water to rise, and by the time the boat had not yet returned, the sun had already set. Because they were being plundered by bandits, [the gate] was opened.
If one agrees to travel together on the same boat, whether going upstream or downstream, and enters the boat, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is already on the boat and one makes the effort to enter but does not do so, or if one agrees to adorn oneself [for the journey], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for all parties involved.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if there was no prior agreement, or if one simply crosses to the opposite shore and enters the boat [without such intent].
If a boatman loses his way while traveling upstream or downstream, or if he is held by force and bound, such that there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya);
or if a bhikṣu knowingly eats food obtained through the cause and condition of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise or exhortation— except for what was previously offered by a donor.
If one does so intentionally, it is a *pāyattika* offense (29).
In Śrāvastī, there was a householder who invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana for a meal.
Thullanandā slandered them as being of low birth, while praising Devadatta and his associates as "dragons among dragons. At that time, Śāriputra and...

They arrived together and immediately announced, "The Dragon among Dragons has arrived. The householder rebuked them. After the two had finished eating, they returned and informed the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the Buddha rebuked Devadatta’s faction and established a precept. Subsequently, the bhikṣus did not know whether there was encouragement to solicit alms or not.
The Buddha said, "If you do not know, there is no offense. Furthermore, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great elder...
He was on intimate terms with Upatiṣya. When Upatiṣya first arrived, he provided offerings to the Saṃgha.

Later, when Upatiṣya returned to the city, a nun went to inform the householder, who subsequently prepared a vegetarian feast. Fearing that he might violate this precept by accepting food, Upatiṣya [refused it];
therefore, [the Buddha] further opened the allowance for a donor who has a prior intention.

Those who teach and transform others: those dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*), those who beg for food (*piṇḍapātika*), those who wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*), those who do not eat after the prescribed time for leftovers has passed, those who eat in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), those who eat from a single alms-bowl (*khalupaścādbhaktika*), those who sit in cemeteries (*śmāśānika*), those who sit in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), those who sit beneath trees (*vṛkṣamūlika*), those who remain seated constantly (*naiṣadyika*), and those who sit wherever they happen to be (*yathāsaṃstarika*).
Carrying the three robes; praising a Dharma teacher who is learned in the sūtras; upholding the Vinaya; and practicing meditation. Regarding food: one may receive food from dawn until midday.
If that bhikṣu knows that the food was obtained through the instruction of a bhikṣuṇī and eats it, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika*.

If he obtains other items such as undergarments, lamp oil, or oil for anointing the feet, it is all a *dukkaṭa*. This applies to actual instruction, as well as the perception of instruction. *Pāyattika*.

If one is doubtful about whether there has been instruction, yet perceives that there was no instruction, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one is doubtful about whether there was no instruction, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one instructs while perceiving that one is not instructing;
or if the nun acts on her own initiative; or if a donor directs the nun to manage the matter; or if one does not intentionally instruct but gives almsfood [to her].
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same road, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika (thirty).
There was a woman from Vaiśālī who had married a man from Śrāvastī; having a dispute with her mother-in-law, she returned to her native country.
At that time, Ānanda was traveling from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī, and that woman wished to accompany him. The Venerable One—

He granted it. The husband pursued him and struck the Venerable One until he was nearly dead. The Venerable One stepped off the path and sat cross-legged in a quiet place, entering the *tejo-dhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi).
The husband waited for him to emerge from meditative concentration, whereupon he prostrated and repented. The Venerable One then preached the Dharma to him and departed.
Upon returning, he informed the community of monks and reported the matter to the Buddha, who established a precept so that such an offense would not occur again. This is the causal origin.
As before. The gravity of the offense is as before. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a monk, at a place where a single meal is offered, being free from illness, should eat only one meal; if he receives more than that, it is a *pāyattika* (thirty-one).
In the kingdom of Kosala, there was an unestablished village where a householder built a dwelling for the bhikṣus.

It was established that they should stay and accept only one meal a day. However, the group of six bhikṣus went there and obtained excellent food and drink; they stayed for a second night and continued to eat repeatedly until this became a frequent occurrence.
Because the householder criticized and resented this, [the Buddha] established the rule. Later, Śāriputra fell ill at that place and feared...
He violated the precepts. As he went along supporting himself while ill, his condition worsened;

therefore, he further added the words "I am not ill. Regarding the "dwelling place," it means staying there for one night. Regarding "food," it refers to even the time of eating. Regarding the "sick person," it refers to one whose illness worsens upon leaving that village.
If one who is not ill accepts food beyond what is permitted, it is a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow. This applies to receiving other garments for the body as well.
Lighting oil lamps or applying oil to the feet constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for all; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if laypeople invite a venerable one to stay, saying, "We shall provide food;
we have prepared this lodging and supplied food and drink for the sake of the śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas."
"One may not [refuse] a Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas; one should likewise accept from others as well.
If a donor invites one to a meal in succession—whether it be men or women, younger brothers or sisters—and one accepts food from this person today and food from that person tomorrow;
or if there is a sudden flood of water, or even difficulties regarding the holy life (brahmacarya) and so forth."
If a bhikṣu eats in succession (at another meal), except at the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense. The remaining times are: when one is ill, and when robes are being given.
These are called the remaining times. (32)
There was a Śramaṇa brāhmaṇa who loaded five hundred carts with food and drink, following the Buddha in hopes of finding an opportunity to provide offerings, but he could find no such chance.

The Buddha permitted the making of cakes and gruel as offerings for the Saṃgha. When the lay devotees heard that the Buddha had permitted the Saṃgha to eat gruel and cakes, they were all greatly rejoiced.
There was a minister of little faith who saw that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had received great offerings.

With the intention that it was a field of merit for nourishing life, he prepared rich and delicious food and invited the monks. However, the monks first ate thick gruel and were unable to eat much more;
the minister resented this. Furthermore, in Rājagṛha, there was a teacher with little faith whose situation was likewise.
The Buddha then established a precept: henceforth, at any place where sick bhikṣus are invited to eat, there must be food appropriate for their illness as well as medicine.

If there is food or medicine prescribed for a specific illness, and a monk fears or hesitates to eat it, the Buddha permitted a sick bhikṣu to take such food by means of a transfer (paṭiggaha-parivattanā).

Furthermore, when one householder had invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and another householder also invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, providing them with food and robes, the bhikṣus were fearful and hesitant and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted taking food by means of a transfer at the time of receiving robes. As for "thick gruel": [it is as follows].
If one draws a line with grass and it does not join [the other lines], one must not eat.

Regarding "eating by passing around," this refers to invitations. There are two kinds of invitations: the invitation in the order of the Sangha and the individual invitation. As for "eating": [it refers to eating after having been invited].
Regarding rice, parched grain, dry cakes, fish, or meat: if a sick person is unable to eat a sufficient amount of fine food while remaining seated for one sitting, [they may take more].
Regarding the gift of robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if there is no *kaṭhina* robe in effect, it is for one month; if there is a *kaṭhina* robe in effect, it is for five months.
Furthermore, regarding the giving of food or robes at other times, or if one receives many invitations on a single day, one should personally accept one invitation and [decline the rest].
"this should be given to another person. When giving in this manner, [the donor says], "Venerable sir, I should go there; I now give this to you.

If a bhikṣu does not relinquish a previous invitation and accepts a subsequent meal invitation, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense. This applies unless he relinquishes the subsequent invitation.
If one accepts a prior invitation to eat, for every swallow there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the other four assemblies, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if what is offered is not food, or if the food is insufficient, or if there was no invitation to eat, or if one obtains food after having already finished eating.

Or if there is food both before and after [the meal] at one location, and a bhikṣu eats separately from the community except during the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense. The remaining times are: when one is ill, when making robes, or when traveling on a journey.
When giving robes; when traveling on a journey; when riding in a boat; when a great assembly has gathered; and when śramaṇas are being given food—these are the proper times (33).
Devadatta’s ill repute spread abroad and his gains and offerings were cut off. Because he was begging for alms from house to house together with five bhikṣus, [the Buddha] established this rule.

Regarding "eating in a separate group": if there are four people, or more than four, except in the case of those who are ill—even down to those with a limp in their heels—[this constitutes a separate group].

Regarding the time for robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, it is one month if there is no *kaṭhina* robe, and five months if there is a *kaṭhina* robe, until even a single "horse-tooth" stitch has been made upon the robe. The time for the bestowal of robes is as explained above. Regarding those on a journey:
Down to half a yojana, there are those who come within and those who go out; it is the same for those traveling by boat. Regarding the gathering of the great assembly:

when four people have sufficient food, the addition of one person becomes a source of trouble; likewise, whether there be five, ten, or even a hundred, the addition of one person becomes a source of trouble.
As for the almsgiving of food to śramaṇas: this refers to those outside the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas—namely, other renunciants.
...as well as those who have gone forth from among the non-Buddhists. If a bhikṣu has no reason for taking food separately from the community, he should immediately arise and announce:
"I have no reason for this separate meal; I wish to go out to seek the Buddha. The Buddha said: "I permit you to go out.
If others likewise have no reason, they are also permitted to go out. If there are two or three people [who do so], it is according to their number.
When the meal is finished—if there are four monks, or more than four—they should divide into two groups and enter the dining hall alternately.
If there is a reason for a separate group to eat and they wish to enter, they must immediately rise and announce their presence; they shall then enter according to the order of seniority.
If a monk eats in a separate group without such a reason, it is an *pāyattika* offense for every swallow. If there is a valid reason but he fails to announce it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson where they invite the bhikṣu to receive cakes, parched flour, or rice;
and if the bhikṣu desires these: [For] a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies [of the Saṃgha], it is a duṣkṛta. If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson... [and so forth].
One should accept two or three bowls. Upon returning to the monastery, one should share them with the other bhikṣus as food.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls and, upon returning to the monastery, does not share them with the other bhikṣus as food, it is a pāyattika (thirty-four).
There was a married woman who had returned to her parents' home and offered food to the bhikṣus. Her husband summoned her to return;
while the bhikṣus were taking all the food she had prepared and before she could return, her husband had already taken another wife.
Furthermore, there was a caravan of merchants who halted for the night. A certain bhikṣu obtained food from a merchant who had faith and devotion;

he then passed the word along to other bhikṣus, requesting that they beg until the food was exhausted. Consequently, those [merchants] went out to purchase provisions and departed before the others could catch up.
Because they were subsequently plundered by bandits on the road, the rule was established.
Regarding the household of white-robed laypeople: there are men and women there. If a bhikṣu goes to such a layperson’s house and is invited to eat cakes, parched grain flour, or rice, he should ask:
"Is this food for a woman returning home, or is it provisions for merchants on a journey?

If they say, "It is for a woman returning home" or "It is provisions for merchants on a journey," he should immediately finish eating and depart, returning to the saṃghārāma to inform [the community].
"O bhikṣus, if there is food from a family where a woman has returned home, or provisions for merchants on a journey, and you wish to eat it, you should leave after having eaten.

If you wish to take some back, you may take two or three bowls; if you take one bowl back, you should share it with the other bhikṣus and say to them: 'In such-and-such a family, there is food from a woman who has returned home.'"
Regarding the provisions for merchants on the road: if one arrives at such a household, one may eat there. If one intends to take food back, one should take two bowls;
I have already taken one bowl back. If one takes two bowls back, one should share them. Furthermore, he said to the bhikṣus:
"In such-and-such a household there is food from a woman returning home, as well as provisions for merchants on the road. If one arrives at that household..."
Regarding this: if one wishes to take food back from there, one should take only one bowl.
If I have already taken two bowls back, or if I am taking all three bowls back, one should say: "You may eat there; do not take any more back. I have now already brought three bowls.
If a bhikṣu, being without illness, goes out through that gate, it is a pāyattika offense. If [he has] one foot [outside...]
If one places one foot inside the gate and one foot outside the gate, intending to depart by means of a stratagem but then remains stationary, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If one takes food without asking whether it is the meal for a woman returning home or provisions for a merchant on a journey, or if one carries it back and eats it alone without sharing it with other bhikṣus, or if one does not inform the other bhikṣus, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa* offense. [The same applies for] a bhikṣuṇī.
A *pāyattika* offense. For the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if he himself brings it to the monastery, or if he himself brings it to the nunnery.
If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal or having accepted an invitation, eats food without performing the ritual for leftover food (*atiriktapiṇḍapāta*),
it is a pāyattika (thirty-fifth).
The World-Honored One praised the practice of eating a single meal. When the bhikṣus followed this precept, their physical complexions became withered and emaciated.
The Buddha then permitted them to eat while remaining seated until they were fully satiated; furthermore, he allowed them to eat rice, parched grain flour, and other such foods until satisfied.

He also permitted sick bhikṣus to eat repeatedly. Because of the discarded leftovers, various birds began to clamor and compete for them. Subsequently, the Buddha permitted those who attend to the sick to eat as needed.
One may eat leftover food, as well as food that has been received and for which the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of "making it leftover") has been performed.
Furthermore, it is permitted for monks to bring food back from that place and eat it after performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa*.
One should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* by saying: "Venerable sir, I have finished my meal; know this, look at this—this is the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍa*. He should then take it.
Having eaten a small amount, he said, "I have stopped; you take this and eat it. This is called the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule of leftover food).
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who was gluttonous; he did not know whether he had eaten enough or not, nor did he know what constituted leftover food or what did not.
Because one obtains [food] and eats it, this rule is established.

There are five factors that constitute having finished eating (*paryāpta-bhakta*): knowing it is rice; knowing it has been brought; knowing the prohibition; knowing the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*); and knowing the relinquishing of the formal deportment.

Once one has finished eating and relinquished the formal deportment, if one obtains food and eats it without performing the *kṛtāvaśeṣa-dharma* (the ritual for leftover food), for every swallow there is an offense of transgression (*pātayantika*).
Pāyattika. There are five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid food): namely, roots as food, stalks as food, leaves as food, flowers as food, and fruits as food;
as well as oil, sesame, black rock-honey, and finely ground powders as food.

If a bhikṣu has finished his meal and, without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), obtains and eats such things, he commits a pāyattika offense for every swallow. If a bhikṣu has finished his meal...

If one performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food) for another, the *khalupaścādbhakti* is not established; it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one knows that another has already finished eating and yet performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* toward them;
or if one performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* while holding the food with one's own hand; or if one performs it by placing the food on the ground;

or if one causes a *kalpika-puruṣa* (a pure person) to hold the food while performing it; or if one performs it in front of a *kalpika-puruṣa*; or if one uses inferior food—[in these cases, the ritual is not established].

If one covers good food with [other food] while preparing it, or if one takes away all of another's *atiritta* (leftover food) after it has been offered according to the ritual, in both cases the *atiritta-vidhi* is not established;

this is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has finished eating and perceives that one has finished eating, it is a *pāyattika*; if one has finished eating but suspects whether one has finished eating, and there is actually not enough food to constitute a full meal, [the offense is as follows].

If one has the perception that the meal is sufficient, yet suspects it is insufficient, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For the other four assemblies, it is also a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if: one eats while perceiving it as non-food;
one does not accept food for which the *atireka-āhāra* (remaining food) rite has been performed; one eats non-food for which the *atireka-āhāra* rite has not been performed;
if it was given to another or received from another who had already performed the *atireka-āhāra* rite; or if it is due to illness, or if it is the leftover food of a sick person.

Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule on leftover food): If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, should— having been invited— insistently offer food to him without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* rite,
saying, "Venerable one, please take this food," for this reason and no other, with the intent to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
(36) [The thirty-sixth case:
A gluttonous bhikṣu was rebuked by others; harboring resentment in his heart, he caused another person to commit an offense for this reason, and thus it was established as a precept.
If he eats it immediately, for every swallow both [parties] commit a *pāyattika* offense.

If he does not eat it, discards it, sets it aside, gives it to another person, or eats it after performing the ritual of "remaining food" (*khalupaṭiggahaṇa*), the one who gave it commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If he gives it to a sick person with the intent to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If he performs the ritual of "remaining food," [the recipient may eat it].

If one has already given [food] to another and intends for that other person to commit an offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has eaten enough and perceives it as having eaten enough, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has eaten enough but suspects whether one has eaten enough, or if one has not eaten enough but perceives it as having eaten enough, or suspects whether one has eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if one did not know beforehand; or if one has eaten enough but perceives it as not having eaten enough; or if one gives [food] with the intention that it be discarded and then eats it.
If one causes [the food] to be lifted up and placed [before him] so that he may eat it; or if one causes someone else to be sent to fetch it for him to eat;

or if one gives it to him and has him perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of "leftover food") before eating; if he does not do these things himself, yet gives what remains from the patient’s meal, he does not cause another to commit an offense.
If he performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* ritual and then gives it, he does not cause another to commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, it is a pāyattika (thirty-seventh).
Nanda and Upananda watched a musical performance; although the crowd gave them food and drink, they continued to watch even after they had finished eating.
He returned only at dusk. When Kāḷudāyin went out for alms at day’s end, a pregnant woman came out carrying food;
encountering a thunderstorm, she caught a fleeting glimpse of his face and, terrified, cried out, "It is a ghost! She immediately fell down.
In her anger she said, "Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, it would be better to break one's own belly than to go begging for food at night. For this reason, the rule was established.
"Proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday; one should follow this time as the rule for the four continents' meals.
"Improper time" refers to the period from midday until the dawn light has not yet appeared. If one receives food at an improper time, there is an *pāyattika* offense for every swallow.
If it is an improper time that has passed its limit, or if seven days have passed the limit of seven days, there is an *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding medicines to be taken for as long as one lives: to take them without a valid reason constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. If it is the improper time (*akāla*) and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.

If it is the improper time but one suspects it is so, or if it is the improper time but one perceives it as the proper time (*kāla*), or if it is the proper time but one perceives it as the improper time, or if one suspects it is so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one goes begging for food at the proper time.

A bhikṣu saw others making black stone honey (kṛṣṇa-śarkarā) containing *kaṇika* seeds; fearing it was not permitted to eat at the improper time, he did not eat it. The Buddha said, "I allow you to eat it;
there is no offense. This is the proper method. When a sick bhikṣu was taking emetic or purgative medicine, by the time the gruel had been heated, the mealtime had already passed.
He should boil barley so that the husks do not break, and drink the strained liquid.
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika (38).
The Venerable Kāla was constantly seated in meditative reflection; at that time, alms-food was easy to obtain. He then had this thought: "Why do I enter the city every day?
It is wearying and troublesome to beg for alms. It would be better to eat what I have first obtained; as for the food obtained later, I shall [eat it later]."
He took it back, and it was exactly as he had thought. At the times of the morning and midday meals, the bhikṣus did not see Kāla and suspected that he had either died or gone on a long journey;
later, when they saw him, they asked about the reason and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
Regarding "stale food": if one has received it today and it reaches tomorrow, for all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas who have received full ordination, it is entirely impure.
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.

If one perceives what was prepared overnight as having been prepared overnight, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is doubt regarding whether it was prepared overnight, and one does not perceive it as having been prepared overnight nor have doubt about it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if the food received overnight has a remainder which is given to parents, to those working for the stūpa, or to those building a dwelling, provided the food is given after calculating its value.
[The Buddha said: "Straightforwardly. Later, while receiving alms from a laborer, his alms bowl had holes and cracks; food entered into them.
Fearing that they would break by picking them out and washing them, he washed it according to the Dharma. If there was any remaining [food] that did not come out, there was no offense.

If he had previously received ghee or oil for the purpose of nasal irrigation, and the ghee or oil came out with the snot when he blew his nose, he should discard it; as for the remainder, there is no [offense].
Offense:
If a bhikṣu, without having received it [with the proper ritual], places food or medicine into his mouth— except for water and tooth-sticks— he commits a pāyattika (thirty-nine).

There was a bhikṣu who constantly went on alms-round and wore rag-robes. At that time, lay devotees (gṛhapati) in the city, for the sake of deceased parents and others, performed sacrificial offerings at crossroads or in shrines. That bhikṣu took the food for himself and ate it.
The lay devotees criticized and disparaged him; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to take tooth-sticks (dantakāṣṭha) for themselves.
Water. The Buddha said: "There is no offense.
There are five ways of receiving: receiving with hand from hand; or receiving with hand from an object held [in the other's hand]; or receiving with hand from an object held [by the giver];
or receiving from an object held [by the giver] with an object held [by the receiver]; or receiving by passing an object from a distance. This applies to both the giver and the receiver.
Knowing that there is no obstruction in the intervening space, [the food] falls into the hand. Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving:
receiving with the body against the body; receiving garment against garment; receiving elbow against elbow; receiving vessel against vessel;

or, having a reason, placing it on the ground to give. If one does not give it [directly] but takes it from the ground and puts it into one's own mouth, for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one does not receive [the food], yet has the perception that one has not received it, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not receive it, but suspects one has received it, or if one receives it but has the perception that one has not received it, or if one suspects one has received it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if, while a *bhikṣu* is begging for alms, food is dropped into his bowl by a bird, or if it is blown into the bowl by the wind, and he wishes to remove it.
One should discard this food until even a fingernail’s worth can be removed; for what remains, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains fine and delicious food—such as milk, curd, fish, or meat—and if, being free from illness, he seeks such fine food for his own sake, it is a pāyattika (fortieth).
Bhadanta went to the house of a merchant leader and requested various foods. The merchant leader asked, "What ailment do you have? He replied, "I have no illness or suffering;
I simply wish to obtain various foods. Because the merchant leader censured him for this, [the Buddha] established the rule.
If one is not ill and begs for fine food for oneself, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow; for the other four assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if one begs while ill, or begs on behalf of a sick person and eats what is obtained, or if one begs for another, or another begs for oneself, or if one obtains it without begging.
If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male follower of another sect or a female follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika (forty-one).
The Buddha instructed Ānanda to distribute cakes to the community of monks. After they had been distributed, there was a remainder, which he then gave to a beggar.
There was a daughter of a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) who was of upright appearance; when Ānanda handed her a cake, the cakes were stuck together, and she said—
He gave this cake to a woman, who passed it to another person, who in turn questioned those from whom she had received it; immediately, suspicion and slander arose.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin who, having finished eating here, was traveling toward the kingdom of Kosala when he encountered a highly devout physiognomist on the road.
He informed [the monks] that he had obtained food from a shaven-headed householder. The physiognomist reported this to the Bhikṣus, who in turn informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhists all voiced complaints. The Buddha then permitted [the food] to be placed on the ground for them to take, or for someone else to give it to them.
Regarding "heretics": these are those of naked asceticism or other heterodox schools. If one gives with one's own hand and the recipient accepts it, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one gives but the recipient does not accept it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one employs a means intending to give but does not actually give, and subsequently changes one's mind and regrets it, [it is likewise a duṣkṛta].

An *dukkaṭa*. For the other four assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one gives it to one's parents, to those working for the stupa, or to those working in a separate room, providing them with the calculated price for their labor. It is also not an offense if [the food] is forcibly seized by someone with superior power.

If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal without having entrusted himself to another bhikṣu, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of receiving robes;
these are called the [permissible] times. (42)
There was a householder who was on intimate terms with Upananda. He prepared a meal and invited the Saṃgha, waiting for Upananda to arrive.
At the time for the morning meal, Upananda went to another house; he did not return until the mealtime had nearly passed. Consequently, the bhikṣus were unable to eat their fill.
Furthermore, a high minister sent sweet fruits to the monastery, also waiting for Upananda to come so that they might be distributed.

After he had finished his meal, he would go to other households and only return when the time had passed. Because this prevented the community of monks from eating fresh fruit, [the Buddha] established a regulation.
Thereafter, the community of monks did not dare to enter the city to accept invitations. The Buddha permitted them to enter the city after having entrusted their bowls to one another;
furthermore, due to specific circumstances, he permitted entering the city without such entrustment during times of illness and so forth.
"Before the meal" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for the meal. "After the meal" refers to the period from the time for the meal until midday.
"Household" refers to a dwelling where men and women reside. "Other monks" refers to those who dwell together within the same boundary (*sīmā*).
Regarding the making of robes and the giving of robes, it is as explained above. If a monk has made an entrustment and, wishing to go to a village, returns on the way, [the entrustment] is lost.
Regarding the formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇā*): if one wishes to go after having previously made an entrustment, one must make another entrustment.

If, having made an entrustment with the intention of going to a village, one does not reach the place to which one was entrusted but instead goes to another house, the previous entrustment is lost; wishing to go, one should make another entrustment.
If, having made an entrustment, one reaches the house of a layperson, or even a storehouse, or a dwelling on the outskirts of a village, or reaches a *bhikṣuṇī*...
If it is at a monastery, or if one goes directly to a layperson’s house, one loses the previous formal entrustment (*ovāda*) upon departing; if one wishes to go, one must entrust oneself again.
If a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation and then visits other households before or after the meal, he must entrust himself to another bhikṣu before entering the village.
A *pāyattika*. If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, and one makes preparations to depart with the intention of going but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if there are no *bhikṣus* present, if one has not made a formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇā*), or if one goes to a storehouse, to the edge of a village, or to a side room, or if one goes to a *bhikṣuṇī*.
At the monastery, he goes to the house of the layperson to whom he was entrusted. If there are many such households, he spreads out his sitting mat and invites the bhikṣus;
