or, if he is constrained by powerful forces, or faces a threat to his life or to his holy life (brahmacarya).
If a bhikṣu sits down forcefully in a house where food is being served while precious objects are present, it is a pāyattika (forty-three).
Kāḷudāyin went to the house of a female lay devotee who was observing the fast and sat down. When her husband asked what he required, he replied that he needed food.
The husband then had his wife bring out food and give it to him. After he had eaten, he did not leave. The husband became angry and went out.
The terminology follows what you have done. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established a prohibition.
Regarding "those who eat" (*āśaya*): men take women as their food, and women take men as their food; therefore, they are called "families that eat. Regarding "jewels" (*ratna*): [text continues].
Regarding the seven treasures, such as gold and silver: if a bhikṣu sits down forcefully while there are treasures present in a household where food is being served, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, or if one stands rather than sitting, these are all duṣkṛta offenses.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pāyattika offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if there are two bhikṣus who have companions; if there is a person capable of identifying them present;

if there is a guest staying in the same place; if they pass through from the front without stopping; if they suddenly fall to the ground due to an outbreak of illness; or if they are held by those with forceful power, or are imprisoned.
Or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place where there is treasure within a family home, it is a pāyattika (forty-four).
Kāḷudāyin sat down again behind the door-panel and conversed with the female lay devotee (upāsikā) who was observing the fast; for this reason, the rule was established.
He sat in the house where food was being served so that his hand could reach the door, allowing the bhikṣu seeking alms to see him.
The rest is as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika (forty-five).
This was also established because [the offense] arose from the person before him.
Regarding whether there is an offense or no offense, all is as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, let us go together to the village;
I shall give you food," yet that bhikṣu ultimately does not instruct [the other] to be given food, but instead says, "Go away; I will stay with you no longer."
If [a monk] finds no pleasure in sitting or speaking with others, but finds pleasure in sitting and speaking alone, for this reason and no other, he should employ skillful means to have them depart;
[if he does so], it is a *pāyattika* offense (forty-six).
Bhadrananda had been fighting with other bhikṣus and harbored a grudge in his heart. On another occasion, he led them to a place where there was no food and wandered about it entirely.
When only a short time remained before they would have to fast, he said to them, "You are great evildoers!
Because of you, I too have been unable to obtain food. Depart quickly! Those bhikṣus left the city and arrived at Jetavana at that time.

[The meal] has already passed; they were unable to eat and became utterly exhausted. The bhikṣus, feeling resentment and reproaching [the offender], informed the Buddha, who then established this precept:
"Regarding 'food,' it refers to food at the proper time. If one uses a pretext to send [a visitor] away, abandoning the place where he can see and the place where he can hear, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one abandons the place where he can see and goes to the place where he can hear, or abandons the place where he can hear and goes to the place where he can see, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one uses a pretext to abandon the place where he can see [himself]," [it is also a *duṣkṛta*].
If one goes from a place where [the offense] was seen to a place where it was heard, or from a place where it was heard to a place where it was seen, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one sends them away by giving them food; or if one is ill;
or if one lacks proper decorum (*airyāpatha*) such that people see them and are displeased, and says, "You go; I..."
When sending food to the saṃghārāma, if that person has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment;

or if they have been formally censured by the assembly, have been expelled, or are subject to expulsion; or if one perceives a threat to life or a threat to their pure conduct—then one may use skillful means to send them away, provided it is not done out of malice or resentment.
If a monk accepts an invitation to receive medicine for four months, a monk who is not ill may accept it;
if he accepts beyond that, except in the case of a regular invitation, a special invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation, it is a *pāyattika* (forty-seven).
Mahānāma, he provided medicine for the community of monks. Out of respect for the elders, he gave them the best quality; whether they asked for it or not, he gave it to them.
When the group of six [monks] went to his house, they intentionally sought out difficult-to-obtain medicines. He replied, "If I have them, I shall give them to you;
if I do not have them, I shall go to the market to buy some and provide them to you. The group of six then acted out of attachment and spoke falsely.
He rebuked him. Because Mahānāma no longer provided medicine for the Saṃgha, this precept was established.

"Four months" refers to the four months of the summer retreat. "The sick" refers to those prescribed medicine by a physician. "One who constantly invites" refers to a person who says, "I shall always provide medicine.
"One who invites again" refers to one who provides it after it has been interrupted. "One who invites by division" [refers to one who provides medicine according to specific shares].

As for "one who brings medicine to the saṃghārāma and distributes it": regarding one who invites [another] for as long as life lasts, that person says, "I shall give medicine for as long as my life endures. There are four kinds of such invitations:

there may be an invitation where the night has a fixed limit but the medicine does not, in which case one establishes a limit for the night but not for the medicine, saying, "I will give you medicine for this many nights."

There may be a case where there is a limit regarding the medicine but no limit regarding the night; in such a case, one establishes a limit for the medicine but does not establish a limit for the night, saying:
"I shall give such-and-such medicine. Or there may be a case where there is a limit regarding the night and a limit regarding the medicine;
in such a case, one says: "For this many nights I shall give such-and-such medicine. Or there may be a case where there is no limit regarding the night and no limit regarding the medicine.
Regarding the limits: it is stated as follows. "I invite you to accept medicine. In this regard, there are four cases concerning the limit of the night and the limit of the medicine:
(1) the night has a limit but the medicine has no limit; (2) both the night and the medicine have limits—one should accept them during the four months of the summer retreat;
(3) the night has no limit but the medicine has a limit; (4) both the night and the medicine have no limit—one should accept them at the time they are offered. If...

To accept food when not ill, except for a regular invitation, a special invitation, an invitation for a specific portion, or a lifelong invitation, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful swallowed.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu goes to view a military array, except for a specific time or cause, it is a pāyattika (forty-eight).
King Prasenajit personally led the six divisions of his army to suppress rebels; the group of six bhikṣus went to view them, and the king was displeased.
Because [a layperson] sent rock honey as a message of inquiry to the World-Honored One, the World-Honored One rebuked him and established a precept.

Later, there were two high ministers in the army who, thirsting with longing, wished to see the bhikṣus; however, the bhikṣus did not dare go. Therefore, the exception for "time-related circumstances" was established.
"An array" refers to a military formation; "an army" refers to an elephant corps, a cavalry corps, a chariot corps, or an infantry corps.

If a bhikṣu goes to view such a military array, moving from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from low ground to high ground, or from high ground to low ground, if he sees it as he departs, it is a *pāyattika*; if he does not see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one intends to observe [the army] through skillful means and adornment, yet does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu is already traveling on the road and the military array arrives later, he should leave the road to avoid it; if he does not avoid it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is led away by force or power.
[If] one departs [from the army], yet the water or land routes are cut off, or there are such obstacles as those to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one need not descend from the road to avoid them.
If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason, he is permitted to remain within the army for two or three nights; should he exceed this, it is a *pāyattika* (forty-ninth).
The group of six monks had a reason for staying overnight among the army. Because householders criticized and disparaged this, [the Buddha] established the rule:
if one stays for a third night, before the appearance of dawn, one must leave the range of hearing and the range of sight.
If one does not leave the range of hearing and sight until the appearance of dawn, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If one leaves the range of sight but remains within the range of hearing...
If one goes from the place where it was heard to the place where it is seen, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if the path by water or land is cut off, or in cases such as those involving threats to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, and at any time observes military arrays and battles,
or observes the strength and power of the marching troops' elephants and horses, it is a pāyattika (fifty).

The group of six monks watched a military array and were struck by arrows; they wrapped them in their robes and returned with them. When a layperson asked about this and learned the reason, he criticized and disparaged them, and thus [the Buddha] established the rule.
Regarding "combatants": whether it be mock combat or actual combat, as for the military, there are one kind of army up to four kinds of armies.

There may be royal armies, bandit armies, or guilds of householders who possess great power—those with the foremost elephant force, the foremost cavalry force, the foremost chariot force, and the foremost infantry force.
As for their battle arrays, they include the four-square array, the circular array, and the crescent-moon array.
The array of Zhang Zhen; the array of Han Xiang; the elephant kings, horse kings, and human kings; whether they violate [the precepts] or do not violate them—all is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika (fifty-one).

The Venerable Bakkula stayed as a guest in the house of a matted-hair Brahmin. He subdued the venomous fire-dragon, whereby the ruler of Kauśāmbī conceived profound faith and came to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
Desiring further to make offerings to the Venerable, the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) requested black liquor for him.
The Venerable became intoxicated and overindulged; midway through his journey, he fell down and vomited, while crows clamored in confusion. The Buddha rebuked them, saying:
If one cannot subdue a small snake now, how much less can one subdue a great dragon?
Furthermore, there are ten faults in drinking alcohol: first, the complexion becomes ugly; second, physical strength diminishes; third, vision becomes unclear;
fourth, it manifests signs of anger and resentment; fifth, it ruins one's fields, livelihood, and means of subsistence; sixth, it increases the occurrence of diseases.
Seventh, they will increase litigation and disputes. Eighth, they will lack renown and their ill repute will spread. Ninth, their wisdom will diminish.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the three evil realms.
From this day forward, those who take me as their teacher must not, even for a moment, place the tip of a blade of grass or wood into alcohol and put it into their mouths.
As for "liquor": it refers to wood-wine, rice-wine made from non-glutinous rice, rice-wine made from other types of rice, barley-wine, or whatever other substances may be used to make wine.
Regarding "wood-wine": this includes wine made from pear juice, wine made from *jambu* fruit, wine made from sugarcane, wine made from *śāluka* fruit, wine made from *mṛdvīkā* juice, and grape wine.
As for "pear juice wine," it is prepared by mixing honey with rock sugar, and so forth.
Drumstick wine (*mṛdvīkā-pāna*) is likewise. As for mixed liquor (*miśra-pāna*): it may have the color, fragrance, and taste of wine;
or it may lack the color, fragrance, and taste of wine; or it may lack the color, fragrance, and taste of wine;
or it may lack the color, fragrance, and taste of wine. In all such cases, it should not be drunk. If it is not wine, yet possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of wine—or...
Whether it be the color of liquor, the fragrance of liquor, or the taste of liquor; or whether it be not the color of liquor, not the fragrance of liquor, but the taste of liquor;
or whether it be not the color of liquor, not the fragrance of liquor, nor the taste of liquor—one should drink [only that which is not liquor].

If a bhikṣu drinks or consumes liquor, or what has been boiled with liquor, or what is mixed with liquor, it is a pāyattika offense. This applies whether he drinks sweet-flavored liquor, sour-flavored liquor, or eats [such substances].

If one consumes yeast or dregs from fermented liquor, it is both cases *duṣkṛta*. If it is liquor and one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt regarding it being liquor, or if it is liquor but one perceives it as not liquor, it is all *pāyattika*.
If it is not liquor but one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt regarding it not being liquor, it is both cases *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if one has such an illness that it is not cured by other medicines and thus uses alcohol as medicine, or applies alcohol to a wound.
If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika (52). While the seventeen groups of monks were playing in the water, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā saw them from atop a terrace.
The Queen sent someone to inform the World-Honored One, and thus this rule was established.

Regarding those who play in the water: acting with unrestrained license, whether going from this shore to the other shore, or with the current or against it, or diving here and surfacing there, or drawing patterns in the water with their hands, or splashing one another, even up to playing with water contained in a bowl—all such acts constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
Excluding water, if it is whey, thin curd-liquid, or thick curd-liquid...

Sour wine, or the liquid of barley beer—playing or sporting with these in a vessel constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī, and a *duṣkṛta* offense for the other three assemblies. There is no offense if one is traveling on a road and crosses water;
or if one is pulling timber, bamboo, or reeds in the water; or if one is gathering stones, sand, or lost property. Or...
The training rule on the practice of tickling: If a bhikṣu tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika (fifty-three).
This was established because one member of the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) tickled a member of the group of seventeen (Saptadaśavargika), causing him to die.
Regarding "fingers": there are ten on the hands and ten on the feet. If one strikes or tickles another with the fingers of the hands or feet, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes or tickles another with a staff, a door-bolt, a broom handle, or other such objects, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one touches someone while they are sleeping in order to wake them.
If one touches [it] by mistake,
or if a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika (fifty-four).
This was established because Chanda wished to violate the precepts and did not comply when the various bhikṣus admonished him.
Regarding one who does not accept admonition: if another person restrains them, saying, "Do not do this; you should not act thus," yet they intentionally commit it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If they know for themselves that what they have done is wrong, yet they intentionally commit it, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if an ignorant person comes to admonish them, and they reply:

"You should ask your teacher or preceptor about the study of the scriptures and the recitation of the sūtras, so that you may understand the method of admonition; only then should you offer admonition.
Furthermore, if [the words] are spoken in jest, as a soliloquy, in a dream, or erroneously, they should not be used."
If a bhikṣu causes another bhikṣu to be terrified, it is a pāyattika (fifty-five).
While the Buddha was walking up and down on the walking path, the bhikṣu Nāgapāla attended upon him. During the first watch of the night, he requested the Buddha to return to his room;
the World-Honored One remained silent. During the middle watch and the last watch, he did likewise, yet he was instead seized and bound. He then... [text fragment ends]
Regarding the sound of non-human terrors: the World-Honored One, having gathered the assembly, rebuked [the offender] and established the precept.
As for "terror": it refers to using form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena to terrify others.

Regarding "form": it means assuming the shape of an elephant, a horse, a ghost, or a bird or beast. Regarding "sound": it includes the sound of a conch, the sound of a drum, the sound of a *bherī* (kettledrum), or the sound of an elephant.

The sound of horses and the sound of weeping. As for odors: the scent of roots, the scent of *sāla* trees, the scent of resin, the scent of bark, the scent of pith, the scent of leaves, the scent of flowers, the scent of fruits—whether pleasant fragrances or foul stench. As for tastes:
whether sour, sweet, bitter, astringent, or the taste of ochre. As for tangibles: whether cold or hot, light or heavy, or...
Regarding the coarse, the fine, the rough, and the smooth: as for the "phenomenon" (dharma), it refers to speaking to another person, saying:
"I have seen such a sign; I have dreamed such a dream. You shall die; or you shall lose your robes and bowl; or you shall abandon the path.
Your preceptor (upādhyāya) and ācārya shall also die, lose their robes and bowls, or abandon the path. Your parents shall fall gravely ill."
If, after [the person] has passed away, one causes them to see, hear, perceive, or know these six sense-objects—whether they are frightened or not—one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If the person before one does not see, hear, perceive, or know them, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one speaks and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks but the meaning is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is likewise.
An *dukkaṭa* offense. There is no offense if: one is sitting in a dark place without a lamp;
or, while at a place for defecating or urinating, one sees something in the distance and thinks it is an elephant, a thief, or a wild beast, and thus becomes terrified;

or, one becomes terrified upon hearing the sound of footsteps, the rustling of grass and trees, or the sound of coughing; or, one looks at a person with a certain expression [of fear] but does not intentionally cause them alarm.

Frightened in mind, if such things were actually to occur, or if he were to actually see such signs, or dream of his imminent death, his renunciation of the path, the loss of his robes and bowl, or the passing of his preceptor (upādhyāya), his teacher (ācārya), or his parents—should such events happen, he would say to them:
"I have seen such portents of your transformation. This applies whether spoken in jest or as private talk.
If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept this; he must not exceed it, except during other times.
This is a pāyattika offense. "Other times" refers to: the heat of the season, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of traveling on a road.
These are the [proper] times. (56)
In the kingdom of Magadha, there was a pond. King Bimbisāra permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in it at all times. Later, during the final watch of the night, the group of six entered the water to bathe.
The king, accompanied by his court ladies, also arrived there. Hearing the sound of the bhikṣus bathing, he waited in silence.
The group of six used various fine medicinal powders to bathe one another until the first light of dawn appeared. The king—
In the end, they were not permitted to bathe. All the ministers, being collectively resentful, established this regulation:
"The hot season" refers to the forty-five days of spring and the first month of summer. "The sick" refers to those whose bodies have become foul-smelling and impure, down to that point.
"One who performs the work" refers to one who sweeps the ground before the house, down to that point. "Wind and rain" refers to even a single whirlwind, down to that point. One.

If raindrops fall upon the body of a practitioner while traveling even as little as half a yojana, whether coming or going, and if they bathe themselves more than once except at other times, it is a *pāyattika* offense if the water drenches half the body.
If one makes preparations to wash but does not go through with it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is compelled by force to bathe;
or if a bhikṣu, being free from illness, lights a fire on open ground for the sake of warming his own body, or instructs another to light it, except when there is a specific reason or occasion.
This constitutes a *pāyattika* (fifty-seven).
The group of six monks, being in the presence of the senior elder, were not permitted to light fires on the open ground outside their cells at will.

At one time, while they were warming themselves by a fire, a venomous snake in an empty tree was driven out by the heat of the flames and emerged from a hollow in the trunk. All the bhikṣus were terrified;
they seized the burning wood and scattered the flying embers, which set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire. Therefore, this rule was established.
Regarding the sick: if there is a circumstance where one must warm the body with fire—such as for the sake of a sick bhikṣu cooking congee, soup, or rice;
or if it is in a heated room (*jentāka*), a kitchen, or a bathhouse;
or for fumigating bowls, dyeing robes, lighting lamps, or burning incense—if a bhikṣu who is not ill lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of warming himself. If...
However, if one burns the branches, leaves, hemp, flax, or *kusa* grass, or cow dung, husks, refuse, or parched grain, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places fire upon the branches, leaves, and so forth, and they burn, it is a *pāyattika*; if they are half-burnt or scorched, it is likewise.
If it is glowing charcoal, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not say to the person before them, "Look at this; know this," it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu conceals another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case— whether he conceals them himself or instructs another to do so—
even if it is done in jest, it is a pāyattika (fifty-eight).
The group of seventeen monks took their robes, bowls, and other requisites and stood in one place practicing walking meditation, waiting for the time of the meal to arrive.

The group of six monks waited until they had turned their backs, then took the items and hid them. When the time arrived and the others went searching for them, the six monks teased them from the front. Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.

For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if one takes and hides [the object] because one truly knows its nature and substance;
or if one takes and hides it because the object has been blown away or soaked by wind and rain.
Furthermore, if the owner of the items is by nature arrogant and keeps his robes and bowl in disarray and neglect, [the monk] may take them up and store them away for the purpose of admonishing him.
Or, if he lends a robe to the other to wear and fears it might be lost because the other does not look after it, he may take it up and store it away.
Or, on account of these robes, bowls, and various belongings, there may be danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Therefore, one takes it and hides it. If a bhikṣu, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī,
subsequently takes it back and wears it without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika (fifty-nine).
This was established because it originated with the group of six monks.
"To give a robe" refers to a *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure gift) of a robe. There are two kinds of pure gifts: first, the *bhūta-pariśuddha-dāna* (true pure gift).
One says: "This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*). It has not yet been purified; now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir. This constitutes a true [purification].
Purification. Second, purification through successive giving (*parivattaka-pariśuddhi*). One says: "This is my long robe (*atireka-cīvara*), which has not yet been purified.
Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir. He should speak thus: "Venerable Sir, listen. You have this long robe which has not yet been purified;
now you give it to me for the sake of purification. I accept it. Having accepted it, one should ask: "Do you wish..."
"To whom? He should reply, "To so-and-so. The other should say: "Venerable sir, you have this long robe which has not yet been purified (*pariśuddha*).
Now, for the sake of purifying it for me, I accept it. Having accepted it, he gives it to the bhikṣu so-and-so, saying: "This robe belongs to so-and-so;
for the sake of so-and-so, you should guard and use it as you please. This is the truth in this matter.

Regarding "pure giving" (*viśuddha-dāna*): one should inquire of the owner and then take and wear [the garment]. Regarding "successive pure giving" (*paramparā-viśuddha-dāna*), it may be done according to one's preference, whether or not the owner is informed.
If a bhikṣu truly receives a gift of clothing and takes and wears it without informing the owner, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of the three types of discoloration, choosing whichever color he prefers among them—such as blue.
If one wears a new garment that is black, madder-colored, or not discolored (dyed), it is a *pāyattika* offense (the sixtieth).
The group of six monks wore white garments while walking; because householders criticized and disparaged this, [the Buddha] established the rule.
"New" refers to either a new garment or one newly acquired; all such items are termed "new garments. "Dyed to an altered color" means dyeing them blue, black, or madder-brown.
If one obtains a new garment and does not dye it in one of these three colors, yet puts on another new garment, [it constitutes an offense].

It is a *pāyattika*. If one keeps heavy robes, light robes, or non-robes, or a bowl bag, a leather sandal bag, a needle and thread bag, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, tweezers, a hot-towel, or a leather-sandal cloth, without having performed the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one entrusts an uncolored robe to a householder’s family, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika (the sixtieth).
Kāḷudāyin did not like seeing crows; he made a bamboo bow and shot them until they were killed in heaps. Because of this, [the rule] was established.
Regarding "animals": those that cannot undergo transformation. Whether one takes their own life, instructs another to take their life, or kills them through various means, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If one employs the means with the intent to kill but does not kill, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies to] a bhikṣu.

A *niḥpāyattika* offense for a nun; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one does not kill intentionally, or if all life is extinguished without any intent to harm.
If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks or uses water containing living beings, it is a pāyattika (62).
This was established because the six groups of monks began [this practice], leading householders to criticize and disparage them.
If there are insects in the water, and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are insects in the water, but one suspects it (or is in doubt), it is a *pāyattika*.

If there are no insects in the water, but one perceives them as such, or suspects they are there, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one was previously unaware; or if there are insects but one perceives them as non-existent;
or if coarse insects touch the water and are driven away; or if one strains the water before drinking it.
If a bhikṣu intentionally annoys another bhikṣu so that he is unhappy for even a moment, it is a pāyattika (62).
The group of seventeen asked the group of six: "How does one enter the first dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna? How does one enter emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one attain the four fruits? They replied: "According to what you have said, you have already committed an offense."

Regarding the *pārājika* rules: at that time, the group of seventeen monks went to question the elders. Knowing that they were causing them doubt and vexation, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
"Causing doubt and vexation" means: whether for the sake of birth, or for the sake of age, or for the sake of receiving the precepts, or for the sake of a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Or for...
If one commits [an offense] for the sake of the Dharma, and there is doubt regarding the time of birth, one asks:
"How long has it been since you were born? He replies: "For such a length of time. One then asks: "It is not that you were born such a long time ago;
you were born like other people, not at such a time. Regarding doubt concerning the age, one asks: "How many years old are you now? He replies: "I am so many."

Regarding the matter of age: if one says, "You are not of such an age as other recipients of the precepts; you have not yet reached that age," and there is doubt concerning the reception of the precepts, one asks:
"At the time you received the precepts, since your age was less than twenty and the *karmavācanā* was performed by a separate assembly within the boundary (*sīmā*), do you have any doubts?
If there is doubt regarding the *karmavācanā*, one asks: "At the time you received the precepts, was the *karmavācanā* not validly accomplished?"
In an illegal assembly, to one who has doubts regarding an offense, saying, "You have committed a *pārājika*, even down to a *dukkaṭa*";
or to one who has doubts regarding the Dharma, saying, "The Dharma you asked about constitutes a *pārājika* offense"—
if a bhikṣu intentionally speaks in such a way as to cause doubt for another bhikṣu and does so clearly, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for a monk; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if the matter is actually so, if one does not intentionally cause distress to another, if it was not permitted that fear or subsequent doubt and regret would arise, or if one accepts the offerings of others or receives the prostrations of a great *bhikṣu* without cause, and then speaks [as follows].
He said, "You were not born that long ago; you do not have that many years. Lest there be doubt or regret later," and so on, until he had paid his respects.
Then he spoke, saying, "You do not have that many years. If you are less than twenty years of age, you would be a separate assembly within the boundary.
Desiring that he know this, so that he may return to his original place and receive the precepts again, he then spoke to him."
If one is under twenty years of age, or if the assembly is divided within the boundary, and the motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the formal act (*karman*) is not accomplished;

this is an illegal division of the assembly (*adharma-vibhakta-saṃgha*). Desiring to make that person aware [of the fault] so that they may return to their original place and receive the precepts again, one says to them:
"Your motion was not accomplished, your formal act was not accomplished; it was an illegal division of the assembly. If that person has indeed committed such an offense, it constitutes a *pārājika*.
Up to the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Desiring to cause him to understand so that he may perform confession according to the Dharma, one says:
"You have committed the four grave offenses (*pārājika*), up to and including the *duṣkṛta*. If his nature is coarse and he does not understand speech, one simply says: "It is as you have said."

To claim for oneself the status of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma) is an offense of defeat (pārājika); one is no longer a bhikkhu. This applies even if spoken in jest, as a soliloquy, in a dream, or by mistake.
If a bhikkhu, knowing that another bhikkhu has committed a grave offense (thullaccaya), conceals it, he commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya). (64)
Upananda frequently committed offenses and told one of his close friends not to speak of them to anyone.

Later, the two of them quarreled, and he immediately spoke of it to other bhikṣus. When the other bhikṣus questioned him and learned the truth, they informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.

Regarding "grave offenses" (*sthūlātyaya*): these refer to the four *pārājika* and thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules. If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, and he learns of it before the meal but speaks of it after the meal;

or if he learns of it after the meal and speaks of it during the first watch of the night; or if he learns of it during the first watch and speaks of it during the middle watch—all these constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If he learns of it during the middle watch and intends to speak of it during the last watch but has not yet spoken when the dawn appears, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) for concealment.

To conceal other offenses, a coarse offense (*sthūlātyaya*), or another person’s coarse offense, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* in all cases. If it is a coarse offense and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*;

if it is a coarse offense but one has doubt regarding it, or if it is not a coarse offense but one perceives it as such, or if it is not a coarse offense but one has doubt regarding it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [if the offender is insane, possessed by a spirit, or suffering from extreme pain; or if the concealment is for the sake of protecting the Dharma, the Sangha, or the individual].
If one did not previously know; if it was a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) but perceived as not grave; or if there was no person toward whom one could speak;

or if, having formed the intention to speak, the dawn had already appeared before one spoke; or if, because of speaking, there would be danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), and one did not speak.

When one has reached twenty years of age, one should receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). If a bhikṣu knows that a person is less than twenty years of age and yet confers the full ordination upon them, this person does not obtain the precepts.
Because those bhikṣus have acted out of folly, they commit a *pāyattika* offense (the sixty-fifth).
There was a group of seventeen youths who were former friends; the eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve.
They sought ordination together, and the bhikṣus conferred the full precepts upon them. At that time, the youths could not endure eating only one meal;
at midnight, they suffered from hunger and cried out loudly. When the Buddha heard this, he established a rule.
If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, and the *upādhyāya* knows they are less than twenty,
and the assembly of monks as well as the candidate for ordination also know they are less than twenty, yet when questioned in the midst of the assembly,
"Are you twenty years of age? the candidate replies that they are twenty, or that they are not twenty, or expresses doubt, or does not know their own age, or remains silent.
If the Sangha does not inquire [regarding the age], the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense and the Sangha commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If the preceptor knows [the candidate] has not yet reached the required age, while the Sangha and the candidate believe he has reached it, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense and the Sangha is without offense.
If the preceptor knows [the candidate] is not yet of age, and the assembly of monks as well as the candidate for ordination suspect it, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense;

the assembly commits a *dukkaṭa* offense. If the preceptor knows [the candidate] is not yet of age, but the assembly of monks and the candidate for ordination do not know it, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense;
the assembly is without offense. If the preceptor believes [the candidate] is of age, but the assembly of monks and the candidate for ordination...
If the person’s age is not yet full, the Upādhyāya is without offense, but the Saṃgha commits a duṣkṛta.
If the Upādhyāya considers the age to be full, and both the Saṃgha and the candidate for ordination also consider it full, all are without offense.

If the Upādhyāya considers the age to be full, but the Saṃgha and the candidate for ordination have doubts, the Upādhyāya is without offense, but the Saṃgha commits a duṣkṛta. If the Upādhyāya considers [the age to be full]...
If the person has reached the required age, but the assembly of monks and the candidate for ordination do not know it, there is no offense for anyone.

If the preceptor suspects [the candidate is not of age] while the assembly of monks and the candidate know he is not yet of age, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* and the assembly commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If the preceptor suspects [the candidate is not of age] while the assembly of monks and the candidate believe he has reached the required age, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika*, but the assembly is without offense.

If the preceptor suspects [an offense], while the community of monks and the person receiving the precepts also suspect it, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense; the community of monks commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the preceptor suspects it, while the community of monks and the person receiving the precepts do not know it, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense;
the community of monks is without offense. If the preceptor does not know it, while the community of monks and the person receiving the precepts know it... [the text continues].
If [the preceptor] does not know [the candidate has reached the age], but the community of monks and the candidate believe he has reached the age, there is no offense for anyone.

If the preceptor does not know, but the community of monks and the candidate doubt [whether he has reached the age], there is no offense for the preceptor, but the community of monks commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the preceptor does not know, and the community of monks and... [text continues].
If the preceptor is unaware, there is no offense for either party. If that bhikṣu knows the candidate is less than twenty years of age and yet confers the full ordination upon him:

when the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the upādhyāya commits a *pāyattika*; when the second *karmavācanā* is completed, he commits three *duṣkṛtas*; when the first *karmavācanā* is completed, he commits two *duṣkṛtas*;
if the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, he commits one *duṣkṛta*; if the formal motion is not yet completed... [or if it is interrupted].

If one has not yet made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), but acts as a preparatory means—whether for shaving the hair, intending to assemble the community, or when the community of monks has already assembled—the preceptor incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;

for a nun, it is a *pāyattika*. There is no offense if one was previously unaware, or if one relied upon the words of a person who had received the precepts, or if one relied upon the testimony of a bystander, or if one relied upon the words of the [candidate’s] parents.
If, after having received the precepts, one has doubts, the Buddha said: "I permit you to count the months of the pregnancy, as well as the intercalary months;
or to count all the fourteen-day periods of the *poṣadha* ceremony as the number of years."
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a matter of dispute has been settled according to the Dharma through confession, should later raise it again, it is a pāyattika (66).
When the group of six had settled a matter of dispute according to the Dharma, they raised it again later and spoke thus: "You are not well-behaved."

Contemplation that fails to become contemplation; lack of skillful understanding, which fails to become understanding; lack of skillful cessation, which fails to become cessation—these cause disputes to arise in the Saṃgha where none previously existed, and they fail to extinguish disputes already present. It is for this reason that the rule was established.
"According to the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instruction. There are four kinds of disputes:

disputes over speech (*vāda-vivāda*), disputes over accusations (*anuvāda-vivāda*), disputes over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes over matters (*kicca-vivāda*). If a monk, knowing that a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, should later raise it again, [he commits an offense].
If one speaks thus: "He did not observe well; his observation was not accomplished. He did not understand well; his understanding was not accomplished. Extinction was not accomplished;
extinction was not accomplished," and if he speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if he does not speak so as to be clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If, after another quarrel or verbal abuse has occurred, he subsequently instigates it again; or if he instigates a matter of quarrel that has already arisen; or if it concerns another person—[the same applies].

Engaging in quarrels and verbal abuse, and subsequently instigating them again, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) in all cases. If one observes [the act] while forming the perception [of it], it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If one observes with doubt, it does not constitute the perception [of it]. If one forms the perception [of it] while doubting, it does not constitute the perception [of it];
this is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one did not know beforehand, or if one observes [it].
One does not practice contemplation. If one does not truly contemplate well, contemplation is not accomplished; if one does not understand well, understanding is not accomplished;
if one does not extinguish well, extinction is not accomplished. This applies to idle chatter, speech in dreams, erroneous speech, and rapid speech.
If a bhikṣu, knowing he is traveling with a band of thieves, makes an agreement to travel together along the same road for even as far as one village interval, it is a pāyattika (67).

A group of bhikṣus traveled as companions with merchants who were smuggling goods through a customs post. They were seized by the customs officials, but King Prasenajit reprimanded them and released them.
The king’s subjects remained dissatisfied; when the Buddha heard of this, he established a prohibition.
Regarding "a band of thieves": it refers to those who have returned from robbing or are about to go out on a robbery. Regarding "making a pact": they agree together to reach a city or a village.
Regarding "the road": it refers to the various paths between villages. The gravity of the offense—whether light or heavy—is as explained in the precept concerning traveling with a woman.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
If one did not know [the rule] beforehand; or if one was not traveling with a companion; or if one was under the influence of force; or if one was bound;
or if there was a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
or if a bhikṣu were to speak thus: "I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha—that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path."
That monk should admonish this monk, saying: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. Do not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak such words. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that the commission of sexual misconduct is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When that monk admonishes this monk and he persists in his refusal to relinquish [his position], that monk...
Up to three admonitions: because of abandoning this matter. If, after being admonished up to three times, one abandons it, it is well; if one does not abandon it, it is a *pāyattika* (sixty-eighth).
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to this evil view; although the other bhikṣus admonished him, he did not relinquish it.
The Buddha then ordered the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure (*prativāraṇīya-karman*) against him, and thereby established this precept.
If a bhikṣu should speak thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should be admonished.
If he accepts the admonition, it is well. If he does not accept the admonition, one should perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) against him.
If they comply with the instruction, it is well. If they do not comply, the first *karmavācanā* is performed;
if they still do not comply when the second *karmavācanā* is finished, it is well. If they still do not comply when the third *karmavācanā* is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.

If they relinquish [the offense] after the second *karmavācanā* is finished, there are three *duṣkṛtas*. If they relinquish it after the first *karmavācanā* is finished, there are two *duṣkṛtas*. [The motion (*jñapti*)...]
If he has already relinquished [the offense], it is one *duṣkṛta*. If he relinquishes it before the formal motion (*jñapti*) is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If he speaks these words—“I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is such that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path”—before the formal motion has been made, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
When other monks admonish that monk, if another monk or a nun obstructs them, [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*].
If others stop you, do not abandon this matter. If the Saṃgha offers admonition, yet you stop them by refusing to be admonished, all incur a *duṣkṛta*;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if: one desists immediately upon the first admonition; if the admonition is given by an unlawful separate assembly;

if the admonition is given by an unlawful united assembly; if the admonition is given by a lawful separate assembly; if the admonition is given by a lawful-similar separate assembly; if the admonition is given by a lawful-similar united assembly;
if the matter is neither Dharma nor Vinaya; if it is not what the Buddha has taught; or if there is no one to offer the admonition.
If a bhikṣu knows that a person has spoken such words, has not performed the formal act [of renunciation], and does not abandon such wrong views, yet he provides them with what they need,
performs formal acts (*karmavācanā*) together with them, stays overnight with them, or converses with them, it is a *pāyattika* offense (69).

Ariṣṭa did not relinquish his evil view. When the bhikṣus informed the Buddha that he had again formed an evil view and would not relinquish it when being formally censured (*utkṣepa*), the Buddha established this rule because the group of six bhikṣus provided him with all necessities and participated in formal monastic acts (*karman*) together with him.
One who speaks thus says: "I have heard the Blessed One teach that engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path.
Regarding those who have not performed the formal act: if they have been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and not yet reinstated;

if they do not relinquish their evil view after being admonished by the Saṅgha; and regarding those who provide what is necessary, there are two kinds: either through the Dharma or through material goods. As for the Dharma:
He teaches the cultivation of higher morality (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*). Regarding material goods:

he provides clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites. Regarding those who perform the same *karmavācanā*: they recite the precepts together. Regarding those who stay overnight: [they share the same lodging].

If there is a dwelling with four walls and so forth, whether one enters before or after [another], or if both enter together, to lie down on one's side against the wall constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣu;
it is a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if the bhikṣu enters to stay overnight without knowing [of another’s presence], or if the bhikṣu is already in the dwelling when such a person subsequently enters. If the bhikṣu...
I do not know. It may be that a house is entirely covered and unobstructed; or entirely covered and half-obstructed;
or entirely covered and slightly obstructed; or entirely obstructed and uncovered; or entirely obstructed and half-covered.

Whether all obstacles are slightly covered, or half-covered and half-obstructed, or slightly covered and slightly obstructed, or neither covered nor obstructed, or again, in an open space—in all such cases, not knowing [the situation] constitutes no offense. This also applies if one has fallen to the ground due to illness.
...up to "the difficulty of the holy life," and so forth.

If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus: "I have heard from the Buddha the Dharma that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying: "Do not, O excellent one, slander the World-Honored One. To slander..."
"It is not the case, World-Honored One; it is not the case that the World-Honored One would speak such words.
For the World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, declared to the śrāmaṇera that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path.

When that bhikṣu admonishes this śrāmaṇera, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should then admonish and rebuke him up to three times to make him relinquish this matter. If, after being admonished up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is well."
Regarding "not relinquishing": that bhikṣu should say to that śrāmaṇera, "From this day forward, you must not say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One.

You must not follow after other bhikṣus. While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with other bhikṣus for two or three nights, you no longer have this privilege. You must leave; depart and be gone! You should not remain here. If [the śrāmaṇera]...
The Buddha said: "I know that if one entices, takes in, and cohabits with a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled from the community for such reasons, it is a pāyattika (seventy).
Baddhananda had two śrāmaṇeras who held such evil views; the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to perform a formal admonition (karma) against them.

He was admonished three times, yet he did not relinquish [his conduct]. Thereupon, the *niḥsaraṇa-pārivāsa* (act of banishment) was performed. This was established because the group of six [monks] knew [of his offense] and yet enticed him to keep [the forbidden items].

As for "banishment" (*niḥsaraṇa*), it refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) that the Saṃgha performs against him. As for "keeping" (*parivāsa*), it means if one keeps [the items] oneself.

If one lures another person, whether luring them oneself or instructing another to lure them, and stays overnight with them—whether arriving before, after, or simultaneously—and lies down on one's side and turns over, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in cases such as not knowing beforehand, and so forth, as explained in detail above.
If a bhikṣu, when other bhikṣus are admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma, speaks thus: "I will not train in this precept now;
I shall instead question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya," it is a pāyattika. However, if it is for the sake of understanding or training, he should indeed question them. (Seventy-one)
This was established because of Cchanda.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to what the Buddha has taught.

When he is being admonished in accordance with the Dharma, if he speaks such words and his speech is clear, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not clear, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [The same applies for] a bhikṣuṇī.
A *pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if the bhikṣu speaks thus because he is ignorant and lacks understanding;
or if the bhikṣu says, "Go back and ask your upādhyāya or ācārya; you should further study, inquire, and recite the sūtras";
or if the matter is actually so; or if spoken in jest, or as a dream-tale, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus: "Venerable sirs, what is the use of reciting these minor and trivial precepts?
When these precepts are recited, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt," because he has disparaged the precepts, it is a pāyattika (seventy-two).
The assembly of bhikṣus recited the True Dharma and the Vinaya. Fearing that they might become proficient, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus frequently raised charges against me, saying:
"If you wish to recite, you should recite only the four matters and the thirteen matters; you should not recite anything else," and so forth.
Other bhikṣus, perceiving their intention to destroy the Dharma, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
When that bhikṣu speaks for himself, speaks on behalf of another, or recites [the precepts], he says:
"Venerable sir, what is the use of reciting these minor and trivial rules? If one wishes to recite, one should recite only the four pārājika offenses and the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses."
Why is this? If, when reciting these precepts, one causes others to harbor doubts, feel vexed, or be ashamed:
if the recitation is clear, it is a *pāyattika*; if not clear, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one reviles the *vinaya*, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one reviles the *abhidharma* or other sūtras, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is likewise.

It is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense in the following cases: if one tells [the other] to first recite the Abhidharma, to first recite the Sūtras, and only then recite the Vinaya;

if one has an illness and must wait until it is cured before reciting the Vinaya; if one does not intend to cause the extinction of the Dharma; or in cases such as joking speech or speaking to oneself.

If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus: "Only now do I know this rule, which is included in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra and is recited every half-month," and other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three such recitations of the precepts, let alone more—then that bhikṣu is ignorant and lacks understanding;
if he has committed an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, this increases the offense of ignorance. He says, "Venerable one, you have gained no benefit; it was not well-obtained by you.
When the precepts were being recited, you did not apply your mind, nor did you listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus. Because of that ignorance, it is a *pāyattika* (seventy-three).
Among the group of six monks, there was one bhikṣu who, recognizing his own karmic obstacles and fearing that a pure bhikṣu might expose them, went ahead and spoke these words to him.
The bhikṣus, having discerned the reason for this, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.

When that bhikṣu, whether during his own recitation of the precepts, when another recites them, or when the precepts are being chanted, speaks in this manner, other bhikṣus should know that this bhikṣu has sat in the uposatha assembly two or three times, let alone more.

He shall be dealt with according to the Dharma for the offense he has committed; furthermore, he should be charged with an additional offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). If it is not so administered, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

There is no offense if one has never heard the recitation of the precepts before and hears it for the first time now, or if one has never heard the detailed exposition before and hears it for the first time now, or if [the words] were spoken in jest, in private conversation, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu, after a formal communal act (karmavācanā) has been performed together, later says,
"The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to personal favoritism," it is a pāyattika offense (seventy-four).
When the monk Trapusa was managing monastic affairs and hosting a gathering, he was unable to attend because his robes were worn out.

The community of monks performed a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to give him their robes. At that time, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) was also present in the assembly;
later, they spoke of this matter again, and thus [the Buddha] established the rule.

"Those who are intimate" refers to those who share the same preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the same instructor (*ācārya*), and who are close in their daily conduct, such as sitting, rising, and conversing.
"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to the items mentioned above: robes, alms bowls, needle cases, sitting mats (*niṣīdana*), and so on, down to drinking vessels and water containers.
If that bhikṣu had previously participated in the formal ritual (karmavācanā) with the community of monks, and later regrets it, saying, "The bhikṣus are partial toward their close associates;
they have given monastic property to them," then if he speaks clearly, it is a pāyattika offense; if he does not speak clearly, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if... [the text continues].
It is indeed so. Or [if it is] in jest, etc.
If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha’s legal proceedings have not yet concluded, rises and departs without having given his consent (*chanda*), it is a *pāyattika* (seventy-fifth).

A group of bhikṣus gathered in one place to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya. The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus, suspecting that a formal ritual (karmavācanā) was being performed against them, rose from their seats and departed.
Because the community of monks stopped [the discussion] but they did not remain, [the Buddha] established this rule.
Regarding "matters": these refer to the eighteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, from "dharma" and "non-dharma" up to "speaking" and "not speaking.

If a bhikṣu rises and departs while a formal legal proceeding of the Saṃgha is not yet concluded, and goes outside the door, it is a pāyattika offense. This applies if even one foot is outside the door, and so forth.
In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*. For the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if there is business for the Saṃgha, business for a stūpa, or business regarding the care of the sick; or if one has given one’s consent (*chanda*) before departing;
or if one is mute and unable to give consent; or if the *karman* is contrary to the Dharma or contrary to the Vinaya.
If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (*chanda*), later regrets it, it is a *pāyattika* offense (76).
Among the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) monks, there was one who had committed an offense; fearing that the Saṃgha would censure him, the six men followed him at all times without parting.
The community of monks was unable to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against him. Later, when it was time to make robes, they were summoned, and he replied:
"You must not go. The Sangha said, "We shall have one or two people bring the *chanda* (consent). Thereupon, they sent one bhikṣu to come.
The Sangha immediately performed the *karmavācanā* for this bhikṣu. When this bhikṣu returned, the group of six asked him about it and learned the reason.
He then said, "Those who performed the *karmavācanā* did so improperly; the *karman* was not valid.
I gave my consent (*chanda*) regarding that specific matter, not for this one. The monks censured him and reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established a precept.
If one has given consent and later regrets it, it is a *pāyattika* offense if the statement was clear; it is a *dukkaṭa* offense if it was not clear.

For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if it was not actually a formal act (*karmavācanā*), or if it was said in jest, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu, after having engaged in a dispute with other bhikṣus, listens to these words and reports them to those [disputants], it is a pāyattika (77).
This rule was established because of the six groups of nuns who initiated the matter.
Regarding "disputes": there are disputes over speech, disputes over seeking, disputes over offenses, and disputes over matters. Regarding "eavesdropping": to listen secretly to the speech of others.
To go and hear it constitutes a *pāyattika*; if one hears it without having gone, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one employs a means to go but does not go, and so forth, [it is likewise].
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If two people are conversing together in a dark place, one should snap one’s fingers or cough to alert them.
If two people are conversing in a secluded place, one should likewise snap one’s fingers or cough.
If two people are walking on a road ahead of one and are conversing together, one should likewise snap one’s fingers or cough. Failing to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for a bhikṣuṇī.
A *pāyattika* offense. For the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one intends to perform an illegal and non-disciplinary (*adharma-aviniya*) formal act (*karma*);

or if it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, or for one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*), up to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and one listens with the intent to cause them harm, disadvantage, or the loss of their right to reside through a formal act.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika (seventy-eighth).
This was established because one bhikṣu among the group of six struck a bhikṣu from the group of seventeen out of anger.
Regarding striking: whether with the hand, a stone, or a staff, it is in all cases a *pāyattika*. This also applies to other door-bolts or curved hooks.
Regarding the handles of a whisk (*cāmara*) or an incense burner (*dhūpakaṭacchuka*): one who strikes them with the finger commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;

for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in cases where, due to illness, it is necessary to push or strike; or when choking, it is necessary to tap the spine;
or if, while conversing, one does not hear [the other], and touches them so that they may hear; or during sleep, when one’s body rests upon another; or when passing by.

[This concludes] the practice. If, while sweeping the ground, one accidentally touches [another], or if a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika (seventy-ninth).
This rule was also established because it originated from a previous person.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

There is no offense if one raises one's hand to ward off another who intends to strike, or if an elephant approaches, or a thief approaches, or a predatory beast approaches, or someone holding a weapon approaches, and one raises one's hand to ward them off. Or...
If one waves a hand to beckon and thereby causes an accidental touch, or if one pokes someone so that they hear one's words,
and if a bhikṣu, out of anger, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika* (eighty).
It is also established as an offense because it arises from a previous person:
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if one speaks the truth to cause reform, or if it is spoken in jest, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkled lineage while the king has not yet gone out and the treasures have not yet been stored away,
and he crosses the threshold of the palace gate, it is a pāyattika (eighty-one).
Queen Mallikā exhorted King Prasenajit; having gained faith and joy, he permitted the bhikṣus to enter and leave the palace gates without obstruction.
When Kālodāyin entered the palace, the king and the queen were sleeping during the day.
Seeing the Venerable One from afar, they immediately rose, adjusted their robes, and prepared a seat for him to sit. The queen, however, lost her garment and was exposed; she was filled with shame.
He remained crouching. When the Venerable One returned to the monastery, he spoke to the bhikṣus, who expressed their disapproval and reprimanded him.
They informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Regarding the "water-sprinkling seed" [rite]: one takes the waters of the four great oceans and the horn of a white bull;
all seeds are gathered and placed within it, which is then set upon a golden palanquin. This is given to the minor kings, while the King receives the foremost portion.
The queen sat together with him upon the palanquin. The great brahmin poured water upon the crown of the king’s head.
If one is of the kṣatriya caste, the king is thus established by pouring water upon his head; therefore, he is called a kṣatriya king of the "water-poured-head" lineage.
If one is of the brāhmaṇa caste, the king is likewise established by pouring water upon his head, and he also [occupies] the position of a kṣatriya.

If the King has not yet been consecrated by the sprinkling of water, if he has not yet emerged [from his seclusion], if the female attendants have not yet returned to their original names, and if the treasures—gold, silver, and all manner of precious jewels and necklaces—have not yet been stored away;
if one enters the royal palace and crosses the threshold, it is a *pāyattika*. If one foot is inside and so forth, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*. If...
If one enters the dwellings of other minor kings scattered like grains, or the houses of wealthy and noble elders, and crosses their thresholds, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For the other four assemblies, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if there is something to report or inform, or if they have invited one to enter.
Or if one is coerced by force; or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

or if a bhikṣu himself takes, or causes another to take, gems or gem-ornaments—except within a monastery or a lodging—this is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu, while in a monastery or a lodging, takes [them]...

[Regarding] jewels: if one uses jewels for adornment, whether holding them oneself or instructing another to hold them, one should form this thought: "If there is an owner who recognizes [them], they shall take them.
One should act according to such causes and conditions, and not otherwise. (82)
There was a non-Buddhist lay follower traveling on the road who forgot a bag containing a thousand pieces of gold.
Several bhikṣus saw it and took it away, intending to wait for its rightful owner. When the lay follower hurried back, they immediately brought it out and returned it to him.

However, he instead considered it insufficient and sued King Prasenajit. The king investigated and realized his deception; he confiscated the man’s household assets and had them entirely forfeited to the state. Therefore, this regulation was established. *Vibhaṅga*.
Śāgaramātṛ removed her jewelry and placed it beneath a tree before going to see the World-Honored One. With her mind fixed upon the Dharma, she forgot to take it back home.
A bhikṣu informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha declared that taking up and securing items within a monastery is permitted.

Furthermore, while traveling through a village without a permanent residence, a bhikṣu stayed overnight at the house of a craftsman. The craftsman left his gold and silver inside the house and departed.
Because the bhikṣus remained awake throughout the night for the sake of guarding [the lodgings], they returned and informed the World-Honored One.

Therefore, he permitted the collection and storage of treasures at the lodging places. "Treasures" refers to gold, silver, pearls, amber, tridacna shell, agate, lapis lazuli, cowries, jade, and wrought or unwrought gold.
"Jewels" refers to those adorned with copper, iron, lead, tin, white wax, and various other precious materials.

If a bhikṣu, while within a monastery or inside a house, should personally take hold of, or instruct another to take hold of, a jewel or a jewel-adornment, he must recognize the characteristics of the bag or vessel, the characteristics of the wrapping, and the characteristics of the fastening. He should open the bag or vessel and know how many [parts] are joined together.
How many are unconnected? How many are square? How many are round? How many are old? How many are new? If there is someone who comes seeking, one should ask:
"What does your object resemble? If it corresponds, one should return it; if it does not correspond, one should say: "I have not seen such an object.
If two people come seeking together, one should ask: "What does your object resemble? If they...
Those who claim it belongs to them should return; if they do not agree, one should say, "I did not see such an object.
If both parties' claims are consistent, one should place the object before them and say, "This is your property; you may each take it away.
If they do not recognize the characteristics of the bag, the wrapping, or the fastenings, or if they open the bag and do not examine how many seams or joints there are—
If they have not been strung together, how many are square? How many are round? How many are new? How many are old? In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;

for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if these are ornaments for the adornment of a stūpa or monastery, and they are collected and stored for the sake of durability.
If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika (83).
Vanaṃdaka entered a village at an improper time and played dice with a householder. When the householder did not win, out of stinginess and jealousy, he said:
"When bhikṣus enter a village in the early morning, it is for the sake of begging for food; why have you entered the village at an improper time?"

Because of such matters, a regulation was established: if there is a matter concerning the Saṃgha, a matter concerning a stūpa, or a matter concerning the care of the sick, one may entrust one's affairs to another bhikṣu and depart.
If one is staying alone in a single room, one should entrust one's affairs to a neighboring room.
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light. "Bhikṣu" refers to a fellow resident who is capable of being entrusted with the matter.
To enter a village at an improper time without having received such an entrustment: upon first crossing the threshold of the village gate, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one foot is inside the gate and so forth, it is a *duṣkṛta* for all [monastics];
for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if the path passes through a village;
or if there is something to be announced; or if one has accepted an invitation; or if one is seized by force; or if one is bound and led away; or if it concerns life...
It is difficult to practice the holy life.
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata, excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes;
once finished, if they exceed this height, it is a pāyattika (eighty-four).
Kālodāyin, knowing in advance that the Buddha would come by this path, immediately prepared a high and fine seat upon the road.
The Buddha, perceiving the evil intent harbored within him, rebuked him, saying: "This foolish man! I have established this rule solely for his own sake."
If one performs it oneself or instructs another to perform it, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense if completed; if not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes another to do it for oneself, it is a *dukkaṭa* whether completed or not. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if the other person has already completed the gift and he cuts it to use it, or if he removes the legs.
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed, a wooden bed, or a large or small mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton,
and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* (85).
The group of six monks did this. Laypeople resented their lack of shame and lack of compassion, as if they were royal ministers;
therefore, it was prohibited. Regarding *tūla*: it refers to the flowers of the white poplar, willow, or reed.
A large mat is for the purpose of sitting and lying down; a small one is for the purpose of sitting. The gravity of the offense is as explained above. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.

For the other three groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if it is made of *kaurava* grass, *manuja* grass, *śāpa* grass, or if it is made of wool, cotton, or tattered rags; or if it is used as a shoulder-support or as a pillow for the head.
If a bhikṣu has a needle case made of bone, ivory, or horn, having carved or scraped it into shape, it is a pāyattika (86). Because there were faithful artisans who,
for the sake of making needle cases of bone, ivory, or horn for bhikṣus, abandoned their household livelihoods and were left without clothing or food,
and because worldly people said that those seeking merit instead incurred calamity, this rule was established.
The gravity of the offense is the same as above. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one uses iron, copper, lead, tin, white wax, bamboo, wood, reeds, or *śara* grass to make a needle case.
Whether they are made as the knob of a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), the handle of a parasol, or the knob of a ladle;

or as curved hooks, scrapers for removing impurities, *maniratna*-shaped toggles, or keys; or as spoons, ladles, hooks for cleaning clothing, eye-salve applicators, tongue-scrapers, or objects for picking teeth;
or as ear-pickers, meditation weights, or nose-irrigation tubes.
If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must make it according to the prescribed measure. The measure here is: two spans of the Buddha’s hand in length, one and a half spans in width;
it may be increased by an additional half span in both length and width. If it exceeds this, having finished cutting it, it is a pāyattika offense (87).

The Buddha, seeing that the bedding and seats of the Saṃgha were defiled by impurities, permitted the bhikṣus to make *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) for the purpose of protecting the body, the robes, and the bedding.
Because the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) then made them excessively large, he established a regulation [limiting their size].
Kālodāyin, being large in stature, was unable to sit [on the small mat]; while on the road leading toward the Buddha’s location, he pulled at his *niṣīdana* with his hands.
Regarding the meditation mat (*niṣīdana*): if one wishes to make it larger, the Buddha, knowing this, permitted an increase of half a *vitasti* (span) in both length and width.

As for the meditation mat, it is spread beneath one’s seat.
