If it exceeds the prescribed measure in length but not in width, or exceeds the measure in width but not in length, or exceeds the measure in both length and width, and one completes it oneself, it is an *pāyattika* offense. [If one does not complete it oneself...]
It constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is the same when instructing another to do so. If one does it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, or makes it less than the measure;
or if one obtains from another a pre-made item and cuts it to the proper measure; or if one folds it double.
If a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. Herein, the measurement is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width.
If he finishes making it exceeding these dimensions, it is a pāyattika (eighty-eighth).
A bhikṣu suffered from a carbuncle, scabies, and sores; the pus and blood stained his body, robes, and bedding. The Buddha permitted him to keep a wound-covering cloth (*vastra*).
However, when he wore the coarse, hairy cloth over the sore, lifting the cloth caused him pain. The Buddha then permitted him to cover the sore with a fine, soft cloth.
When putting on the *nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī*, the group of six [monks] made them excessively large and long; therefore, it was prescribed:

"The wound-covering robe (*vastra-ābādhika*) is for various types of wounds and illnesses; one should use it to cover the body. The rules regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not are the same as above.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measurements. Herein, the measurement is six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width.
Should it exceed these, it must be cut down; [otherwise] it is a pāyattika (89).
It was also established because it originated with the group of six [monks]. The rules regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not are as stated above.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to that of the Tathāgata, or makes one exceeding that size, it is a pāyattika. In this matter:
Regarding the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s robe: it is ten *vitasti* (handspans) in length and six *vitasti* in width; this is called the dimension of the Tathāgata’s robe (90).
The Venerable Nanda was four fingers shorter than the Buddha. When the bhikṣus saw him from afar, they all thought it was the Buddha and immediately rose.
They went out to welcome him, only then realizing it was Nanda; both felt ashamed.

When the Buddha ordained that Nanda should wear black robes, he prohibited the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) from making robes equal in size to the Tathāgata’s or larger than them. Thus was the rule established.
The offenses and non-offenses are the same as before. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The sixth of the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas:
If a bhikṣu enters a village and, being without illness, takes food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
Regarding "eating": that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable sir. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession) (1).
At that time, grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain. Whenever the nun Utpalavarṇā received food through begging, she would immediately give it to the bhikṣu.
Later, a certain elder riding in a carriage went to have an audience with the king; the nun, avoiding the path, fell into a muddy pit and lay there prostrate upon the ground.

The elder ordered his attendants to assist him out. Upon questioning, he learned the reason for the incident; because he resented the monk’s lack of propriety in yielding the food, he established this rule:
if one who is not ill receives food with one's own hand and eats it, there is a *pāṭidesanīya* offense for every swallow. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one is ill, or if the food is placed on the ground to be given, or if someone else is made to hand it over.

Whether it be given in a monastery, or given outside a village, or given within a nunnery—if a bhikṣu goes to the house of a layperson to eat and there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who points out [food], saying, "Give such-and-such a person soup;
give such-and-such a person rice," that bhikṣu should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows: "Sister, please stop for a moment."
The bhikṣus must wait until they have finished eating. If there is not even one bhikṣu present, they should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, please stop for a moment; we must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating. If this occurs, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying:

"Venerable sirs, I have committed a censurable act which ought not to have been done. I now confess my transgression before you, venerable sirs. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).
(2) When the group of six bhikṣus were eating at the home of a layperson, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs requested soup and rice for them,
skipping those in the middle and serving out of order, thereby preventing the bhikṣus in the middle from eating. It was therefore established as a precept.

For the other four assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if a nun herself acts as the donor, or if the donor directs the nun to make the distribution, and she does not intentionally give preferentially.

If a *kula-karma* (formal act regarding a family) has previously been performed for a family, and a bhikṣu, without having been invited by such a family and while not being ill, accepts food with his own hand and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"I have committed a censurable act which ought not to be done; I now confess this to the Venerable One. This rule is called the *deśanā-dharma* (the rule of confession). (3)
There was a householder couple who both attained faith and joy. They gave to the bhikṣus without any sense of stinginess until they eventually fell into poverty.
Their neighbors criticized them, so the Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the *kula-karma* (formal act concerning a family) and established this precept.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one has previously accepted an invitation; or if one is ill;

or if the food is placed on the ground and given; or if it is received from another person; or if that family’s wealth and goods have returned to abundance and they request the Sangha to revoke the *kuladūṣaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring a family corrupt), and the Sangha grants them the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation), and one goes there after the revocation has been completed.
If a bhikṣu dwells in an araṇya that is remote and subject to suspicion or fear,
and while staying in such an araṇya, he does not first inform a donor, and then— without being ill—
accepts food with his own hands outside the monastery and eats it inside the monastery, he should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir..."
Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done. I now repent before the Venerable one.
This rule is called the Rule of Repentance (4).
Various women, carrying food and drink, went to the monastery to make offerings. Thieves heard of this and waylaid them on the road, harassing them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, you should tell the women not to go out, as there are thieves on the road who cause fear.
If they have already left the city, you should tell them not to go into the monastery, as there are thieves on the road who cause fear."
This precept is thus established.
There is no offense if one has first informed the donor; or if one is ill; or if the food is placed on the ground for one to take; or if one instructs another to give it;
or if the person comes to receive instructions or listen to the Dharma, at which time the bhikṣu gives them his own private food.
The Seventh Section of One Hundred Śikṣākarāṇī Dharmas (all enacted because they originated with the group of six bhikṣus):
One should learn to wear the antaravāsaka properly and neatly. (1)
Regarding "not being neat": sometimes it is worn low, and sometimes it is worn high; sometimes it is shaped like an elephant's trunk, or like the leaves of a *tāla* tree;
and sometimes it has fine pleats. "Low" means tied at the waist below the navel; "high" means hitched up level with the knees.
"Elephant trunk" refers to having one corner hang down in front. "Tāla leaf" refers to having two corners hang down in front. "Fine pleats" refers to pleated folds encircling the waist.
If done intentionally, it is an offense requiring confession (*sāpattika duṣkṛta*); because it was done intentionally, it is also an offense of improper conduct (*aduṣkṛta*).
If not done intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The following cases for the other four assemblies should be understood accordingly.
The same applies here. There is no offense in the following cases: if a sore has developed at the navel and it is worn low; if there is a sore on the calf and it is worn high;
or if one is inside a monastery, outside a village, engaged in work, or traveling on a road.
One should wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner; this is how one should train (2). As for what is not neat:
letting them hang down past the elbows so that the ribs are exposed; wearing them too high so that they rise above the calves; letting one corner hang down;
letting the two front corners hang down while hitching up the back with high, narrow pleats and securing the edge. There is no offense if [the robe covers] the shoulder and arm.
If there is an ulcer, one may place [the hand] underneath; otherwise, it is as stated above.
One must not enter the house of a layperson with the robe tucked up behind the back; this is a training rule (3).
"Tucking the robe up behind the back" means either tucking the left or right side of the robe up onto the shoulder. There is no offense if [it is tucked up] at the ribs.

If one has sores, whether within a monastery, outside a village, while traveling on the road, or while working, one must not sit in the house of a layperson with one's robe tucked back over the shoulders; this is how one should train (4).
One must not enter the house of a layperson with the robe wrapped around the neck; this is a training rule (5).
"Wrapping the neck" means grasping both corners of the robe and placing them over the left and right shoulders. There is no offense if there are sores on the shoulder or arm;
otherwise, it is as explained above.
One should train oneself: (6) not to enter the house of a layperson with one’s robe wrapped around the neck while seated.
One should train oneself: (7) not to enter the house of a layperson with one’s head covered.

Regarding covering the head: whether with tree leaves, fragments of material, or clothing, there is no offense if one is suffering from cold, or has a sore on the head, or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered while seated (8).
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson by jumping (9).
"Jumping" means leaping with both feet together. There is no offense if, at times, one has such an illness;
or if struck by someone; or if there are thieves; or if there are wild beasts; or if there are thorns and brambles; or if crossing a canal.
Whether crossing a ditch or wading through mud, one must not leap across to enter the house of a layperson and sit there; this is a training to be observed (10).
One must not squat while inside the house of a layperson; this is a training to be observed (11).
Regarding squatting: whether on the ground or on a bed, if the buttocks do not touch the ground, there is no offense.
Exceptions include cases where sores have developed on the buttocks, or when one is giving something, performing a prostration, confessing an offense, or receiving instruction.
One must not walk into the house of a layperson with hands placed on the hips; this is a training rule (twelfth).

"With hands on the hips" means to place the hands upon the waist, supporting the elbows. There is no offense if sores have developed under the ribs, or if one is within a monastery or similar location.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my hands resting on my hips while seated" (13).
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while swaying my body" (14).
"Shaking the body" means turning the body to the left or right while walking.
"Not committing an offense" refers to instances such as when one has a certain illness, or when struck by another person and turns the body to the side to avoid the blow;

or when a rogue elephant approaches, or is threatened by bandits, lions, or other fierce beasts; or when encountering someone carrying thorns—turning the body to avoid such things—or when crossing [a river].
In muddy water or when crossing a ditch or canal, one may sway the body to pass through; or at times, having put on the robes, one may turn the body to check that they are properly arranged.
One must not sway the body while entering the house of a layperson to sit down; this is how one should train. (15)
One must not walk into the house of a layperson with swinging arms; this is a training rule (16).
"Swinging arms" means swinging the arms back and forth while walking. There is no offense if one is walking with companions who are falling behind and uses the hand to beckon them;
otherwise, it is as stated above.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with arms swinging about while seated (17).
One should train oneself to enter the house of a layperson with the body well-covered (18).
One should train oneself to sit in the homes of white-robed laypeople with the body properly covered, not exposing it here and there.
This is not an offense if one is bound, or if the wind blows the robe away from the body (19).
One must not walk into the house of a layperson while looking left and right; this is a training rule (the twentieth).
"Looking left and right" means gazing about in various directions. There is no offense if one looks up to observe the time or the season.

If there is danger to one's life or danger to one's holy life (brahmacarya), and one seeks a means of escape by looking here and there, one must not sit in the house of a layperson while looking around; this is how one should train. (21)
One should train oneself to enter the homes of laypeople in silence (22).

One who is not silent means one who speaks loudly or calls out at the top of one's voice. There is no offense if it is for the sake of entrusting [the meal], or if one must call out loudly to give food.
There is no offense if one is deaf and must call out loudly, or if one must entrust [the meal] loudly, or if one must give food loudly, or if there is an emergency.
It is difficult to practice the holy life;
one should train oneself to run away with a loud voice and sit silently in the house of a layperson (23).
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson while laughing or joking (24).
"Laughing and joking" means to laugh with the teeth exposed. There is no offense if the lips are painful and the teeth cannot be covered, or if one laughs out of joy while recollecting the Dharma.
One must not sit in the homes of laypeople laughing and joking; this is how one should train. (Twenty-five)
One should train oneself to eat with mindfulness (26). Regarding "not eating without mindfulness":
this refers to discarding soup or rice while eating. There is no offense if, because the bowl is small, one discards rice while eating, or if it falls back onto the table.
One should train oneself to receive food with a level bowl (27).
"With a level bowl" means not overflowing it; the rest is as explained above.
One should train oneself to receive soup with a level bowl (28).
One should train oneself [in the following]: regarding food such as soup and rice, [one should not eat] unequally.

"Unequally" means that the soup has not yet arrived while the rice is already finished, or the rice has not yet arrived while the soup is already finished. There is no offense in the following cases: [if the meal is interrupted by another person, or if one is ill].
Sometimes one may need only rice and not soup; sometimes one may need only soup and not rice; or when the time for eating is about to pass;
or when there is danger to life or danger to the holy life—one may eat quickly.
One should train oneself to eat in proper sequence (thirtieth).
To eat out of sequence means to take food from various places within the bowl and eat it.

There is no offense if one picks at the cool parts because the rice is hot, or if the time for the meal is about to pass, or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life, and one eats quickly.
One must not eat by scooping from the center of the bowl. This is how one should train (31).
"Scooping" means to push the food toward the four sides, leaving the center until reaching the bottom of the bowl. The rest is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu is not ill, he must not seek out plain soup and rice for himself; this is a training rule (thirty-second).
There is no offense if he seeks it for himself when ill, or if he seeks it for another, or if another seeks it for him.
One should not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more; this is a training rule (33).
One should not look into the bowl of a neighboring seat-mate; this is a training rule (34).

"Regarding 'observing': one observes who has more and who has less. Regarding 'not transgressing': if the person sitting nearby is blind, one must observe whether they can see the food or not, whether it is permissible or impermissible, and whether it has been received or not."
One should eat with the thought that one's alms-bowl is tied [to one’s waist]; this is how one should train (35).
"With the thought that the bowl is not tied" means looking around to the left and right; the rest is as explained above.
One must not take large mouthfuls of rice when eating; this is how one should train (36).
A "large mouthful" is one that cannot be accommodated within the mouth. There is no offense in cases such as when the time for eating is about to expire.
One must not wait for food with the mouth wide open; this is how one should train (37).
Regarding "waiting with the mouth open": before the morsel of rice has even arrived, one first opens the mouth wide in anticipation. The rest is as explained above.
One must not speak with food in the mouth; this is a training rule (38).
To speak with food in the mouth means that when rice remains in the mouth, one’s speech is indistinct and causes others to fail to understand. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one is choking and seeks water; or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if one makes a sound while eating.
One shall not form a lump of rice and cast it into the mouth from a distance; this is a training to be observed (39).
One commits no offense if one is bound [in fetters].
One shall train so as not to let food fall [on the ground] (40).
Regarding "dropped": half has entered the mouth and half remains in the hand.
There is no offense if one eats thin cakes, scorched rice, or if [the food consists of] melons, sugarcane, vegetables, *āmra* fruits, *bījapūra* fruits, grapes, medicinal leaves, or medicinal hearts.
One shall not eat with cheeks puffed out; this is a training rule (41).
"Eating with cheeks puffed out" means intentionally filling the mouth so full that both cheeks bulge, resembling the appearance of a monkey.
There is no offense in cases such as when the time for eating is about to expire.
One should not eat making noise while chewing rice; this is a training rule (42).
There is no offense if one is chewing dry cakes, scorched rice, or the like.
One should not take large mouthfuls of rice when eating; this is a training rule (43).
Regarding "sucking at food": one should not open the mouth wide and call out from afar while sucking.

There is no offense if the mouth is painful, or if one is eating soup, curd, or curd-milk and the like, as it is not permitted to lick with the tongue; this is how one should train (the forty-fourth).
"Regarding licking with the tongue: one shall not lick the balls of rice with the tongue while eating.
There is no offense if one is bound, or if the hands are soiled with mud such that one cannot shake them to eat; in these cases, one should train accordingly. (45)
There is no offense in the following cases: if there is grass or insects in the food; if one wishes to shake off impurities from the hand;
or if the hand has become defiled by touching food that has not yet been formally received, and one shakes it off.
One must not eat by holding scattered grains of rice in the hand; one should train [in this] (46).
"Scattered grains" refers to rice that has been dropped or discarded; the remainder is as explained above.
One must not hold a drinking vessel with soiled hands; this is how one should train (47).
"Soiled hands" refers to hands that have rice mixed with oil clinging to them. There is no offense if one receives [the drink] on grass or on a leaf.
One should receive [food] with washed hands.
One must not discard bowl-washing water inside a layperson’s residence; this is how one should train (48).
Regarding "bowl-washing water": it is water mixed with rice. There is no offense if one receives the water in a basin and carries it outside to discard it.
One must not void excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva upon living grass or vegetables, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (forty-nine).

There is no offense if one voids excrement or urine in a place where there is no grass or vegetables, but it subsequently falls onto living grass or vegetables, or is blown by the wind or carried by birds into living grass or vegetables.
One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water, except when ill; this is a training rule (50).
One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is a training rule (51).
There is no offense if one is bound, or if the feet are covered with filth and grime;
if one is unable to fold the robe over the shoulder; or if one is preaching the Dharma to a person who lacks respect—except in cases of illness. One should train oneself accordingly. (52)
There is no offense if one is a king or a high minister;
however, one must not preach the Dharma to someone who has wrapped a cloth around their neck, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train. (53)
One should not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (54).
One should not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads wrapped, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (55).
One should not preach the Dharma to one who has their hands on their hips, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (56).
One should not preach the Dharma to one wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (57).
One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (58).
One must not preach the Dharma to those riding on vehicles, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (59).
One must not stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it; this is how one should train (the sixtieth rule).
There is no offense if one is seized by force, or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
One must not conceal wealth or goods within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of securing them; this is a training rule (61).
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa wearing leather sandals; this is a training rule (62).
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in my hands.
(63) One should train oneself: "I shall not circumambulate a Buddhist stūpa while wearing leather sandals. (64)
One should train oneself not to wear leather footwear while entering a Buddhist stūpa (65).
One should train oneself not to carry leather footwear while entering a Buddhist stūpa (66).
One must not sit and eat beneath a stūpa, leaving grass or food to defile the ground; this is how one should train (67).
There is no offense if one gathers [the refuse] by one's feet and carries it away for disposal when departing.
One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa; this is a training rule (68).
There is no offense if one must travel by that path or if one is constrained by force.
One must not bury a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a training rule (69).
One must not cremate a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a training rule (70).
One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a training rule (71).
One must not burn a corpse on the four sides of a Buddha-stūpa so that its foul odor enters within; this is a training rule (72).
One should train oneself: it is not permitted to pass beneath a stūpa carrying a corpse’s garment or a bed, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed with incense (73).
One should train oneself: it is not permitted to defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha-stūpa (74).
One should train oneself not to defecate or urinate toward a Buddha-stūpa (75).
One should train oneself not to defecate or urinate around the four sides of a Buddha-stūpa so that the stench enters within (76).
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination; this is a training rule (77).
There is no offense if the path passes through such a place, or if one is held by force.
One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick beneath a Buddha stūpa.
(78) One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick facing a Buddha stūpa. (79)
One should train oneself not to chew tooth-sticks within four paces of a Buddha stūpa (80).
One should train oneself not to spit or sneeze beneath a Buddha stūpa (81).
One must not spit toward a Buddha-stūpa; this is a training to be observed (82).
One must not spit on the four sides of a stūpa; this is a training to be observed (83).
One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa; this is how one should train (84).
There is no offense if there is a partition between [the stūpa and oneself] or if one is held by force.
One must not occupy an upper room while placing the Buddha in a lower room; this is a training rule (85).
There is no offense in cases of danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
One should train oneself thus: when another is seated and one is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
(86) One should train oneself thus: when another is lying down and one is seated, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. (87)
If another person is seated and one is not seated, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (88).
If another person is on a high seat and one is on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (89).
When another person is walking ahead and one is walking behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (90).
When another person is on a higher walking path and one is on a lower walking path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness;
this is a training rule (91).
If another person is on the path and oneself is not on the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when they are ill;
this is a training rule (92). One should train so as not to walk along a path holding hands with others (93).
There is no offense if one has impaired vision and requires assistance;
however, one must not climb a tree higher than a person's height, except under special circumstances. This is how one should train. (94)
One must not walk with a bowl placed in a net-bag, suspended from the head of a staff over one’s shoulder; this is a training rule (95).
There is no offense in cases such as being seized by force.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who carries a staff and is disrespectful, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (96).
There is no offense in the case of kings and great ministers.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (97).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a spear, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (98).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (ninety-ninth).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (one hundredth).
The Seventh Method for Settling Disputes, the Eighth [Section] (contained within the *Khandhaka on Settling Disputes* in the Third Division).

There are four kinds of disputes. First, a dispute over speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*): when bhikṣus engage in verbal dispute with other bhikṣus, citing eighteen grounds for dispute—namely, what is Dharma and what is not Dharma, up to what has been spoken and what has not been spoken. If they thus engage in verbal dispute based on such characteristics, it consequently...

They fight with one another. Second, disputes regarding accusations: a bhikṣu accuses another bhikṣu of an offense based on three grounds—breaking the precepts, breaking views, or breaking conduct—and through what has been seen, heard, or suspected; he thus seeks out the offense in such a manner.
Third, disputes regarding transgressions: there are seven kinds of offenses: first, pārājika; second, saṃghāvaśeṣa; third, pāyattika; fourth, pratideśanīya; fifth, sthūlātyaya...

Lanchara. Six *duṣkṛta*s. Seven *durbhāṣita*s. Regarding the four types of disputes: they are the matters arising from disputes over speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*), the matters arising from disputes over searching (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*), and the matters arising from disputes over offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*).
Among these, disputes over speech are settled by two *vinaya* methods: namely, *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *yadbhūyaḥ-kṣānti* (settlement by the majority).
Or, they may be settled by one *vinaya* method: namely, *saṃmukha-vinaya*. Disputes over searching are settled by four *vinaya* methods.
Extinguishing (nirodha): that is, either by being present, by recollection, or by being present and non-delusion;

or by being present at the site of the offense, regarding the dispute over an offense, through the three *vinayas*—namely, by being present, through confession (*pratijñā-kāraka*), or by being present, through the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
Regarding disputes over matters, they are to be settled by all forms of *vinaya*.
According to the offense committed, one should apply the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused);
where *pratyakṣavinaya* is appropriate, it should be applied. Once Kālodāyin and the group of six had gone to the river to bathe, Kālodāyin finished bathing and stepped out onto the bank.
The group of six monks wore their robes thinking them to be their own; they departed without checking.
When the group of six reached the shore, they did not see their own robes, but saw only those of Kālodāyin. They immediately said, "Kālodāyin has stolen our robes.
Without the person being present, they proceeded to perform an act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (excommunication). Kālodāyin informed the Buddha, who then asked him about the matter.
[The monk] takes it with the thought, "This is my robe," and not with a thieving mind. The Buddha said: "There is no offense.
However, one should not wear a robe without having inspected it. One should not perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) in the absence of the person concerned. [These include:

the *karmavācanā* of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), the *karmavācanā* of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the *karmavācanā* of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), the *karmavācanā* of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople (*apratisaṃkhyāna-karman*), the *karmavācanā* of suspension (*utksepaṇīya-karman*), and the *karmavācanā* of formal reconciliation (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*)."
*Karmavācanā*. If a *karmavācanā* is performed and it is not validly accomplished, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

From this time forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) for the extinction of disputes. It should be explained as follows: What is "presence"?

Presence of the Dharma, presence of the Vinaya, presence of the person, and presence of the Saṃgha and the boundary. What is the presence of the Dharma? It is that which consists of the Dharma upheld for the extinction of disputes.
What is the presence of the *vinaya*? It is that which settles disputes by means of the *vinaya* as upheld.

What is the presence of the person? It is the exchange of words regarding the meaning [of the matter]. What is the presence of the Saṃgha? It is when they assemble together in one place for a common *karmavācanā*.
One who does not come is subject to formal instruction. One who is present and capable of being rebuked but is not rebuked is [one who has committed an offense].

What is "presence within the boundary"? It is when a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed within the boundary by those who have established a restriction. If a matter of dispute has been settled, yet it is raised again...
A *pāyattika*. To have given one’s consent and later regret it is a *pāyattika*. The same applies to the six subsequent methods of settling disputes (*vinayātyaya*).
One should grant the *smṛtivinaya*; when one ought to grant the *smṛtivinaya*, one shall grant the *smṛtivinaya*.
In the case of Trapusa-māra-putra, because he had not committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), the monks questioned him persistently;
he should be granted the *smṛti-vinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness). He should make three requests within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
I, so-and-so, have not committed a heavy offense. Yet the monks say that I have committed a heavy offense—a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*. The monks...
The Venerable Kāśyapa asked me, "Do you remember committing a grave offense? I replied, "I do not remember committing a grave offense;
I do not recall having committed such a grave offense. "Venerable elders, there is no need to repeatedly interrogate and press me," I said.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to interrogate and press me without ceasing. Therefore, I now request from the Saṃgha the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness).
"O Bhikṣuṇī, may the Saṃgha grant me the *patisāraṇīya-vinaya* out of compassion. The Saṃgha then performs the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This [monk] So-and-so has not committed a grave offense—whether a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
Yet all the bhikṣus claim he has committed a grave offense—ranging from a *pārājika* to a *sthūlātyaya*. The bhikṣus have questioned him..."
"Tell me, do you remember committing a grave offense, such as a *pārājika* or even a *sthūlātyaya*?
He does not remember committing a grave offense and immediately replies, "I have not committed a grave offense; O Elders, there is no need to interrogate me further."
Yet these bhikṣus continue to interrogate him without ceasing; he does not recall his offense and now requests from the Saṃgha the *vinaya* of recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: this is the formal motion (*jñapti*) for granting him the *vinaya* of recollection.

Regarding the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), it is stated: "What is the *yadbhūyaḥsammatā* (recollection) *vinaya*? That bhikṣu’s offense should no longer be formally raised, nor should the *yadbhūyaḥsammatā* be applied;
rather, the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict for one not insane) should be granted. The *amūḍhavinaya* shall indeed be granted."
The bhikṣu Nanda was deranged and his mind was disturbed, whereby he committed many offenses. Later, when he regained his sanity, the bhikṣus interrogated him incessantly;

therefore, the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict for one who is no longer insane) should be granted to him. He should make three requests within the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha should perform the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for him.
This should be understood as being according to the preceding rules. What is the *amūḍha-vinaya*? Regarding that bhikṣu’s offense, [it shall not be further...]
One should not bring it up; one should not cause him to be reminded of it.
He should be dealt with according to his own confession; he should indeed be dealt with according to his own confession.
When the Blessed One was reciting the precepts, there was one who had committed an offense who sat near the Buddha. The Buddha remained silent and did not speak. Maudgalyāyana...
He even knew this; he seized the man by the arm and dragged him out. The Buddha said, "One should not do so. He had the man acknowledge his guilt, and only then did he assign him the punishment.
How should one speak for oneself? One speaks of the name of the offense, the category of the offense, and performs repentance. How is the punishment administered? One says, "Reproach yourself;
let your mind give rise to weary detachment."
He should be granted the *tassapāpiyasika* (the procedure for searching out the offense). This is the formal determination of the offense.
When the bhikṣu Hastibala was debating with an outsider and was questioned intensely, his words were contradictory from beginning to end;
when questioned within the Saṃgha, his words were likewise contradictory from beginning to end; he intentionally uttered false speech in the midst of the assembly.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reviled and censured him. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the establishment of a place of censure (*āpattisthāna*).

Having assembled the Saṃgha, they performed the act of formal accusation (*codanā*) against him; having performed the accusation, they performed the act of calling to mind (*smṛti-vidhāna*); having performed the calling to mind, they imposed the offense upon him.

The motion was made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This son of the Śākya, Hastibala, is fond of debate. When he engaged in debate with the non-Buddhists and was subjected to pressing questions,"
Your words are contradictory from beginning to end. Even when questioned within the Saṃgha, your words are likewise contradictory from beginning to end;

you have intentionally uttered falsehoods before the assembly. If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now perform the *karmavācanā* for the place of punishment against the Śākya son, Hastika.
You, Hastika, have gained no benefit and have not attained what is wholesome; you shall be subjected to rigorous interrogation.
At that time, his words were contradictory from beginning to end; even when questioned by the Saṃgha, he was likewise so.

He intentionally uttered false speech in the midst of the assembly. The formal motion (*jñapti*) is made accordingly, and the ritual procedure (*karman*) is performed based thereon. What is the locus of the offense?
It refers to that monk’s offense for which the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and the formal act of calling to mind (*sativinaya*) are to be performed.
One should apply the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (decision by the majority). One must apply the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*. The monks of Śrāvastī were disputing;
the Saṃgha sought to determine the offense. The Buddha said: "The words of those who know the Dharma in great number should be employed. It is permitted to distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*).
A person to distribute the tallies shall be appointed through a formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). There are five qualities for which one should not be appointed."

Attachment, aversion, fear, delusion, and ignorance regarding what has been done and what has not been done—regarding those who possess the opposite of these five qualities, there are three ways to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*):

first, openly; second, in secret; and third, by whispering. Even if there are many unrighteous monks within the assembly, provided that their preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and others are all righteous, one should distribute the sticks openly; two types [of procedures] should be performed.

The voting sticks (*śalākā*) are of two kinds: those that are broken and those that are intact. One should announce: "Those who speak thus shall take up the intact sticks; those who speak thus shall take up the broken sticks.
Once the sticks have been distributed, they should be counted in a separate place. If those who act according to the Dharma are in the majority, he should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"For those who speak thus, the matter of dispute is settled. If those who act according to the Dharma are in the minority, one should simply pay respects and depart.
Arise and depart! Send a messenger to the place where the bhikṣus reside and announce within the Saṃgha: "In that residence, there are many bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma.
It would be well, O Elders, if you could go there; if the bhikṣus who speak according to the Dharma are numerous, the dispute will be settled and great merit will be gained.
Upon hearing this, those bhikṣus should go. If they do not go, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. If [the messenger] among the assembly...

Although there may be many bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma, if their preceptors (upādhyāya) and elders (sthavira) do not act in accordance with the Dharma, one should fear that the bhikṣus will follow their preceptors and others by taking up the voting sticks (śalākā). In such a case, the voting sticks should be distributed in secret.

Furthermore, even if there are many bhikṣus in the assembly who act in accordance with the Dharma, if those preceptors and others speak what is contrary to the Dharma, one should whisper [the instructions] into the ear.

The voting sticks (*śalākā*) are to be distributed. When distributing the voting sticks, one should sit with sufficient spacing so that there is room for one person’s body between each, providing a slight visual screen.
That bhikṣu should whisper to them, saying: "Your preceptors and others have already taken their voting sticks; it would be well if you also take a voting stick."
Out of compassion: if there are many bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma, the matter of dispute will be extinguished and much merit will be gained.
After the voting sticks have been cast, count them on one side.
"One should grant the *tṛṇaprastāra* (covering with grass); one shall grant the *tṛṇaprastāra*.

The monks of Śrāvastī were disputing; many of those monks had violated various rules of discipline and non-śramaṇa practices, both performing them and speaking of them, entering and leaving without restraint. Later, the monks thought to themselves: 'If we were to return...'"
They questioned one another about this matter, causing the dispute to become increasingly grave and heavy.
It persisted for months and years without being settled, preventing the Saṃgha from attaining peace and happiness. They reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"This dispute should be settled by the 'covering over with grass' (tṛṇaprastāraka) method. Then, a wise and capable bhikṣu from that community rose from his seat and knelt on his right knee.
Joining their palms, they spoke as follows: "Venerable Elders, regarding this matter of dispute among us, we have committed many offenses that are contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Our speech has been without moderation, and our coming and going, our movements and conduct, have not conformed to the rules of decorum.

If we were to investigate this matter thoroughly, we fear it would cause our offenses to become even more grave, and we would be unable to act in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the instructions of the Buddha."
The dispute has been settled, yet it causes the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort.
If the elders will forgive me, I now perform a "grass-covering-the-earth" confession for these offenses on behalf of the elders. The same should be said before the second assembly.
Those bhikṣus should then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents..."
Listen. The Sangha shall cause this matter of dispute to undergo the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) confession. The motion (*jñapti*) is as follows.
Having made this motion, one performs the *tṛṇaprastāraka* confession. One who possesses wisdom and capability kneels on the right knee, joins the palms, and makes this announcement:
"Venerable Elders, regarding these matters of dispute of mine and the offenses I have committed—excluding grave offenses and those that obstruct [the path]—"

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for entering the house of a layperson: "If the elders will permit it, for the sake of the elders and for those who have already performed the 'covering with grass' (*tṛṇapraticchādana*) confession, the second assembly should also speak in this manner. What is meant by "covering with grass"?
One who does not proclaim the name of the offense, but confesses the category of the offense, is [a true repentant].

According to the Vinaya texts, the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) are augmented by the addition of the *sthūlātyaya* to form six groups (*ṣaḍ-varga*), which are still listed after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Seven.

Thus, within the Vinaya, *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) are categorized as *dauḥśīlya* (misconduct). The term "section" (*pāda*) is derived from its specific articles, while the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) receives its name according to the gravity of the offense.
As listed and explained in the *Sìfēn lǜ shìchāo*, neither "sections" nor "aggregates" exist [as literal categories]; they are merely translated according to their semantic meaning.
The meaning of *pārājika* in the *Mahāsāṃghika* tradition is that it constitutes an ultimate evil. It is explained through three aspects: first, falling away;
because one has violated this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path. Second, not living in communion;
it is not merely that one loses the Path, but one also may no longer dwell together with the Saṃgha. Third, falling; after casting off this body, one falls into the hells (*niraya*). As...
When a person’s head is severed, they cannot rise again.
The *Śāriputra-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "This offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there is a remnant within the Saṃgha.
Because one confesses before the assembly of monks, it is extinguished. This is called a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* says: "As [for example]..."
When a person is maimed by another, it is called "maimed" (*saṃghādisesa*) when they still possess a throat.
If they obtain a skilled physician and excellent medicine, they may recover; if not, they cannot recover. It is the same for one who commits an offense involving the *saṃghādisesa*.

There is a principle by which this may be slightly repented. If one obtains a pure assembly that can preach the method for repentance and the removal of offenses according to the Dharma, then these offenses may be eliminated. If there is no pure assembly, they cannot be extinguished.

*Thūlaccaya* is translated as "great obstacle" (*mahā-āvaraṇa*). It is also translated as "great offense" (*mahā-āpatti*), and is further called "coarse and evil" (*audārika-pāpaka*). This [category] is of two kinds:

first, those arising from [other offenses], which refers to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the first two categories of offenses; these are also termed "causal *thūlaccaya*" (*hetu-thūlaccaya*). Second, those that are independent (*mukhya*).
This refers to the derivative offenses (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) of the first two categories, which are also called *phala-dukkaṭa* (resultant offenses) and *svabhāva-dukkaṭa* (intrinsic offenses).

Each of these two types of offenses is further divided into three grades. Regarding the three grades of causal offenses (*hetu-dukkaṭa*): the preparatory stage (*upakrama*) for a *pārājika* offense is termed the "superior grade.

This includes, for example, desiring to engage in sexual intercourse and making physical contact with a female body, or desiring to steal an object of value and selecting it before it has been removed from its place, and so forth.

Among all the Sangha, one should confess and eliminate the offense. The *pārājika* [offenses], as well as the preparatory acts (*upakkama*) for them and the proximate preparatory acts (*āsannūpakkama*) for the *saṃghādisesa*, are termed "middling.

For example, if one intends to engage in sexual intercourse and grasps the body of a clothed woman, or intends to fondle her to cause the emission of semen, but stops before it occurs, and so forth—one should confess and eliminate the offense before four bhikkhus outside the boundary (*sīmā*). This applies to the preparatory acts for the *saṃghādisesa*.
This is designated as the lower grade (*mṛdu*). It is like grasping the genitals with the hand but not yet manipulating them, or desiring to touch a woman’s body but not yet reaching it;

such [offenses] should be confessed and removed before a single bhikṣu. Regarding the three types of *phala* (fruits): for example, being a leader who destroys the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), stealing four *kārsāpaṇa*, killing a deity, and so forth.

These are termed "superior" offenses. If one causes a schism in the *saṃgha* through formal procedure (*karmabheda*), acts as an associate in causing a schism in the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-bheda*), or steals two or three coins and the like, these are termed "middling" offenses.
If one shaves the hair, goes naked, keeps human skins, stone alms bowls, raw flesh or blood, or wears the robes of non-Buddhists;

Stealing one *māṣaka* or more is termed an "inferior" offense; the method for repentance follows that of a *sthūlātyaya*. This category of *sthūlātyaya* encompasses both primary and derivative offenses, and its nature includes both light and heavy degrees.
Among the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*) and six groups (*ṣaṭ-nikāya*) of offenses, the *sthūlātyaya* is included in all of them, occurring either in the higher or lower grades.

There is a reason for this distinction. Among the Vinaya rules, those that follow the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (monastic offenses) are so called because they are categorized as "heavy" (*guru*) due to being included within the division of precepts.
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: *naiḥsargika* means "to be relinquished" (*śe*), and *pāyattika* means "falling" (*duo*). That is to say:
This is because one falls into the hell of burning, boiling, and obscuration. There are one hundred and twenty matters in total;
among them, thirty arise from matters concerning wealth. Because one has committed offenses out of greed and arrogance and must forcibly relinquish the items to the Saṃgha, it is said:
"These objects should be surrendered to the Saṃgha," and a *pāyattika* offense should be confessed. As for the remaining ninety matters, they are termed *nissaggiya*.
There is no dharma of relinquishment; there is only the confession of transgression. If one considers the nature of the offense itself, it is a single grade of repentance;
therefore, within the *pien-chu* (the categories of offenses), they are all combined into one.
The meaning of *pāṭidesanīya* is translated as "confessing to another. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:

"This means that when bhikṣus are currently residing in the same dwelling place, one must individually confess before each of them. Because this differs from other offenses, it receives its distinct name."
Furthermore, once a transgression has been committed, it must be confessed immediately without delay; this differs from other offenses.

Regarding *duṣkṛta* (translated here as "evil action"), all the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, the methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), the rules of decorum according to the Vinaya, as well as the remote preliminary stages (*pūrvaprayoga*) of the first two categories and all the preliminary stages of the third and fourth categories, all fall under this category.
This category is called *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline) in the Mahāsāṃghika school, while in the Mūlasarvāstivāda it is called *dharmātikrama* (transgression of the dharma).

This category is further divided into two sub-categories: first, *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and second, *durbhāṣita* (wrong speech). The old [Chinese] interpretation holds that bodily offenses are termed *duṣkṛta* and verbal offenses are termed *durbhāṣita*;

however, this is likely not necessarily the case. For while the preceding five categories collectively govern the seven branches of conduct (*sapta-varga*), these two names here are instead distinguished separately.
Regarding body and speech: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are *duṣkṛta* offenses requiring formal confession (*pratideśanīya*) and those requiring mental reprimand (*cittotpāda*).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* mentions *vinayātikrama* offenses and *vinayātikramasamutthita-citta-āpatti*. This refers to the fact that for serious offenses, one must confess before another person to purify the transgression;
this is termed *duṣkṛta*. For minor offenses, one need only mentally reflect and verbally express self-reproach; this is termed [mental reprimand].

*Karma* is here translated as "performing the ritual" (*zuofa*). It is also rendered as "action," "that which is done," "the matter," or "the performance of the matter.

There are three types in total. The first is the *jñapti-karman* (single-announcement *karma*), which refers to such acts as appointing someone to instruct others in private, or for the recitation of the precepts and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

The second is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), such as the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and the receiving of a day’s grace (*divasa*).

The third is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), such as the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the granting of training rules (*śikṣā-prada*).
There are three types of *karmavācanā*, totaling one hundred and one items; thus they are called the "one hundred and one *karmas*.
However, as the various schools differ in how they categorize and combine these, they simply subsume them according to their respective categories, which involves no contradiction or obstruction.
Postscript to the *Viniya-Zhenjing Lu*:

During the intervals between my late teacher’s lectures on the *Vinaya*, he personally compiled various articles from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and arranged them into an upper and lower volume, titled the *Viniya-Zhenjing Lu*.
This title was taken from what is stated in the World-Honored One’s bequeathed teachings. Alas! Such was the intention of our teacher.
Profound indeed! The ten grave precepts and forty-eight rules of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas were established all at once;

the two hundred and fifty rules of the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas were formulated gradually according to circumstances. The Tathāgata repeated his exhortations three times, yet the wording was voluminous and could not be abridged.

These were compiled into five sections and four divisions, resulting in a vast number of scrolls. For those of dull faculties in this degenerate age, it is not easy to peruse them. The Master, therefore, adapted to the needs of the times.
Because of this skillful means, I have recorded its items and outlines; they are clear, concise, and easy to follow, so as to accord with the capacities of beings.
Alas! The Master’s intent is profound. Monks of the Dharma-ending age rarely uphold the precepts; for generations, they have followed the ways of birds, mice, lions, and insects.

As for the parable of the swan and the pearl tied to a blade of grass, such a thing has never been heard of. Looking at the present through the lens of antiquity, one truly cannot help but shed tears. It is precisely because I wish to rely on this [text] to exhort [the practitioners]...
He diligently upheld the Vinaya and instructed his disciples so that they might perfect their fivefold Dharma-body. Alas!

This record was only recently completed when the Master passed away. It has long remained in a chest, unable to be carved into woodblocks for publication, because offerings had not yet gathered and there had been no leisure for collation and editing.
Recently, my elder brother Xin-yi and Master Xu Suhua have slightly revised and edited it, and are now soliciting contributions.
This carving [of the text] can truly serve as an eye for recent times and a wise counsel for ten thousand ages.

In this endeavor, our late Master was not only a meritorious contributor to the Deer Park (Rakuen), but Brother Shin was a filial son of the Lotus Abode (Renju), and Master Nikkō was a respected friend of our own.
I am ashamed that I have never studied the Vinaya and am unskilled in composition; nevertheless, [I have undertaken this].
Knowing the Master’s intention in compiling this collection, I could not help but be moved by it. Thus, I have excerpted its beginning and end as follows, together with a record of the date.
It was the year of Kǒu-yǒu (the tenth year of the Chóngzhēn era).
